comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 The earlier answer was too categorical. I found **no explicit per-cluster request or active-connection cap in the checked-in Iris proxy or ingress configuration**, and the parent does not send a cluster's traffic through one relay stream. There is still shared capacity: each CoreWeave cluster has [one controller pod](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/controller.py#L249), each relayed request gets a [target decision from the public parent's private Python listener](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/rust/src/lib.rs#L540), and the requests traverse the child's Traefik ingress. Any of those stages can saturate without an explicit limit. We have not established a threshold at 900 trials; the child proxy's measured mean in-flight request count was 339–374 in the cited later windows, and trials are not simultaneous HTTP requests.

I also need to correct my earlier connection-pool claim. [PR #9480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9480), merged September 27, changed the Rust upstream client to retain up to **256 idle connections per host for 90 seconds**. That is an idle-reuse ceiling, not a cap on active connections. I have not verified which controller image was deployed during the incident. The checked-in Traefik route has an IP allowlist, with no request-limit middleware configured; the live Traefik settings remain unverified because the earlier Kubernetes read was denied.

The existing [Finelog comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10318#issuecomment-6283946880) shows added time between the parent and child proxies for the POST workload, but its counters cannot distinguish the parent's decision, connection setup, and the child's ingress. So adding timings is useful, but it is not the only action: check the deployed image and live Traefik/controller resources, then run the same GET/POST mix at roughly 450 and 900 trials while timing the public route and the parent-to-child route separately. Change whichever stage shows the added wait, then verify the latency and error rate under the same load. Until an authenticated alternative is validated, off-cluster Daytona agents should use the capability URL; in-cluster clients can use their registered endpoint address. I corrected the [incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/795) to remove the stale zero-idle-connection claim.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## Goal

Run a weight-merging loop on spare Marin compute: merge Snowball checkpoints on CPU (reserved v4 hosts in us-central2-b), screen the merges cheaply with TPU vLLM on preemptible single-host slices, and promote winners to the H100 policy evaluation. This issue tracks the project end to end.

## Pins

- Marin base `24ce375f06`
- vLLM fork `fb02daf1d7139d2adaeb0588448649591657d1e3`, tpu-inference `ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d` (head of marin-community/tpu-inference#27, stacked on #29 and #28), applied job-locally
- Evalchemy `3bb8278`, MATH500 full set, harness seed 19311
- S = `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02` @ `50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e`

## Status

| Step | State |
|---|---|
| Inventory, feasibility, campaign matrix | done 2026-10-15 |
| Parents S, C, A5, M staged and sha256-verified in `gs://marin-us-central2/scratch/karan/rsi-merge/parents/` | done 2026-10-16 |
| Merge toolkit: allowlisted BF16 to F32 widening for M's router biases (branch `task/197`) | done, no PR yet |
| TPU scoring smoke test | done: TPU scores 6-7 points below H100 |
| Matched H100 control | done 2026-10-17: 0.944 |
| Quantized serving on v5e | blocked: the pinned fork rejects every quant config for GrugMoE |
| Localize the TPU gap | in progress (#10250) |
| Iteration-one merges (3 recipes) | not started, waiting on the scoring path |

## MATH500 scores for S, same model revision, same Evalchemy pin, same effective sampling

| Server | Score |
|---|---|
| H100 policy config, 2026-10-03 record | 0.950 |
| H100 policy config, 2026-10-17 | 0.944 |
| TPU v6e-8 TP8 bf16 (two runs) | 0.878, 0.882 |
| TPU v5p-8 TP4 bf16 | 0.884 |

Per item: 421 right everywhere, 39 right on both H100 runs and wrong on TPU, 12 wrong everywhere. The 39 are long solutions; 22 of them drift onto a different problem mid-solution.

## The TPU gap (#10250)

Teacher-forced logprobs on the same 10 items match the H100 within noise up to token 2047 and diverge from exactly token 2048, which is S's `sliding_window` (`global_every` 4). The gap grows to about 0.14 nat mean absolute logprob difference by 3-4k tokens.

Ruled out: truncation, thinking mode, sampling (Evalchemy strips temperature and seed, both servers run vLLM defaults), batch dependence, sharding degree and chip generation (v5p-8 TP4 scores the same), cross-request contamination, mask off-by-one (training, FA3 and the TPU kernel all keep the last W tokens including self), KV block eviction (the TPU runner keeps one full-attention cache group), per-layer window plumbing (reaches the TPU kernel unchanged; global layers get no window), KV cache dtype (bf16 on both).

Not valid controls at this pin: `grugmoe_attention_mode=dense` (never read by the vLLM model), a GPU TP8 run (GPU GrugMoE requires TP=1), the experimental batched RPA kernel (fails to compile: its SMEM schedule is sized from a reported capacity above the compiler's 1 MiB limit).

A standalone probe of the pinned ragged-paged-attention v3 kernel against its dense reference with random inputs passes 22 cases around the window boundary (error flat at bf16 noise). Random inputs spread attention over about 2048 keys, so that probe cannot see an edge or sink effect. Running now: a kernel probe with peaky scores, a BOS-like sink key and position-bucket values, and a TPU serving control with the window disabled.

Consequence for the loop: TPU vLLM cannot rank merges until this is fixed. One H100x8 MATH500 run costs about 14 minutes of box time per candidate.

## Related

- #10250 TPU sliding-window divergence
- #9400 tpu-inference pin bump and hardware checks
- #8323 Snowball TPU serving
- #7555 earlier long-context divergence on TPU
- marin-community/tpu-inference#28 custom router selections, #29 host storage release, #27 TP8 head padding (the stack every TPU run here used)
- Two Evalchemy integration gotchas found on the way: the pinned Evalchemy strips `temperature` and `seed` from requests, so the server's defaults apply; and marin's FineStore result reader expects native results JSON while Evalchemy `3bb8278` writes parquet tables, so the parent eval job reports FAILED although the child succeeded and the score is in `data/evalchemy_results/`.

## Open decisions

1. Score iteration-one merges on H100 now, or wait for the TPU fix.
2. Open a PR for the merge-toolkit change on `task/197`.
3. File the Iris autoscaler tier-blocking issue (a v6e-4 group in backoff blocks v6e-8 demand in the same zone).

The pinned Evalchemy writes parquet tables while Marin's result reader looks only for `results_*.json`, so a successful child can leave the parent failed. comments.body:
## Localization update: the TPU/H100 gap is the sliding window, and the TPU side matches training

Teacher-forced logprobs on the same 10 MATH500 prompts (Snowball S, `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02@50fe2f48`), now in five configurations: H100 and TPU v6e-8 each with the model's 2048 sliding window and each with the window disabled (`--hf-overrides '{"sliding_window": 262144}'`), plus an H100 repeat for run-to-run noise. Mean |Δ logprob| per position bin:

| positions | H100 vs TPU, window off on both | H100 vs TPU, window on | H100: window on vs off | TPU: window on vs off | H100 repeat noise |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0–2047 | 0.014–0.016 | 0.015–0.017 | 0.013–0.015 | 0.000 | 0.013–0.015 |
| 2048–2111 | 0.012 | 0.026 | 0.013 | 0.025 | 0.012 |
| 2112–2303 | 0.012–0.014 | 0.037–0.039 | 0.018–0.024 | 0.038–0.041 | 0.011–0.014 |
| 2304–2431 | 0.011–0.017 | 0.040–0.066 | 0.037–0.084 | 0.058–0.114 | 0.010–0.014 |
| 2432–3071 | 0.014–0.015 | 0.066–0.079 | 0.124–0.186 | 0.143–0.211 | 0.012–0.015 |
| 3072–4095 | 0.021 | 0.142 | 0.703 | 0.700 | 0.013 |
| 4096–8000 | 0.033 | 0.133 | 1.123 | 1.096 | 0.010 |

1. With the window off on both platforms, H100 and TPU agree at every position to within 0.03 nats. The whole divergence is in how the 2048 window is applied.
2. On TPU (tpu-inference `ae387b8`, ragged paged attention v3) the window takes effect at token 2049 on every long item. Three standalone kernel probes (random, peaky/sink, and serving's per-shard head geometry and request classes) put exactly zero attention mass outside the window. This matches levanter's training mask (`splash_attention_mask.LocalMask(window_size=(W-1, None))` AND causal, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/splash_attention.py`).
3. On H100 (vLLM fork `01911be`, FlashAttention 3) the window's effect stays at noise until about token 2150, is about half the TPU's around token 2340, and equals the TPU's from about 2460 on. Past 3072 the two effects are the same size, so every local layer is windowed on both platforms; the H100 differs only in the first few hundred tokens past the boundary, i.e. it keeps seeing some early tokens that the exact window drops.
4. Ruled out on the TPU side: the kernel, the batched kernel (does not compile at this pin), KV block eviction (one cache group on TPU), KV dtype, per-layer window plumbing, RoPE, prefill chunk size (knee stays at 2048 with 1536-token chunks).

Open: which code path in the FA3 backend produces the loose boundary (an FA2 run is in flight), and why the looser window scores higher on MATH500 (0.944 H100 vs 0.878–0.884 TPU). Data: `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/karan/task236/teacher-{h100x8,h100x8-nowindow,h100x8-fa3repeat,v6e8,nowindow-v6e8,chunk1536-v6e8}/`.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
## TPU serving defect localized: global attention layers get the sliding window

Follow-up to the seven-way comparison above. The TPU-side defect is now named and fixed by a config override; the proper fix is in tpu-inference.

**What happens.** tpu-inference registers a vLLM general plugin (`tpu_inference/layers/vllm/__init__.py`, `register_layers` -> `_register_grugmoe`). Whenever the TPU stack is present it sets `_CONFIG_REGISTRY["grug_moe"] = GrugMoeHfConfig`, replacing the vLLM fork's `GrugMoeConfig`. `GrugMoeHfConfig` (`tpu_inference/models/jax/grugmoe.py`) is a plain `PretrainedConfig` with name aliases; it never sets `layer_types`. The fork's `GrugMoeConfig` sets `layer_types` from `grug_moe_layer_types(num_layers, global_every)`. Plugins load in `EngineArgs.__post_init__`, before the model config is built, so on TPU `hf_text_config.layer_types` is `None`. vLLM then sets `cache_config.sliding_window = 2048` (arg_utils: "only set CacheConfig.sliding_window if the model is all sliding window"), and the fork's GrugMoE model, which passes `per_layer_sliding_window=None` for its 7 global layers (3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 25 of 26), gets 2048 for them through the `Attention.__init__` fallback. A static trace of the TPU engine shows all 26 layers at `sliding_window=2048`. On H100 the plugin is absent, the fork config is used, and the engine builds 4 KV cache groups with the global layers unwindowed. The fork model derives its own layer pattern from `global_every`, so nothing crashes; the window is just applied to the wrong layers.

**Verification.** Passing `--hf-overrides '{"layer_types": [...]}'` (the fork's list: `full_attention` at 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 25, `sliding_attention` elsewhere) changes the trace to 7 layers at `None` and 19 at 2048, with 4 KV cache groups. Teacher-forced probe (same 10 MATH500 items, 35,801 positions) against the exact-window eager reference, mean |delta logprob|:

| positions | TPU, override | TPU, default | H100 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0-2048 | 0.015-0.018 | 0.015-0.018 | 0.014-0.016 |
| 2048-2304 | 0.013-0.016 | 0.023-0.038 | 0.012-0.014 |
| 2304-3072 | 0.015-0.017 | 0.054-0.080 | 0.014-0.016 |
| 3072+ | 0.012-0.015 | 0.132-0.142 | 0.011-0.014 |

TPU with the override vs H100 directly: 0.011-0.017 at every position. MATH500 with the override (Evalchemy 3bb8278, seed 19311, same settings as the TPU runs above): **0.940** (470/500, 500 generated and scored, 1421 s), against 0.878-0.884 for TPU without it and 0.944 / 0.950 for the two H100 runs. The gap is closed.

**Fix.** Proper fix is in tpu-inference: `GrugMoeHfConfig` should set `layer_types` the same way the fork does, or the plugin should not replace a registry entry the fork already provides. tpu-inference `main` at 340444337772 (2026-10-19) still has the overwrite. Until then, TPU serving of any GrugMoE checkpoint whose `config.json` lacks `layer_types` needs the override above. Pins: vLLM fork fb02daf, tpu-inference ae387b8, Step12 @50fe2f488aee.

issues.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
issues.body:
The October 20 Tier 2 Datakit canary exhausted its 14,400-second Actions wait while Iris still reported the ferry as running. Normalization made no progress: its Zephyr worker job had 98/98 tasks pending, with the scheduler reporting `Insufficient memory (need 32.0GB, available 20.7G...)`. This is an infra/scheduling failure.

Reproduce:
1. Run the scheduled [Tier 2 ferry workflow](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/39423437260).
2. At the wait deadline, inspect the uploaded `datakit-tier2-diagnostics/job-tree.txt` and the normalization worker job under the Iris job ID below.

Expected: normalization workers are placed and the ferry finishes within the wait budget, or Iris reports the resource shortage early enough for the canary to fail with that cause.

Evidence: The worker job was submitted at 12:49 UTC and remained pending at the 16:36 UTC timeout. `iris job describe` showed 0/98 workers completed and 98 pending; a worker requested 2 CPUs, 34.36 GB memory, and 10.74 GB disk. The tier-2 ferry calls `normalize_step` without `worker_resources`, so `normalize_to_parquet` requests `ram="32g"`. Finelog `zephyr.stage` had no completed stage for normalization execution `20261020-124354-cbb30502`; the concurrent bloom stage completed at 12:54 UTC. The uploaded diagnostics report contains the same pending job and no collection errors.

The canary ran in lane `datakit-tier2` on 2026-10-20 UTC under Iris job `/runner/iris-run-job-20261020-123608`. Its [Actions run and diagnostics artifact](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/39423437260) and [W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/datakit-tier2-ferry-39423437260-1) provide the run context.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Smartie revisited multi-domain reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) on Snowball, a 67B-total / approximately 2B-active-parameter model. Run `2026.10.15.32` produced the checkpoint released as [Marin Snowball 67B-A2B v0.1](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-67B-A2B-v0.1). At its released update 14, recorded native validation pass@1 rose from **41.21% to 50.22%**. NVIDIA task mean reward rose from **40.59% to 55.50%**, while structural-task mean reward fell from **39.09% to 32.92%**. The experiment shows useful task learning and recorded structural regression. It does not establish successful balanced joint optimization.

The intended mixture combined four domains from [NVIDIA Nemotron-RL-Ultra-Training-Blends](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Ultra-Training-Blends): calendar reasoning, competitive coding, Reasoning Gym puzzles, and STEM multiple-choice questions. These are called the NVIDIA cohort below. Synthetic structural-compliance tasks formed the other cohort. The launch configuration left shuffling disabled: domain-grouped NVIDIA rows preceded the structural rows. The training-reward spike near update 16 therefore cannot be interpreted as a sudden general capability gain. The fixed-validation curves are the evidence used here.

## Setup

The run started from [Grug Merge Campaign2 DARE-TIES-02](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign2-DARE-TIES-02-2026.10.10/tree/153f5369f69a0c0a7203779099ec94e98c66748f), with a fresh optimizer. It did **not** start from the separately released Marin Snowball v0, which is a Campaign3 merge. [The model provenance report](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14#provenance-report) records the initializer's merge parents.

Training used asynchronous RLOO-N, a leave-one-out policy-gradient estimator with neutral treatment of masked infrastructure failures, and truncated importance sampling. The learning rate was `4e-6`, with 512 accepted prompt groups and 16 responses per group per update. The run used 64 H100 policy GPUs and 48 separate inference GPUs. There was no KL, entropy, or auxiliary FTPO loss; structural tasks used the same verifiable-reward objective as other tasks. Loss reduction was token-mean. The [exact submitted launch config, resolved config, and source patch](https://gist.github.com/penfever/40f0f81dd4fba022697e4fa5aeabb91d/b79646603c23bd466969ff498661a0e313b1024a) are public.

The N means neutral: a masked infrastructure-failure sample gets zero advantage and is excluded from other samples' leave-one-out baselines. Model failures can remain zero-reward samples in the baseline. A group contains responses to the same prompt; 512 accepted groups is the optimizer-batch target, not 512 arbitrary completed responses. The configuration requires at least four baseline-eligible responses per group; fully masked, stale, undersized, or contract-invalid groups cannot contribute normally, and constant-reward groups provide no relative learning signal. Exact accepted groups and valid loss-token shares per domain were not reconstructed. File row proportions must not be treated as optimizer exposure.

The [exact public data release](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-Data/tree/cb728a7636caad3fc6fa6b6ba85a49194d9d69a3) contains 69,487 training tasks and 910 native validation tasks. Training rows comprise 741 calendar, 7,553 competitive-coding, 1,918 Reasoning Gym, 1,911 STEM, and 57,364 structural tasks. These are task inputs for online generation, not a static collection of model answers. Structural families cover JSON objects, arrays, nesting and string escapes, code fences, reasoning delimiters, tool-call delimiters, and repeated-opener retention. A continuation task can ask the model to finish a supplied JSON prefix without adding fields or changing reference content. Valid syntax alone does not pass that content-preservation check.

## Results and limits

| Fixed native validation measure | Initializer, update 0 | Released update 14 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Combined recorded pass@1, 910 tasks (%) | 41.21 | 50.22 |
| NVIDIA mean outcome reward, 667 tasks (%) | 40.59 | 55.50 |
| Structural mean outcome reward, 243 tasks (%) | 39.09 | 32.92 |

Grading coverage was 654/667 NVIDIA tasks and 235/243 structural tasks at initialization, versus 667/667 and 226/243 at update 14. Structural mean among graded tasks also fell, from 40.43% to 35.40%, so missing grades do not fully explain the recorded structural regression.

Each validation task has one sampled response. Mean outcome reward averages per-task rewards in `[0,1]`; missing grades remain zero outcomes in the fixed denominator. The combined native metric is task-count weighted, not an equal average of source means. The runtime's recorded pass@1 uses an explicit pass verdict when available and otherwise positive reward; partial-credit tasks can count as passing. Reasoning Gym exhibits this distinction: its initial mean reward is 76.48%, while recorded pass@1 is 82.04%. Mean outcome reward and pass@1 are therefore different measures. These repeatedly inspected development results are not an independent final test or a statistical-significance claim.

Update 12 had the highest recorded native pass@1, **50.33%**, but its weights had already been removed by checkpoint retention. Update 14 was the best surviving checkpoint, at **50.22%**, and was exported with that limitation recorded. The [complete public W&B metric archive](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-Artifacts/tree/20a22f8a7bdcbca7edf38279b7c24d22826693a3/wandb-full-20261019) covers 22 returned history rows: the pre-training row 0 and recorded optimizer steps 1–21, with native validation through step 20. This does not establish whether an additional unlogged update occurred before cancellation.

The separate in-line BFCL-Parity, SWE-bench Verified, and OpenThoughts-TBLite panel suffered execution failures. Its incomplete results were not used as valid zero-accuracy benchmark measurements. A later independent release-policy evaluation and baseline comparison is published in [#10283](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10283); it is separate from the native validation curves in this report.

Later campaign runs tested shuffled mixtures, Harbor-native Mini-SWE-Agent execution, task-source repairs, and staged SWE-Smith repository setup. They do not contribute weights to the Step14 release. The active `.57` job is deliberately left running; its later results will be reported separately. This issue closes the historical publication record, not that live job.

## Reproducibility and conclusion

The release includes public weights, exact Step14 training/native-validation Parquets, launch configs, frozen metric history, figure inputs, and source revisions in the [campaign artifact archive](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026/tree/9f01d8146fc48d7c5eb9c95d08d46d86b81c0f66). The archive's [reproduction guide](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026/blob/9f01d8146fc48d7c5eb9c95d08d46d86b81c0f66/REPRODUCING.md) collects the historical revisions, submitted patch/config, input mapping, and original launch command. Code is recorded in [Marin #10190](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10190), [MarinSkyRL #1030](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/1030), and [Harbor #277](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/277). These are code-publication links, not claims that the PRs have merged. Historical reproduction uses the submitted source pins. Marin's latest-main RolloutEngine API integration remains pending in its draft PR; the two runtime fork worktrees were refreshed against main.

Existing private repositories remain private. Raw conversations, restricted TaskForge inputs, uncleared third-party task assets, secrets, and transient environments are excluded from this public artifact upload. Those exclusions limit independent reconstruction of later restricted-data runs and trace-level failure analyses. The original Megatron optimizer checkpoint and a complete raw rollout history are not included, so bitwise training or export reproduction is not claimed.

The main next experiment is shuffled joint exposure with measured per-domain optimizer admission and valid-token contribution. A separate comparison can test sequence-mean loss to reduce response-length weighting. Structural retention needs an explicit checkpoint-selection constraint. Agentic benchmark claims require complete, graded benchmark cohorts; a training-reward increase alone is insufficient.

🤖

## Historical campaign tracker

This is the campaign TRACKER snapshot, with public artifact links replacing local paths. Iris and W&B links are operational references that may require authentication; Step14 evidence is mirrored publicly. The tracker includes failed and preparatory runs. A dash in a score column means no usable recorded score; in other columns it means missing or not applicable. Inaccessible raw evidence is labeled as unavailable.

The real/structural mean-reward columns use the tracker's graded-only convention and may differ from the fixed-denominator means in the release figure. `Real` denotes the four NVIDIA domains in `.32`, but later runs change the cohort. `Recorded optimizer step` is the run's counter, separate from initializer ancestry; it can reset with a fresh optimizer and continue across a training-state resume. The `.32` value is 21, the last optimizer step in the public metric history, not the 22 returned history rows that include baseline step 0.

BFCL/Pi means the Harbor BFCL-Parity adaptation using the Pi coding-agent harness; SWE is SWE-bench Verified; OT is OpenThoughts-TBLite. Historical benchmark columns use their linked audited scored-trial denominators, which differ by run. A documented early comparison uses 123 BFCL tasks and 498 SWE tasks; the failed `.32` in-line panel instead attempted 30 tasks per benchmark. Compare rows only when their linked paired audit establishes matching tasks, harness and settings. These historical rows are not recertified under a later policy. comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 Update: Smartie `2026.10.19.57` completed 12 recorded optimizer updates and was stopped on October 20 after later agentic validation scores declined. [Update 8 is exported publicly](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.19.57-step8). This is an experimental continuation; it does not replace the earlier Marin Snowball v0.1 release.

The initializer was [Smartie `.32` update 14](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14), with a fresh optimizer. The run used asynchronous RLOO-N, a configured training batch of 512 groups × 16 responses per update, AdamW at `4e-6`, token-mean loss, and no KL or entropy auxiliary loss. [W&B](https://wandb.ai/dogml/snowball-smartie-rl/runs/v1vksnkr).

### Per-domain results and artifacts

The [public artifact bundle](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/e0d611e5e5d10ce2ba7b1f807e3a8a/runs/2026.10.19.57/update-20261020) contains PNG/SVG figures, CSV/JSON plot values, selected numeric W&B metrics, plotting code, the launch configuration, and exact data links.

![Per-domain validation reward](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/e0d611e5e5d10ce2ba7b1f807e3a8a/runs/2026.10.19.57/update-20261020/per-domain-validation-reward.png)

All values below are mean verifier scores among graded attempts, scaled to percent. Scores can include partial credit, so these are not uniformly binary success rates. They differ from fixed-denominator averages in some earlier campaign figures. These are repeatedly inspected development panels with one sampled response per task, not full release-policy evaluations. [Exact graded/attempted counts for every domain and checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026/blob/6662745944e0d611e5e5d10ce2ba7b1f807e3a8a/runs/2026.10.19.57/update-20261020/validation-curves.csv).

| Validation domain | Initializer | Update 8 | Update 12 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| SWE-Smith full issue repair | 27.16 | 34.34 | 9.78 |
| CalibForge | - | - | - |
| NL2Bash | 71.00 | 57.58 | 27.00 |
| Competitive coding | 51.28 | 45.07 | 26.87 |
| Structural compliance | 36.36 | 63.20 | 76.09 |
| TaskForge | 72.88 | 6.26 | 0.88 |
| SWE-bench Verified, Terminus-2 | 3.33 | 33.33 | 6.67 |
| BFCL-Parity, Terminus-2 | 53.33 | 66.67 | 13.33 |
| OT-TBLite, Terminus-2 | 6.90 | 13.33 | 0.00 |

CalibForge has no valid grades: all four tasks fail agent startup at every checkpoint. SWE-Smith grade coverage is 81/100, 99/100, and 92/100 at the three tabulated checkpoints. The decline also holds on the same 64 SWE-Smith tasks graded at all seven evaluations (updates 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12): 28.13% initially, 42.19% at update 8, and 14.06% at update 12. Update 8 was selected for export by the user; it is not uniformly best across domains.

![Validation grading coverage](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/e0d611e5e5d10ce2ba7b1f807e3a8a/runs/2026.10.19.57/update-20261020/validation-coverage.png)

### Training mix and exact data

Training used 3,322 rows: **1,661 SWE-Smith Stage 1 repository-setup tasks and 1,661 structural tasks**, with shuffle enabled. Stage 1 asks the agent to prepare the correct repository, branch, commit, and installation; it does not ask for a bug fix. SWE-Smith validation still tests full issue repair. CalibForge and the other domains above are validation-only in this run.

![Training-source reward](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/e0d611e5e5d10ce2ba7b1f807e3a8a/runs/2026.10.19.57/update-20261020/training-source-reward.png)

- [Exact training Parquet](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/task-trove-smartie-continuation-private/blob/3cd8b45655637b5d1b79ca607d007537706e2981/releases/2026.10.19.1/stage1-structural-mixture/train.parquet).
- [Exact 573-row validation Parquet](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/task-trove-smartie-continuation-private/blob/3cd8b45655637b5d1b79ca607d007537706e2981/releases/2026.10.19.1/stage1-structural-mixture/validation.parquet).
- [Source-owned agent profile and task requirements](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/task-trove-smartie-continuation-private/blob/3cd8b45655637b5d1b79ca607d007537706e2981/releases/2026.10.19.1/stage1-structural-mixture/README.md).
- [Launch config](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/e0d611e5e5d10ce2ba7b1f807e3a8a/runs/2026.10.19.57/update-20261020/training-launch.yaml) and [data hashes/provenance](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/e0d611e5e5d10ce2ba7b1f807e3a8a/runs/2026.10.19.57/update-20261020/data-provenance.json).

The exact data files remain **private and access-controlled**. Validation includes restricted TaskForge payloads, and the complete task bundle has not been cleared for public redistribution. Both Parquet hashes were verified against this pinned HF revision. Exact reproduction requires data access.

Validation used the same declared release, URI, and file as `.56`; the release README also records that rows were copied unchanged from the preceding cohort. The 573 rows comprise 100 SWE-Smith, 100 NL2Bash, four CalibForge, 85 coding, 41 TaskForge, and 243 structural tasks. Three additional panels of 30 tasks each (BFCL, SWE-bench, and OT-TBLite) are configured in the launch file.

### Interpretation and follow-up

Structural scores improved while later issue-repair and tool-use scores declined. Original Harbor traces from 30 SWE-bench and 30 BFCL tasks at each of updates 8 and 12 show increased parser-error fractions (73.99% to 87.62% for SWE-bench; 74.95% to 88.56% for BFCL). These evaluation traces were recovered independently of the training-trace publisher. A confirmed training-path defect clears earlier action tokens after history resets, leaving the final segment to receive whole-task reward. [Marin #10326](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10326) records the evidence and required TITO safeguards.

The defect's contribution to the reward decline has not been isolated experimentally. A separate trace-publisher failure limits late-run training evidence. The next training run needs verified preservation of all action segments and repaired trace retention before testing whether the narrow setup/structural mix itself harms broader behavior. No replacement run was launched as part of this update.

Rebuilding from the archived material has not been tested on a fresh machine, so this is not a self-contained execution release. Keep private tests, gold solutions, and verifier resources outside model access.

CalibForge's environment admission checks cover fixture equivalence and setup/verifier execution, with oracle solution execution explicitly skipped. Its public v2 release includes train/validation splits. The public NL2Bash and full SWE-Smith releases contain task cohorts and review decisions; their campaign-specific splits are in the private archive. Private downloads require access to the Open-Athena repository.

The archive contains historical and rejected candidates as well as admitted data. Use each version's admission manifest rather than treating all archived rows as approved training examples. Raw source mirrors, mounted source volumes, caches, and operational log directories were excluded. The file manifest records SHA-256 hashes and exclusions; no archived dataset is silently relabeled as public or fully runnable.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
Since 2026-10-18 05:49 UTC, every mini-swe-agent trial on Harbor main fails before its first model call, and SWE-bench Verified scores read 0. Marin main pins Harbor `18e71265`, so any SWE eval launched from marin main today is affected. Harbor `38742b0f` on `benfeuer/eval-campaign-09-25-runtime` has the fix, but Harbor main does not.

Harbor installs the agent inside each sandbox with `uv tool install mini-swe-agent==2.1.0` ([`mini_swe_agent.py` L456 on main](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/18e712655917ee1c5f82624809339daff3a26a9e/src/harbor/agents/installed/mini_swe_agent.py#L456)). mini-swe-agent 2.1.0 requires only `litellm>=1.75.5`. litellm 1.106.0, released at 05:49 UTC, raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mcp'` on the first query.

Symptom: the vLLM server logs `/tokenize` requests but no `/v1/chat/completions`. Each trajectory has 2 steps and 0 prompt/completion tokens. The orchestrator log does not show the import error, because the captured agent stdout is cut off before it. The shootout's plain-arm SWE r100 screen read 0/99: 98 trials ended in `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`, 1 in `VerifierRuntimeError`, 1 in `AgentTimeoutError`.

Local repro, against any OpenAI-compatible server set in `HOSTED_VLLM_API_BASE`:

```python
# uv run --no-project --with mini-swe-agent==2.1.0 --with litellm==1.106.0 repro.py
from minisweagent.models.litellm_model import LitellmModel
LitellmModel(model_name="hosted_vllm/m", model_kwargs={"api_key": "EMPTY"}).query(
    [{"role": "system", "content": "s"}, {"role": "user", "content": "u"}]
)
```

It raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mcp'` and sends no request. With `litellm==1.103.5` the request goes through. With Harbor 38742b0f's install (`uv tool install mini-swe-agent==2.1.0 --with mcp==2.3.0`) it also goes through: litellm 1.106.0 + mcp 2.3.0.

Who is affected: every mini-swe-agent eval and SWE-smith generation trial whose sandbox installed after 05:49 UTC on 2026-10-18, on Harbor `016dd78b` (the September campaign pin) or `18e71265` (marin main). Terminus-2 (TBLite, TB2), Evalchemy and BFCL do not install mini-swe-agent and are unaffected. The task204 LR-sweep SWE screens finished before 05:49 UTC and are valid.

Fix options:
1. Recommended: port 38742b0f's install change (`--with mcp==2.3.0` plus the setup-time import check) to Harbor main, then advance marin's Harbor pin. The setup check turns this kind of dependency drift into a setup failure, not a 0 score. Runs on the fix use litellm 1.106.0 instead of the earlier < 1.106 client, so comparisons should rerun their baseline under the same install.
2. Add `--exclude-newer 2026-10-18T05:00:00Z` to the install. This reproduces the pre-incident dependency set exactly, but the date must be bumped by hand later.
3. Pin `litellm<1.106` in the install. This is narrower, but leaves the other mini-swe-agent dependencies unpinned.

The shootout reruns its SWE screens (three arms plus v0) on 38742b0f. Shootout: #10213. Eval policy: #10197.


Incident note: https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/789

issues.author: XenonMolecule
issues.body:
## Description

The current pipelines for transforming web scrape data to training data for LLMs are multi-stage and a somewhat specifically engineered [[1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11794)] [[2](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.840/)].  We hypothesize that LLMs may do a better job at converting raw web data into useful tokens for pre-training or mid-training, especially on more challenging to parse contents like latex, tables, math, etc. [[3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06786)].

Preliminary testing has been positive for getting better quality extraction from LLMs rather than heuristic rules ([writeup here](https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4)) however this is way too expensive to run at the full web scale.  Our 8b LLM curator is predicted to take 42 years even on the generous compute we do have.

That is why we are currently experimenting with more efficient distilled pipelines from our 8b model.  The lifecycle would thus be: **Write spec for curation** -> **Run with LLM on subset of internet** -> **Distill into faster pipeline** -> **Run at webscale**.  We also noticed that a lot of decent data OUTSIDE of math/code/science is getting discarded by current pipelines.  Our new spec ([See below](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/2351#issuecomment-5074349445)) keeps way more data, and we are making the bet that data mixing/data selection will be a better fit than data filtering for deciding how to weight data for training.  This way we preserve web content that may be decent quality but not beneficial to math/code/science benchmark scores.


### Definition of Done

Two main deliverables with more additional artifacts.

1. **A scientific paper on our spec driven curation methodology and philosophy**: Preliminary drafts are [already completed](https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4), but a more polished version for ICLR is in progress.
2. **A 30T+ token dataset of more diverse common crawl data (extracted better)**: Using our distilled pipeline and new design philosophy (optimize data for coverage NOT "quality") we plan to re-run extraction on common crawl and build a production ready data pool for marin with removal of copywritten content.  With any additional time we will also incorporate [safety pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16980) practices into the dataset.

comments.body:
# Progress this week (1/26-1/30) My progress on this task this week spans quite a few categories. For easy reading I am writing each up in collapsible sections. My primary focus was on benchmarking LLMs for web content extraction. To this end I achieved these main goals: 1. Identify Axis of Evaluation (Content Preservation, Spec Adherence, Quality Filtering Calibration, Diversity) 2. Curate benchmarks for these axis 3. Iteratively improve existing LLMs on these axes (primarily through prompting) I am defining these axes as such: - **Content Preservation**: Does the LLM extractor include all main content or omit important details? - **Spec Adherence**: Given a controllable text spec does the LLM adhere to requirements in the spec - **Quality Filtering Calibration**: Two measures - when we say to filter to top X% of documents, what percent actually remain, AND what is the accuracy (are they actually the top X% of docs) - **Diversity**: When we sample from an LLM extractor at a certain temperature with the same doc and spec how different are the actual outputs (might be a useful signal if LLM extractors help with implicit deduplication) I also identify a few challenges and how I have addressed them or how I plan to address them. ---
Article Extraction with Spec The first quick thing to discuss is an update from last week. With the article extraction benchmark (see above) we hypothesized that with a bit more guidance from the benchmark specs that LLMs would do even better on the benchmark. I found these specs for the benchmark from the tech report: ``` For a fair evaluation, we need to define what should be included into the article body (main content), and make sure that all systems follow the same goals. Underlying principle is that the article body should be “clean text”, without other fields (like author), navigation elements, ads, etc. At the same time we want to include all sub-headings, block-quotes and other elements which constitute article content. Here is a list of items not included into an article: • other fields such as authors, publication date, keywords, image captions, etc., and markup around them • share buttons and suggestions to share an article • comments and UI related to comments (e.g. “Comments” header, forms, links to comments) • “related” articles, "read next" links, "recommended to you", etc.: any links which are not part of the article and whose goal is to keep the reader on the platform • newsletter signup links, generic calls to action, various forms • advertisements • author information, usually at the end of the article (such as "X X is an X reporter ..."), as this is not directly related to an article • control elements around images which produce unneeded text (e.g. number of images in a gallery, buttons overlaid over an image/video, etc.) • blocks denoting reading time of the article • other items unrelated to the article content Here is a list of items that should be included into an article (except for the article body proper): • links to read in more detail, to the source, or to other content directly related to this article: these might require deeper understanding of the article content to annotate correctly • embedded posts related to the article, such as tweets/instagram/facebook posts • copyright notices at the end ``` I added them to the prompt for the extractor to make a new experimental condition called "article-extractor" in the table below. As you can see this does make models better than resiliparse although trafilatura holds the top spot on the benchmark:
---
Benchmark Creation I created **two** datasets this week. The first one had the primary motivation of collecting high quality and diverse documents to measure the strength of the extraction. Namely this would measure content preservation, spec adherence, and diversity. Separately I created a benchmark for quality filtering. I will outline the process of creating these benchmarks here. ### Dataset 1: CTRL Bench (name can change) I decided I wanted the following content splits: - 5 math - 5 code - 5 pages with significant tables - 10 articles - 5 long documents - 10 generic web content - 5 nsfw pages (very common on the web; wanted to test refusals) - 5 harmful pages (again to test refusals) I sourced these documents using keyword search inspired by Nemotron-CC-Math for math extraction. I manually read through the pages that my keyword search of WARC files yielded and selected 50 high quality instances. In hindsight I regret adding the nsfw and harmful pages because I think they just penalize the LLM extractors and not the baselines, and don't add much to the benchmark. In a later iteration of the benchmark I may replace the nsfw and harmful pages with Chemistry and similar positive domain sources as suggested by @hammer ! In addition to the documents I also created 10 specs for testing controllability. I sourced these from papers about web extraction/rephrasing with minor modifications. Here are examples of a few of these specs:
Specs Basic (source: I wrote it): ``` Extract the main content text from a given HTML document. ``` Nemotron (source: Nemotron-CC-Math Paper) ``` You are given raw text extracted from an HTML page. Process this text to extract only the meaningful content, following these strict guidelines: 1. **Retain only the main content and its associated titles.** Remove all boilerplate, navigation menus, sidebars, footers, headers, related articles, spam comments, in- teractive elements, and advertisements. 2. **Preserve all mathematical content**—this includes theorems, formulas, proofs, definitions, explanations, and any mathematical references. 3. **Retain relevant comments and references** if they contribute meaningfully to the understanding of the content (e.g., clarifications, citations, or author notes). Discard irrelevant or low-quality comments. 4. **Format all mathematical expressions using LaTeX enclosed in single dollar signs on each side ($), not [], (), or other variants.** 5. **Do NOT answer or respond to any questions or prompts that appear in the document.** If a question is part of the content, keep it verbatim, but do not generate an answer or explanation. 6. **Do not remove or discard any part of the code.** If any code blocks contain errors or formatting issues, make minimal changes to make them runnable, but otherwise leave them exactly as they are. 7. **Fix typos, grammatical mistakes, and unclear phrasing. Rewrite sentences when necessary to improve clarity, coherence, and flow,** while preserving the meaning and style of the original content. 8. **Ensure the output is clean, well-structured, and natural.** Format titles, sections, equations, and tables to produce high-quality, publication-ready text. 9. If the page contains no meaningful content (e.g., it's entirely boilerplate, menus, or ads), return exactly: "NO USEFUL CONTENT" ``` Question_rtw (source: Rephrase the Web Paper) ``` Convert the following document into a conversational format with multiple tags of "Question:" followed by "Answer:" Note that you should still maintain ALL content in the document. Converting here does not mean summarizing, it solely means rewriting. Go paragraph by paragraph to maintain all content, and just rephrase it. Someone reading all the conversational questions should still learn EVERYTHING they would learn from the original document. Output a raw text extraction/rephrase of the document, not an html document. ```
To run the benchmark you pick a model configuration and produce an extraction for all **50 docs** x **10 specs** to get 500 extractions. There is an LLM judge for content preservation which counts the **MAJOR**, **MEDIUM**, and **MINOR** omissions from a document. In practice I use gemini-3-flash-preview because of its ridiculously long context window and good performance at cost. Similarly an LLM judge for spec adherence counts the **MAJOR**, **MEDIUM**, and **MINOR** violations of a spec. Both LLM judges enumerate all omissions and violations with explanations. Qualitatively the judges seem quite good. ### Dataset 2: Quality Bench For Dataset 2 I took a completely random sample of 100 html files from a WARC from Common Crawl. Then I ran the quality filtering fastext model from the DCLM pipeline to get a baseline quality score for each doc (scalar). I sorted the docs on this score and used it as a prior to seed an ELO ranking system where I was presented with two docs and selected which was higher quality. I did 251 votes until I realized this was impractical at this scale (need 2000 to 3000 votes to stabilize), so using the new rankings that my pairwise comparisons yielded as a starting point I made a list of the 100 sites that I could drag and drop to reorder based on quality. I used this to produce a ground truth ordering of the 100 sites. See examples of the tiers of webpages below:
Web pages in the Quality Benchmark #### Number 1 (Best): **Interview with a USAA financial expert on how to boost your credit score (very informative and interview style)** #### Number 2: **Interview with a religious author about his new book** #### Number 5: **Article on 2008 Financial crisis**: #### Number 10: **Summary of New Orleans council meeting**: #### Number 25: **License Agreement**: #### Number 40: **Brief Biographical details about Composer Caleb Simper** #### Number 60: **Article Preview about Easter Travel** #### Number 80: **Photo Gallery with a non-descriptive caption**
After obtaining ground truth ratings for the 100 documents I made the following template to add to the end of the spec prompt for any LLM extractor runs on the benchmark: ``` Additionally I am trying to filter low quality documents out of my corpus. I want to train on only the top {PERCENT}% of quality documents. This is not a percentile, that is the ratio of documents I want to RETAIN out of all documents. If you believe this document does not meet the quality threshold, then rather than extracting the content please respond with the exact phrase "NO USEFUL CONTENT" as the extraction. ``` For now I just ran with the BASIC SPEC ("Extract the main content text from a given HTML document.") but theoretically this is compatible to mix and match with other specs.
---
Content Preservation GPT-OSS-120B is quite good at content preservation without explicitly asking to emit reasoning (predict better than cot): We see that technically Resiliparse > GPT-OSS-120B > GPT-OSS-20B > trafilatura > Llama 3.2 3B **HOWEVER** Note the high refusal rate (empty extractions). These come from NSFW and Harmful docs that the LLMs refuse but not the parsers. Also adding a preprocessing step to remove script tags seems to be useful (See more in the long context section later)
---
Spec Adherence GPT-OSS-120B is again quite good here: Some specs are harder than others (for instance the rephrase the web ones which lead to lower content preservation and lower spec adherence. Rephrasing is probably a mix of harder to do and harder to judge than extraction. GPT-OSS-120B is clear winner (See SA column)
---
Quality Filtering With the Quality Filtering it is important to note that there are two measures: **Calibration** and **Accuracy**. **Calibration**: When we request the top X% of docs do we actually get only X% of docs? Measured with MSE of acceptance rate. **Accuracy**: Of the top X% of docs requested what is the **recall** of those docs actually being in the top X% We compare against a highly calibrated baseline: DCLM's quality filter fastext model where we run once to get all the scalar scores and then cutoff at each threshold. This is perfectly calibrated so the baseline is just for recall comparison. This plot is a bit messy so we will dive into specifics in a second, but the main takeaway is that the LLM extractors are not super calibrated even with fewshot examples, although they do have high recall (but this might be unfair since the low calibration) Overall GPT-OSS-120B wins again and this time explicit cot beats just direct predictions but only by a small margin: This is an area where we are not super strong so might be worth discussion about how to fix this before trying to scale up.
---
Diversity Since I ran the ctrl benchmark extractions for 3 trials it was possible to measure the Levenshtein distance, distinct n-grams, exact matches between extractions, etc. The rephrase prompts clearly have the highest diversity. The lowest diversity comes from specifying EXACTLY what you want to include/exclude in the extraction, but the outputs there are still somewhat diverse. Might be worth more exploration, but the thing that is clear is that no two extractions are the same. The 0.06 rate of no variation comes from docs that exceed the context length. If a doc is processed then one out of the three will always have something different.
--- ## Challenges
Long Context The Rate of Empty Extractions is quite high: This is a combination of documents being too long and exceeding the context window of the LLM, but also of harmful/nsfw documents that the LLMs refuse to extract from. 0.75% of the documents in a WARC will exceed the context window of GPT-OSS-120B We can bring this down to 0.33% of docs by stripping to JUST the tags and removing contents. This is the row "preproc body" in the table above and you can already see that it helps!
---
Quality Filtering For more details please read the Quality Filtering section above, but to recap our calibration for LLM quality filtering is quite bad and so far adding fewshot examples has not made it much better. Without Fewshot: With Fewshot: The fewshot is adding an example of a top 1%, 10%, 25%, 50%, and 75% document. I still feel careful prompt engineering can get us somewhere better here (maybe with DSPy??) but as it stands right now the Quality Filtering is horribly uncalibrated.
--- For next steps I want to: - [x] High Priority: Fix the calibration to a reasonable level for Quality Filtering - [x] High Priority: Test content preservation and spec adherence together with Quality Filtering prompt too so we know the QA isn't messing things up with extraction - [x] High Priority: Kick off GPT-OSS-120B-predict extractions with 20 diverse specs to produce 200M training tokens - [x] Low Priority: Remove NSFW and Harmful from ctrl-bench and add in science extractions

# Progress this week (2/2-2/6) Progress this week was a bit lighter given my travels for a workshop in Munich however my primary focus of the week was derisking the big GPT-OSS-120B run that we decided to hold of on until next week. The main things that I wanted to test were about the composability of specs for steering extraction as well as the accuracy of spec based filters. The main findings of this week are: 1. Kimi and Deepseek are pretty on-par with GPT-OSS-120B but GPT-OSS-120B is cheaper and faster so makes sense to stick with that. 2. Seems order does not matter for what comes first in the prompt for spec vs doc 3. COMPLETE spec adherence (following ALL specs) drops below 50% accuracy after 5 specs in context. 4. We see that general filtering performance is decently strong 5. Filtering accuracy remains decently high even as the number of formatting specs increases ---
More models on ctrl bench Kimi and Deepseek are pretty on-par with GPT-OSS-120B but GPT-OSS-120B is cheaper and faster so makes sense to stick with that.
---
Can we flip the order of the spec and the doc in the prompt to the extractor? Unfortunately the exact results are still running here, but preliminary results are promising (only 100 docs processed out of 550) **Seems order does not matter for spec vs doc**
---
Composable Spec Benchmark In order to test the composability of specs I decided to filter to 10 of the best docs from the ctrl_bench of last week. Then I worked to define both rule-verifiable and llm-verifiable specs that span both FORMAT and FILTERING. In total I had 25 specs; 15 FORMAT and 10 FILTERING **Format Specs**: **Filter Specs**: Then it is possible to run subsets of 15 choose N sets of specs for formatting. For filtering I always run one at a time because it seems unrealistic to want to say filter to only Math AND filter to only code AND filter to only science, etc. and more naturally it seems you'd write one spec that says filter to Math or code or science, with some more detail so to an extent if felt better to avoid automatically composing those. There are also 10 docs I pulled from the quality benchmark. For formatting experiments we test on the 10 ctrl_bench docs and for filtering (and filtering + formatting) we test on 20 documents (10 from ctrl_bench and 10 from quality_bench) It's worth noting I also updated ctrl bench with 10 science (chemistry, biology, nutrition) webpages however I have not rerun all the numbers with those. **Examples of the new science data:**
---
Format Spec Adherence The first thing to look at is adherence for each spec when that spec is the ONLY spec being tested. Next we look at how this changes when we combine with more specs We see interesting degradation patterns per spec This is a generally stable trend across specs There are also interference patterns between particular specs But perhaps the most important thing to focus on is how this impacts the aggregate performance. In other words **how well does the spec adherence scale with more specs?** On average things are pretty fine, however **COMPLETE spec adherence (following ALL specs) drops below 50% accuracy after 5 specs in context.**
---
Filter Spec Adherence **First we see general filter performance is decently strong**: This is exciting and a nice contrast to some of the lackluster quality filtering results of last week.
---
Intersecting the two (Format Spec and Filter Spec) When we bring the format specs and filter specs together the important question is do we see the same levels of degradation in filter quality that we saw in format quality? The answer is seemingly this is NOT as big of a problem Overall, **filtering accuracy remains decently high even as the number of formatting specs increases**. There is a drop-off from 90% to 80% accuracy, but this feels much more reasonable than the 50% or even 100% drop-off from earlier.
---
Planning the 200M token data collection - I believe this will cost $3,869.25 or let's just round to $4k. - I want to generate 1000 complete specs seeded from about 40 realistic composable specs. We can mix them together in a rules based way and use an LLM to rephrase (maybe just GPT-OSS-120B). **Note this is a change** my prior plan was handwriting 20 specs and scaling that up, but Will pointed out that this might lead to lack of generalization. - Half of the tokens (100M) can be generated spec first and half of the tokens can be generated doc first (100M) - I will duplicate documents about 4x in the training data, but each time with a different spec. I am not fully sure if this makes sense because maybe no duplicates is just the better way to do this, and in this case we only get ~50M diverse tokens... There are two core dimensions we can tweak for distilling these models: 1. How many specs do we need for us to learn general extraction from specs and not just exactly how to extract from one spec 2. How much data diversity do you need to achieve this versus just training on the same docs over and over again Let's discuss this data collection design just a bit more to be sure this is ready to kick off this week.

In an effort to include even more of the process publicly available I am including some of the next steps discussed in the team meeting for this project today (2/12): **Next steps (both big and little picture)**: - Eventually take the Kimi model, train on as much data as we need, and that can be our final run. Fine to keep iterating on GPT-OSS for now - The main experiment will be to run on DCLM and compare - An immediate next step is to run the closed models on our benchmark **Some ideas** - Possibly adding url to input of the rewriter (what domains look reasonable could be a signal for filtering) - Case studies would be feasible for the paper (we rewrite to remove content discussing AI behaving poorly or unsafe content, essentially replication studies of [this](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10160) and [this](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16980) However beyond case studies there is an even stronger result: - Take the same webpages as DCLM - Can extract as many tokens as you want (“Extract as much juice out of the data as possible”) - See if we exceed performance We can just start there and don’t worry about the compute as much. Later we can worry if we need to run controls with similar token budgets/compute budgets. ### Results (Qwen3-8B, ~84 HTML pages) | Ver | Lines | Words | Filter Rate | Key Change | |-----|-------|-------|-------------|------------| | v1 | 3 | 22 | 5.5% | Baseline — just "extract the main content" | | v2 | 9 | 62 | 4.1% | Added markdown formatting, code/math preservation | | v3 | 45 | 333 | 20.0% | Full role prompt with hard gates — too verbose for 8B | | v4 | 22 | 178 | 38.9% | Simplified to flat checklist, added specific reject categories | | v5 | 23 | 189 | 36.9% | Added social media rule, `$` math delimiters | | v6 | 25 | 200 | **47.6%** | Tighter product rule, tag/archive rule, ~100 word threshold | ### Common mistakes & successes per version | Ver | False Accepts (should have been filtered) | Correct Behaviors | |-----|------------------------------------------|-------------------| | v1 | Login walls, profiles, galleries, product pages, non-English | Basic extraction works | | v2 | Same as v1 — formatting rules don't help filtering | Better markdown output, code fencing | | v3 | Product pages, galleries, "who posted" forum pages | First real filtering (language, utility pages) | | v4 | German page accepted, product pages slip through, used ` ```latex ` for math | Catches profiles, galleries, empty search, paywalls, short content (<50 words) | | v5 | 4 stochastic regressions (peoplemag, giftcards, simonseeks, sportsfanfare) | Social media stubs filtered, correct `$` math delimiters | | v6 | 1 stochastic regression, ~3 borderline thin pages remain | Product pages w/ prices caught, tag/archive pages caught | ### 1.7B comparison (v6 prompt) | Model | Filter Rate | Notes | |-------|-------------|-------| | 8B | 47.6% | Best overall | | 1.7B | 31.0% | Misses non-English (Portuguese, Chinese), product pages, profiles. Extraction quality is fine — gap is in rejection reasoning. |
Example outputs (v6, 8B) **Good extraction — math content (math03)** ``` # Time Complexity of $T(n)=T(n-2)+\frac{1}{\log(n)}$ **Question:** > Solve $ T(n)=T(n-2)+\frac{1}{\log(n)} $ for $ T(n) $. I am getting the answer as $ O(n) $ by treating $ 1/\log(n) $ as $ O(1) $. The recursive call tree of this is a lop‑sided tree of height $ n $. Hence, considering the amount of work done in each step, the answer comes out to be $ O(n) $. Please verify my answer, and tell me if I am correct. ## Answer 1 If $ T(n) = T(n-2) + \frac{1}{\log(n)} $, then $$ T(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{}T(0)+\sum_{k=1}^{n/2}\frac{1}{\log(2k)}&\text{if }n\text{ is even}\\T(1)+\sum_{k=1}^{(n-1)/2}\frac{1}{\log(2k+1)}&\text{if }n\text{ is odd}\end{array}\right.\tag{1} $$ Note that $$ \begin{align} \sum_{k=1}^{(n-1)/2}\frac{1}{\log(2k+1)} &\le\frac{1}{\log(3)}+\int_1^{(n-1)/2}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(2x+1)}\\ &=\color{#C00000}{\frac{1}{\log(3)}+\frac12\int_3^8\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)}}+\frac12\int_8^n\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)}\tag{2} \end{align} $$ and $$ \begin{align} \sum_{k=1}^{n/2}\frac{1}{\log(2k)} &\le\frac{1}{\log(2)}+\int_1^{n/2}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(2x)}\\ &=\color{#C00000}{\frac{1}{\log(2)}+\frac12\int_2^8\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)}}+\frac12\int_8^n\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)}\tag{3} \end{align} $$ For $ n\ge8 $, we have that $ \log(x) \le 2(\log(x)-1) $, thus $$ \begin{align} \frac12\int_8^n\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)} &\le\int_8^n\frac{(\log(x)-1)\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)^2}\\ &=\frac{n}{\log(n)}\color{#C00000}{-\frac{8}{\log(8)}}\tag{4} \end{align} $$ Combining (1) through (4), we get that $$ T(n)\le\color{#C00000}{C}+\frac{n}{\log(n)}=O\left(\frac{n}{\log(n)}\right)\tag{5} $$ ## Answer 2 $$T(n)=T(n-2)+1/\mbox{log }n=T(n-4)+1/\mbox{log }(n-2)+1/\mbox{log }n=\cdots $$ So $$T(n)=a+\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{1}{\mbox{log}(n-2i)}\leq a+\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{1}{b}=a+bn/2=O(n) $$ Where $ a=T(0),T(1) $ and $ b=\mbox{log }2,\mbox{log }3 $ depending on even or odd $ n $. This shows that $ O(n) $ is an upper bound. ## Answer 3 $ T(n) = T(n-2) + \frac{1}{\log(n)} $ $ \implies T(n-2) = T(n-4) + \frac{1}{\log(n)} + \frac{1}{\log(n-2)} $ So, $ T(n) = T(n-2r) + \sum_{0 ≤ 2s < 2r} \frac{1}{\log(n-2s)} $ If $ n $ is even, $ 2r \leq n-2 $, $ T(n) = T(2) + \sum_{0 ≤ 2s < n-2} \frac{1}{\log(n-2s)} $ If $ n $ is even, $ 2r \leq n-1 $, $ T(n) = T(1) + \sum_{0 ≤ 2s < n-1} \frac{1}{\log(n-2s)} $ In either case, $ O(n) = \frac{n}{\log(n)} $. ``` **Good extraction — forum Q&A (sprinklertalk)** ``` # Richdel 500 PRI controller error **Question (jrebcarlson, Monday, June 11th 2012, 5:40 pm):** When a particular station is ready to turn on (7), the controller displays and blinks a FU 5 error. Do you know what that means? I am without an owners manual. Help? **Answer (Wet_Boots, Monday, June 11th 2012, 7:53 pm):** short circuit – probably a bad solenoid **Answer (GatorGuy, Tuesday, June 12th 2012, 8:36 am):** boots is right. Except it's FUS, not FU5. From the manual: Display is stuck on a zone and "FUS" is flashing in the display. 1. Faulty valve solenoid. 2. Shorted wire connection. ``` **Correct rejection — product page (sportsfanfare)** ``` [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] ``` (Page was a Kansas State jersey listing with price, item #, and warehouse availability) **Correct rejection — blog tag page (downthedrive)** ``` [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] ``` (Page had only two post titles with 1-line teasers and dates, no actual article content)
---
Inference on TPU/marin Did a deep audit of marin's current inference stack (`lib/marin/src/marin/generation/`) and researched modern vLLM + Ray Data patterns. The current system has several architectural problems that compound on our highly preemptible TPU cluster. Summary of findings and improvements: | Problem | What's Happening | v2 Improvement | |---|---|---| | **TPU sits idle during preprocessing** | Template formatting, tokenization, and truncation all run *inside* the vLLM actor on the TPU node. TPU waits for CPU work to finish before each `generate()` call. | Separate CPU preprocessing stage from TPU inference stage (a la `ray.data.llm.build_processor`). Each scales independently via backpressure. | | **Scaling stuck at 1 replica** | Ray requests a custom resource name (`TPU-v5p-8-head`) — if the cluster doesn't register that exact string, scheduling silently fails. Zero logging of how many replicas are actually running vs. pending. No way to tell "Ray chose 1" from "Ray can't find the resource." | Validate resource names at startup (fail fast). Log replica counts periodically. Explicit `min_replicas`/`max_replicas` config. | | **Head node is the bottleneck** | The entire `run_inference` function runs on the head node — including GCS glob resolution, checkpoint scanning (batches of 20 files, 120s timeout), and write orchestration. With 10k+ output files the checkpoint scan alone takes 20+ minutes and saturates head node I/O, which also kills other people's jobs. | Head node only partitions work and writes a lightweight shard manifest. All heavy I/O (reads, writes, checkpoint tracking) moves to CPU workers. | | **10+ min recompilation on every preemption** | JAX compilation cache lives in `/tmp` — wiped on every preemption. Each restart triggers full XLA recompilation. | Cache XLA compilations to GCS (`gs://marin-{region}/compilation-cache/{model_hash}/`). After first compile, restarts take seconds. | | **Checkpoint resume is O(millions)** | On restart, every output file is scanned to extract processed row IDs into a Python set, then the entire input dataset is filtered row-by-row against that set. Stragglers that time out at 120s are silently dropped, causing those rows to be reprocessed. | Shard-based checkpointing: partition input into small shards (~5-10 min each), track completed shards in a manifest. Resume = skip completed shards. Bounded data loss on preemption. | | **Confusing config API** | Single `filetype` field means both input and output format; `output_filetype_override` bolted on separately. Resolution logic copy-pasted in 3+ places. Checkpoint glob can use the wrong filetype and silently miss old outputs. | Clean config with separate `input_format` and `output_format` fields. Each used exactly once. No override, no ambiguity. | A big part was moving to **Zephyr**. On a single v5p8 node I got from 400 tokens per second to close to 1k!!!
---
Midtraining Experiments My initial Midtraining experiments were kinda a bust. ~10M tokens on Llama 3.2 1B: Learning rate warmup was bad, way too few steps for signal. Even using 100M tokens from gpt-oss was not enough steps, although it was better. These were not leading to meaningful eval changes. I spoke with @Helw150 and we came up with a better experiment. Go to checkpoint 35000 of [this nemotron run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/exp2166-scaling-ladder-nemotron-validation-optimal-1e+20-9563f0?nw=nwuserheld) of a 1.3B model and replace the cooldown: However the cooldown is still 2.3B tokens. It is important to train on that many steps but how do we get that many tokens when inference isn't too fast on somewhat limited compute (most of the week I could only get 1-2 tpus nodes) We decided to mix in with the existing cooldown and target about 10% of the data being from my rephraser. I kicked off a run last night with 25 WARC files. I managed to get close to ~10 tpus consistently overnight so this actually ran relatively fast! I used the v6 prompt I engineered above. This is the outcome of the token generation vs a DCLM baseline I purposefully selected to be around 10% of the size needed. | Metric | Rephraser | DCLM | |---|---:|---:| | shard_ledger rows | 83,834 | 244,203 | | `.stats.json` total_tokens | 45,904,757 | 307,051,596 | | Avg tokens/row | ~548 | ~1,257 | Looks like I need about 6x as many WARC files: | Metric | Rephraser Cooldown | DCLM Cooldown | |---|---:|---:| | Added source tokens | 45.9M | 307.1M | | NemotronCooldown tokens | 2,558.7M | 2,558.7M | | Added source % | 1.76% | 10.72% | | NemotronCooldown % | 98.24% | 89.28% | This took 5 hours to process inference so it might be closer to 30 hours unless we can scale up tpus. 10 at a time already feels pretty high though... This is worth a discussion! The two runs are going now, but I feel there is too little data on the rephrased run: - rephraser: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/cooldown-rephraser-d7d976d3-v2-1cdc5a?nw=nwusermichaeljryan - dclm: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/cooldown-dclm-100m-v2-32bcbc?nw=nwusermichaeljryan
---
Plans for Future Experiments (Contingent on Midtraining working) Some ideas: - The full pretrain experiment comparison to DCLM - Reproduce RephraseTheWeb results but now we can just do our pipeline - Reproduce Nemotron-CC-Math but with just our pipeline - Reproduce Alignment Pretraining but with just our pipeline Another next step is to convert the data to be Kimi K2 instead of GPT-OSS which I can hopefully do on the cluster now.
---

# Cooldown data "midtrain" experiment ## Baseline run we’re pulling from (Nemotron 1.3B) - We are evaluating cooldown variants starting from the same Nemotron 1.3B training run / checkpoint lineage. - W&B link: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/exp2166-scaling-ladder-nemotron-validation-optimal-1e+20-9563f0?nw=nwuserheld ## What this experiment is We start from a **pre-cooldown checkpoint** (step 35000) and run cooldown training with different data mixtures. The main question: - does replacing part of the standard **Nemotron cooldown data** with **DCLM** or **Rephraser** data improve downstream benchmark performance? - More fundamentally to us: Does our **Rephraser** beat **DCLM**? ## Headline result **Nemotron-only is the best aggregate condition** in these runs. In aggregate our rephraser might beat DCLM but individually DCLM outperforms our rephraser.
Experimental design Headline full-cooldown conditions: - **Pre-cooldown**: checkpoint before any cooldown - **Post-cooldown (Nemotron-only)**: standard cooldown with no auxiliary mixin (this is just the final checkpoint) - **DCLM-300M**: large DCLM mixin chosen to approximately match the large rephraser run by token count - **DCLM-filtered-6M**: DCLM text extracted from the **same 150-WARC pool as Rephraser-362M**; those WARCs were selected to be **after the DCLM cutoff**; only ~6M tokens survive filtering - **Rephraser-362M**: rephraser-generated text from that same **150-WARC post-cutoff pool** Important implementation note: - Rephraser data is produced using the **8B rephraser model** trained to checkpoint 1318 on 16M reasoning tokens and 10M output tokens. See prior week reports for more details Primary metric: - **choice_prob_norm**: Normalized probability of selecting the correct answer choice on a multiple-choice benchmark, computed from the model’s log probabilities over answer choices. Rephraser Prompt:
Prompt used to generate the rephraser data (8B rephraser model) ``` Extract the main content from the provided HTML into clean Markdown. First, check if the page should be rejected. Output exactly [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] if ANY of these apply: - Not primarily in English - Login, signup, account, checkout, paywall, or subscribe page - Error page, captcha, cookie wall, bot check, or "session expired" - Empty or near-empty page, directory index, or navigation-only page - User profile, member page, or "who posted" page - Image gallery or photo album listing without articles - Search results page with no actual results - Page where the main content is behind a login wall or paywall - Product listing, gift card, or e-commerce page with prices/availability - Social media post that is just an image or a single short caption - Blog tag page, category page, or archive page that only lists post titles and teasers - After removing boilerplate, the remaining useful text would be under ~100 words If the page passes, extract with these rules: - Output Markdown only. No commentary or analysis. - Preserve original wording. Do not summarize or rewrite. - Remove boilerplate: navbars, footers, sidebars, ads, share buttons, related links, breadcrumbs. - Preserve all technical content exactly: code blocks verbatim with language tags, math/LaTeX using $$ delimiters, chemical formulas, tables. - Do not truncate or simplify content due to length. - Include comments/replies only if they add real information (answers, corrections). - Start with the page title as a top-level heading if available. ```

It is not reliable enough to replace downstream eval when choosing between nearby variants. ---

# Math SFT Experiment The purpose of the SFT experiment is to show how the rephraser can be useful for curating SFT datasets. ## Experimental Design I took my 8B rephraser trained on 1318 steps (see prior weeks) with the following prompt: ---
Prompt ``` EXTRACTION_SPEC = """\ Extract and restructure this math help forum HTML page into a clean Question/Reasoning/Answer format in Markdown. First, check if this is an actual math discussion thread with a math question. Output exactly [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] if ANY of these apply: - Not a math question/discussion thread (e.g. forum index, category listing, user profile, search results) - Software announcement, product news, or tool tutorial without a math problem - Page is empty, login-only, error page, or has no substantive math content - Not primarily in English If the page is a valid math thread, extract and restructure it. Remove all boilerplate: navigation, footers, sidebars, ads, user signatures, join dates, post counts, reaction buttons, and related thread links. Do not include any raw HTML tags in your output. Output format: - Start with the thread title as a top-level heading. - Use up to three sections: ## Question, ## Reasoning, ## Answer. - **Question**: The original poster's problem, cleaned up but preserving the mathematical content faithfully. - **Reasoning**: The key steps, explanations, and worked-out logic from the discussion thread. Synthesize the useful replies into a coherent explanation. - **Answer**: The final answer or solution clearly stated (if it is present in the thread) Rules: - Output Markdown only. No meta-commentary. - Preserve all mathematical content exactly: LaTeX/MathJax using $ or $$ delimiters, equations, formulas, and notation. - Preserve code blocks verbatim with language tags if applicable. - If the thread contains multiple distinct questions, use a separate ## Question, ## Reasoning, ## Answer block for each. Solve each question independently — do not mix answers between questions. - If no clear answer was reached in the thread, omit the Answer section. Do not fabricate or guess an answer.\ """ ```
--- I pointed it at content from [mathhelpforum.com](http://mathhelpforum.com/) which is the number one source of data for Nemotron-CC-Math (8.44% of documents) Using CDX index lookups of WARC files I was able to locate 506,072 docs from [mathhelpforum.com](http://mathhelpforum.com/) from 28 WARCs from 2018–2022. I parsed this data using both our 8b rephraser and resiliparse (**separate experiments** NOT together) to produce 113,162,322 tokens and 262,127,845 tokens respectively. Our 8b rephraser filtered down from the 500k docs to 260,865 docs. I provide some examples of what the parsed pages look like here: ---

First, check if it's a math discussion thread: Yes, contains differential equations problem. Now extract content. Thread title: "Differential Equations" (from

Differential Equations

) Original poster's problem: In post 1 (KayPee) content includes: "1. Obtain the solution to the differential equation dy/dx=(1+y^2)/(1+x²) 2. The first order differential equation dy/dx-xy=x has the solution y= ? These are both separable. 1) $\displaystyle \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1 + y^2}{1 + x^2} \rightarrow \frac{dy}{1 + y^2} = \frac{dx}{1 + x²}$ 2) $\displaystyle \frac{dy}{dx} - xy = x \rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx} = x(1+y) \rightarrow \frac{dy}{1 + y} = x dx$ Someone kindly finish up for me..I kind of confused at this stage." We need to clean up but preserve math. Then answer: In post 4 (Prove It) provides step-by-step solution. Also post 5 (mr fantastic) comments but not answer. Thus answer is the solution from Prove It. We need to produce Question, Reasoning, Answer. Question: The original problem. Reasoning: The key steps from the discussion: The steps given by Prove It. Answer: The final answer: y = ... for each question. Let's extract the final answer from Prove It: For first equation: Solution: arctan y = arctan x + C => y = tan(arctan x + C). Could be expressed as y = tan(arctan x + C). But they didn't simplify further. The answer could be written as y = tan(arctan x + C). However they might want explicit expression: y = tan(arctan x + C). We'll present. Second equation: y = Ae^{(1/2)x^2} - 1. Thus answer. Now produce markdown. We need to preserve LaTeX. Let's format: ## Question 1. Obtain the solution to the differential equation $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1 + y^2}{1 + x²} $$ 2. Solve the first order differential equation $$ \frac{dy}{dx} - xy = x $$ ## Reasoning The first equation is separable: $$ \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ Integrating both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \int \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ Which gives: $$ \arctan y + C_1 = \arctan x + C_2 $$ Simplify to: $$ \arctan y = \arctan x + C $$ Thus the solution is: $$ y = \tan(\arctan x + C) $$ The second equation is also separable. Rewrite: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = x(y + 1) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = x\,dx $$ Integrate both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = \int x\,dx $$ Which yields: $$ \ln|y + 1| + C_1 = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C_2 $$ Simplify to: $$ \ln|y + 1| = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C $$ Exponentiate both sides: $$ |y + 1| = e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2 + C} = e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Thus: $$ y + 1 = \pm e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Let $ A = \pm e^C $, so: $$ y = A e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2} - 1 $$ ## Answer 1. $ y = \tan(\arctan x + C) $ 2. $ y = A e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2} - 1 $ Make sure to include markdown headings. Now produce output with required fields. [[ ## text ## ]] # Differential Equations ## Question 1. Obtain the solution to the differential equation $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1 + y^2}{1 + x²} $$ 2. Solve the first order differential equation $$ \frac{dy}{dx} - xy = x $$ ## Reasoning **First equation** The equation is separable: $$ \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ Integrating both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \int \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ Which gives: $$ \arctan y + C_1 = \arctan x + C_2 $$ Simplify to: $$ \arctan y = \arctan x + C $$ Thus the solution is: $$ y = \tan(\arctan x + C) $$ **Second equation** Rewrite the equation: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = x(y + 1) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = x\,dx $$ Integrate both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = \int x\,dx $$ Which yields: $$ \ln|y + 1| + C_1 = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C_2 $$ Simplify to: $$ \ln|y + 1| = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C $$ Exponentiate both sides: $$ |y + 1| = e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2 + C} = e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Thus: $$ y + 1 = \pm e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Let $ A = \pm e^C $, so: $$ y = A e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2} - 1 $$ ## Answer 1. $ y = \tan(\arctan x + C) $ 2. $ y = A e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2} - 1 $ [[ ## completed ## ]] ```
