# Weekly Sync 8/3 - 8/7 ---
Extraction Unit Tests Ran some other benchmarks: Pretty universally it seems like we get way higher recall but lose on precision. HOWEVER I looked into these benchmarks and they reward things like removing titles, authors, copyright info, and comments sections which are all things I deliberately chose to KEEP in the document, so we can either remove copyrightten documents or include interesting discussion about articles. This is not to say that we don't incidentally extract some stuff that is genuine garbage. Sometimes author bios for articles end up being advertisements for something that person wants to sell you, sometimes related articles are not that useful (however sometimes related questions end up being a nice QA style chunk of questions AND their answers so it is an edge case). On our own unit tests we look pretty good. The unit tests are comprised of domain specific evals. 13 code, 10 math, 9 tables, 29 prose, 12 attribution, 5 structure, 24 negative. We are worst at the "negative" case which has to do with removing content. | system | total | code | math | table | prose | attribution | structure | negatives | |---------------|:-------:|:----:|:----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----------:|:---------:|:---------:| | GOLD (self-test) | 102/102 | 13/13 | 10/10 | 9/9 | 29/29 | 12/12 | 5/5 | 24/24 | | **marin v1.1 (ours)** | **90/102** | **13/13** | **10/10** | **9/9** | 28/29 | **12/12** | **5/5** | 13/24 | | resiliparse | 92/102 | 13/13 | 10/10 | 8/9 | 27/29 | 12/12 | 5/5 | 17/24 | | ORIGINAL spec | 84/102 | 13/13 | 9/10 | 7/9 | 24/29 | 8/12 | 5/5 | 18/24 | | Dripper | 84/102 | 13/13 | 7/10 | 9/9 | 26/29 | 2/12 | 4/5 | 23/24 | | trafilatura | 78/102 | 13/13 | 7/10 | 7/9 | 23/29 | 3/12 | 5/5 | 20/24 | https://claude.ai/code/artifact/ccb92af7-09dc-42ae-b37a-0d40aad802b7
---
Mixing Results View Mixes: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/83283a3a-90b4-46a1-b88d-de18510578f4 View Eval Results: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/c283aebd-ed3a-4685-823d-62e8e3a70884 Better version but can't be shared publicly because of script tags: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/dae91143-af49-401c-acac-e3a1627929a5 Note our high coverage spec is still extracting so this is still somewhat preliminary exploration of data mixing. Mixing for 3 Targets: --- **OLMO Base Easy Evals:**
Details Spec-Driven Mix: On the OLMO dev set this was optimized for it is great: Even overall on OLMO full set it is pretty great: However on DCLM Core it doesn't move the needle very much:
--- --- **DCLM Core v2:** Since OLMO dev set optimization didn't move things that much for DCLM maybe optimizing on it directly will?
Details Spec-Driven Mix: Surprisingly it doesn't move DCLM that much, although it makes HQ competitive with DCLM: Fully inverts the OLMO scores though when you mix for DCLM instead:
--- --- **BLEnD Cultural QA:** From here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.09948
Details Spec-Driven Mix: Interestingly the DCLM data is better for cultural QA than our old spec, but I suspect our new spec will be better: I also suspect this might have more to do with models being good at in-context MCQ than cultural understanding
---
---
The Problem with DCLM Core DCLM Disaggregated: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/dc5f1cf5-eb62-4c99-9e2f-70472b28797e OLMO Disaggregated: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/ce4e61f6-f3e9-433b-ae76-805a12015ee5 DCLM Core is super noisy. Some are higher signal (basically hellaswag), and with mixing we can improve over Hellaswag: But many **many** are just noise, and no sense of trying to win on them at this scale: In contrast OLMO bpb seems to be pretty high signal: Although there are some that are still noisy here too: My thought: **maybe we forget about DCLM Core and showcase wins on OLMO Base Easy instead at least for spec-driven project at smaller scale** This is where we already win, no new specs, no mixing needed!
---
Distillation Progress Distilling back into our FastText -> ModernBERT -> Resiliparse/JustText pipeline for LLM_Curated_v1.1. **FastText**: **ModernBERT**: Still training - ModernBERT 1M: 40.3% (step 1,575 / 3,906) — on pace to finish tonight, F1 lands right after in its end-of-run eval. - ModernBERT 10M: 11.1% (step 4,317 / 39,062) — the multi-day flagship, pace steady at ~5s/step, ETA roughly 2 days out. **Resiliparse (instead of JustText since it is faster)**:
---
Plan **Experiment Idea**: Scale everything down by 20x. So instead of a 100B model we are training a 5B, and instead of nemotron producing 7T tokes we sample 350B tokens. And instead of a 2T token target or similar we have a 200B token target. Once I extract 5% of the internet I will have about 3-4T tokens or so. We would be comparing 350B tokens of nemotron to 2T tokens of my data, on a 200B token target for a 5B model. We can do whatever data mixing we choose but at the end of the day we need to find the best 200B tokens to train that 5B model. This seems like the most fair way to compare the data at smaller scale and should be achievable within a week or so of launching my big run.
---

# Wednesday August 12th Sync Today I intend to talk about: - How for the scale we are working at we should move away from DCLM Core v2 (until we can do some larger scale runs) - The two main thrusts I have been iterating on: **data mixing** and **pipeline distillation** - The current status of the 10k extraction - Some planning for what we should prioritize next Some of this is overlap with the notes I added to the thread last Friday, but this should be a cleaner version --- > [!NOTE] > This should be the **final** week we have to look at old "high_quality" results rather than the new "llm_pipeline_v1.1" spec ---
Why possibly we should ditch DCLM (for this scale) Full Viewer: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/dae91143-af49-401c-acac-e3a1627929a5 Unfortunately because it includes javascript Anthropic won't let me share it publicly. **GENERAL THOUGHTS ABOUT DCLM CORE v2**: From [Olmo 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.13961): Recommendation from chatting with David Heineman: - BPB based evals are higher signal for models under around 10^22 flops - Above this threshold you can switch to accuracy based evals but need to average over a large set **WHERE WE ARE AT WITH DCLM CORE v2**: Even when I mix directly for it **high_quality** does not exceed **DCLM** (note we are still just a bit out from getting **llm_pipeline_v1.1** which could change things). But when we disaggregate... There is a lot of noise: It is not all noise though: **IF WE TURN TO OLMO BASE EASY (which is bpb based)**: Without mixing we might already be the best or tied for the best: Closer look: After mixing we are FULLY better:
**TAKEAWAY** > [!TIP] > I think we need to do one of three things going forward: > - Convert DCLM Core to a BPB based eval > - Ignore the results at this scale and collect enough data to realistically train a 10^22 flop model for comparison > - Switch to trusting the OLMO Base Easy results instead ---
Data Mixing The Data Mixing setup seems to be working. We are getting clear benefits on what we mix towards: **OLMO Base Easy** **DCLM CORE** **BLEnD** NOTE with Blend I spoke with Will Held yesterday and I am not setting up the evals properly so this one needs to be rerun.
How I currently run it ``` The following are questions about everyday life in South Korea. Question: What is a common snack for preschool kids in South Korea? Answer: cookie Question: What is a popular food to go with beer in South Korea? Answer: fried chicken Question: What is the most popular fruit in South Korea? Answer: ``` **Take the logprobs of the correct answer** -- this comes from OLMO base easy multiple choice scoring

American Football B. hide and seek C. soccer D. stick game Answer: ``` **Take the logprobs of letter and answer** -- something Will figured out from scaling MMLU
The movement from the BLEnD mix is sensible: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/83283a3a-90b4-46a1-b88d-de18510578f4 HQ: DCLM:
**TAKEAWAY** > [!TIP] > Our Olmix clone works for getting data mixes that better steer towards particular benchmarks > > However, **high_quality** is not better than **dclm** after mixing at all benchmarks. We need to see if our coverage bet played off for **llm_pipeline_v1.1** when that is ready next week. ---

Formula on the 115 annotated-equation docs: ours 0.3838 · Dripper 0.1579.
**CLASSIFIER CASCADE** Had Claude try a bunch more architectures: Seems like **ettin68** from this [JHU paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11412) training optimal encoders and decoders is nearly as good as modernBERT but twice as fast. Also using Rav's pooled tranformer shallow architecture is 172x as fast as modernBERT but only slightly worse. **WITH THIS I HAVE THE FOLLOWING SETTINGS**: One version that is currently running: Coverage looks promising: http://localhost:8096/#coverage Will get me the **10k WARCs later today and I will immediately start mixing** to compare with **DCLM**, **High_Quality**, and **Resiliparse** (running now) Another promising version: Half the time, but similar performance. **CURRENT BRANCHES I AM STILL EXPLORING** - Running filtering AFTER extraction since our new resiliparse-rust version is so fast - 10x the data on Rav's pooled transformer architecture since it is also much faster to train. So modernBERT takes 5 days to train on 10M docs, but we can train this on ~100M docs in similar time.
**TAKEAWAY** > [!TIP] > Our exploration of different architectures to distill the pipeline into has yielded a really fast and really quality pipeline. I am still exploring a few more knobs to tweak but we are getting ~0.85 F1 on filtering decisions and ~0.8 Levenstein similarity to LLM based spec-driven curation. ---
10k WARC Extraction Status LLM Pipeline v1.1 has 1 week to go if we decide this is the best use of cluster time:
**TAKEAWAY** > [!TIP] > We need one more week to extract LLM Pipeline v1.1 if we choose to use the cluster time for that. ---
Planning **RISKS** 1. **Maybe you really shouldn't get too much data and then mix it**. We are getting mixed results from **high_quality** vs **dclm**, however this is only mildly concerning because **high_quality** was never meant to be the "super high-coverage data source". **llm_pipeline_v1.1** is supposed to be this so if we can't mix it we are in trouble. === **DERISK:** Don't wait on the 10k extraction, get that mixing later today on the distilled version!! 2. **Everything looks great at sub 10^22 flops, but once we scale up...**. I think we need to test things at real scale SOON. This was out of the question for llm extraction, but I think it is feasible with our distilled pipeline now. **DERISK:** It might be time to train with no epoching, something like 3B models for 200B tokens or similar so we can trust benchmarks like DCLM Core. 3. **There is no distinction between good data and good data for human-centered applications**. I don't believe this, but **dclm** was beating us on blend. **DERISK:** I think we need more human-centered benchmarks. **NICE TO HAVE** - Safety pretraining style rewrites. **MUST HAVE** - High quality copywrite filtering to remove copywritten content from common crawl. With both of these we know that 3k WARC files is enough to get decent distillation from an llm filter. We could consider even training these as fastText classifiers or text rules (in the case of copywrite) - though safety might be more advanced, and run this once we are already starting to process the dataset. I presented this plan to Diyi and Will (separately). Diyi liked it but Will was more inclined to say this should all be one thing: **NEXT STEPS:** - [ ] Run training and evals on the new data from the distilled pipeline at 10k WARCs - [ ] Compare with resiliparse - [ ] Finish architecture sweeps for the distilled pipeline - [ ] Launch more data extraction on the distilled pipeline so we can test things at scale - [ ] Add more human centered benchmarks besides BLEnD

Release Options: 1. Common Crawl: https://data.commoncrawl.org/contrib/index.html 2. If we release it we could just release an index of what is kept and only release text if it was rephrased (e.g. for safety) 3. We could upload everything to huggingface under OpenAthena, Common Crawl, or Stanford - Should I include all the llm_pipeline stuff in an ICLR paper or is that complexity not needed? The old spec (so much simpler) performs similarly on the benchmarks we care about even if the new spec is better in our data mixing argument world - What does the right division of ideas and artifacts look like? The above is just one proposal. **Paper Changes:** Current Framing (https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4): - Introduce Spec-Driven curation - Explain how we trained the model to do this - Show that we get more tokens and better data - Show that by changing the spec you make the curation more budget aware (with scaling for quality) - **Show that you can revise the spec to make it better for math, code, medicine** New Framing: - Introduce Spec-Driven curation - Explain how we trained the model to do this - Show that we get more tokens and better data - Show that by changing the spec you make the curation more budget aware (with scaling for quality) - **Show that revisions to the spec lead to interpretable changes to the data distribution**
> [!TIP] > We can submit to ICLR by the end of September, have our initial data processed by end of September, and hopefully have a plan for data to be "release ready" by end of October. Most of these dates besides ICLR are flexible and end of October is generous in that we can push to be done sooner if needed. ---

More principled FLOP estimation ## Inference FLOPs of the fast curation cascade **Estimate: 1.3e10 to 1.7e10 FLOPs per extracted document, 5.1e14 to 6.7e14 per WARC, and 4.0e21 to 5.3e21 for the 8M-WARC run (7,925,398 WARCs).** The low end charges each document its real token count; the high end charges the padded length the chip actually runs. ettin68 accounts for 98% of the total. | | Actual lengths | Padded lengths | |---|---|---| | Per extracted doc | 1.3e10 | 1.7e10 | | Per kept doc | 6.9e10 | 9.0e10 | | Per WARC | 5.1e14 | 6.7e14 | | Per kept token (ModernBERT tokens) | 5.1e7 | 6.7e7 | | 8M run total | 4.0e21 | 5.3e21 | The rest of this note explains how the numbers are produced. The deployed pipeline (`lpv11_fastpipe_v2_1_fused`) scores every extracted document with three classifiers in sequence: fastText, a pooled super-token transformer, and ettin68. Each stage only sees the documents the previous stage passed on, so the cost per document is an expectation over the stages a document reaches. ### Stages and reach rates | Stage | Model | Context | Condition to run | Share of extracted docs | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | fastText w640 | full doc | always | 100% | | 2 | pooled transformer (90M-doc ckpt) | 8192 | fastText prob ≥ 0.0048 | 58.2% | | 3 | ettin68 | 2048 | pooled prob in [0.079, 0.8883) | 20.1% | Of the documents the pooled model scores, 18.3% are accepted outright, 47.2% are dropped, and 34.6% go to ettin68. Overall, 19.2% of extracted documents are kept. Rates are measured from production catalogs (52 shards, 12,824 WARCs). Per WARC: 39,464 records, 38,560 extracted docs, 22,423 fastText survivors, 7,749 band docs, 7,413 kept docs. ## Expected cost per document ``` E[FLOPs per extracted doc] = c_ft + p_ft * E[ c_pool(min(L, 8192)) | passed fastText ] + p_ft * p_band * E[ c_ettin(min(L, 2048)) | in band ] p_ft = 0.5815 p_band = 0.3456 ``` Each stage's cost is averaged over the token-length distribution of the documents that actually reach it. Those distributions come from the 100k comparison sample, which stores every stage's score per document: we tokenize its deployment text with the ModernBERT tokenizer and apply the production thresholds. The sample's reach rates match production within two points. **How padding works.** Within a WARC, the scorer sorts a stage's documents by length, takes batches of 32, and pads each batch to the smallest bucket in (128, 256, ..., context) that fits the longest document in that batch. The last batch is filled to 32 rows with empty rows. Because batches are length-sorted, all 32 documents in a batch are close in length, so the padded cost is well approximated by charging each document its own bucket; simulating the real per-batch procedure on the sample gives the same mean within 1%. Padding raises the mean charged length by 1.37x for the pooled stage and 1.30x for ettin68, which is the gap between the two columns below and in the headline table. | Stage | Reach rate | Mean tokens, actual (capped at context) | Mean tokens, padded | Cost per doc, actual | Cost per doc, padded | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | fastText | 100% | 1,318 (no cap) | n/a | 2.0e5 | 2.0e5 | | pooled | 58.2% | 1,010 | 1,380 | 4.1e8 | 5.7e8 | | ettin68 | 20.1% | 608 | 792 | 6.5e10 | 8.5e10 | ## 8M run document counts (7,925,398 WARCs) | | Count | |---|---| | Docs scored by fastText | 3.1e11 | | Docs scored by pooled | 1.8e11 | | Docs scored by ettin68 | 6.1e10 | | Kept docs | 5.9e10 | For reference, 4.0e21 to 5.3e21 FLOPs is the 6ND training cost of a 1B model on 700B to 900B tokens. ## Caveats - FLOPs and chip time diverge. Measured chip time from the catalogs implies MFU of 0.1 to 0.4% for the pooled stage and 1.4 to 5.7% for ettin68. All-in, the run is 26.2 v6e-8 slice-seconds per WARC (about 58k slice-hours for 8M WARCs), which is 0.35% MFU against the FLOP total. - fastText FLOPs count arithmetic only. Its measured cost is 0.55 CPU-ms per document, mostly hashing and table lookups. - Token counts use the ModernBERT tokenizer, not the training tokenizer. - Reach rates are from the current ladder's crawl mix.
Conventions - Forward pass only; a multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs. - Embedding lookups, layer norms, softmax, activations, and the pooling reduction count as zero. - Length `L` includes the two special tokens and is capped at the stage context. The padded variant rounds `L` up to the next bucket in (128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192). - Empty tail rows in a WARC's last batch are included in the per-batch simulation and add under 1%.
fastText formula dim 100, word bigrams, no character n-grams (read from the model header). Features are words plus bigrams, about twice the word count; words are taken as 0.75 of ModernBERT tokens. One add per dimension per feature, then a 100 x 2 output layer. ``` F = 2 * 0.75 * T c_ft = 100 * F + 2 * 100 * 2 ≈ 150 T + 400 ``` At T = 1,318 this is 2.0e5.
Pooled transformer formula Levanter's `PooledTransformerConfig.flops_per_token`, called directly. `L` padded tokens, `S = L / 64` super-tokens, hidden `D = 512`, pooled input width 768 (mean, max, min of 256-dim embeddings), feed-forward 2048, 4 layers, 2 labels. ``` proj = 2 * 768 * D * S layer = 2 * 4 * D^2 * S # q, k, v, o projections + 2 * 2 * S^2 * D # QK^T and AV + 2 * 2 * D * 2048 * S # MLP head = 2 * D * 2 c_pool(L) = proj + 4 * layer + head ``` About 4.1e5 FLOPs per input token, nearly flat in `L`.
ettin68 formula Hand-derived (Levanter's generic helper adds a vocabulary-head term a classifier does not have). Hidden `D = 512`, GeGLU feed-forward 768, 19 layers, 8 heads, global attention on every third layer starting at layer 0 (7 layers), sliding window 128 on the other 12. ``` linear_per_token_per_layer = 2 * 4 * D^2 # q, k, v, o + 2 * D * 2 * 768 # GeGLU up and gate + 2 * 768 * D # down attn_per_token_per_layer = 4 * span * D # span = L (global), min(L, 128) (local) c_ettin(L) = L * sum over 19 layers of (linear + attn) ``` Linear term 8.5e7 per token (two times the 42M non-embedding parameters); attention 3.2e7 at L = 2048; total 1.17e8 per token.
Data sources - Reach rates and per-WARC counts: fused catalogs, 52 random shards of the 404 to 8079 ladder. - Per-stage length distributions: 100k comparison sample (`extractor_compare/high_quality_200warc`), deployment text tokenized with `answerdotai/ModernBERT-base`, production thresholds applied to stored scores. - Model shapes: checkpoint `config.json` for pooled 90M and ettin68; fastText hyperparameters from the model binary header. - Chip time: catalog columns `pooled_s` and `score_s` times device count, per device type.
> [!TIP] > The distilled pipeline is projected to take about 5e21 flops to run on the full 8M WARC files. > The previous 8B model running on all of the internet was projected to take between 3e25 and 1.8e26 flops depending on if I used the pipeline version or the single call spec. > The fact that it is taking a month is likely somewhat due to poor MFU ---
Updated Main Results from Mixing
> [!TIP] > Finally showing signs of how the "more data" really helps at scale (100B+ tokens) ---
Beta Paper Outline Old Paper: https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4 New Paper (extremely preliminary for now, will auto-update here): https://www.overleaf.com/read/tzzfngmmyqsp#daf616 **Introduction:** Something about how we should spend way more compute on data curation but it doesn't need to be more complicated. **Background**: Current data curation pipelines including data mixing **Method**: Spec-Driven Curation, as well as the distillation into FastText, Pooled Transformer, and Ettin68 (modernBERT) **Swapping the spec enables control of the data distribution**: We show different specs lead to expected changes in data downstream
Plots
We then argue that because of the mixing and the growing demand for tokens we opt to use the coverage spec. **Spec-Driven Curation Yields Bigger and Better Data**: We show that by using our high coverage spec distilled pipeline we get more data and can mix it to be better at many domains.
Plots **Bigger**: Everything else bends upwards, but we can train on 100B+ tokens from just 10k WARCs. If we 800x (which is a bad way to do this bc no accounting for dedup), then we should be able to train on 80T tokens without issue. **Better Coverage**: We can mix for several downstream target capabilities.
**Ablations**: When we remove parts of the system how much does it impact performance. All ablations will be done on the olmo base easy eval set.
Plots **THESE ARE JUST STAND IN PLOTS, I HAVE TO RUN THESE EXPERIMENTS:** **Original Resiliparse vs Our "AutoResearch" Resiliparse**: **Spec for Quality ("High Quality") vs Spec for Coverage ("High Coverage")**: **Distilled Pipeline into Classifiers vs Original**: **Mixing vs No Mixing**:
**Discussion**: Scaling this up to the full internet **Conclusion**: Invest more flops into the pretraining data curation.
> [!TIP] > I tore apart the old paper but tried to keep the focus around the spec-driven idea. Interested to discuss if this is the right framing :) ---

> [!TIP] > Turns out most of the atrocious performance we were seeing is attributed to the vllm-tpu bug (discussed below) but `rewrite` pages do have a high rate of hallucination still. ---
Why do TPU and GPU differ? RoPE bug in vllm-tpu version :( Our TPU inference stack (vLLM + Google's `tpu-inference`) has two ways to run a model: a JAX re-implementation of each architecture (the default for dense Qwen3, Qwen2, Llama) and a path that runs vLLM's PyTorch model definition through torchax. The JAX Qwen3 implementation reads the model's RoPE settings from the Hugging Face config like this: ```python self.rope_scaling = getattr(config, "rope_scaling", None) ... if rope_scaling: # truthy dict -> apply Llama-3 long-context scaling timescale = apply_rope_scaling(timescale, rope_scaling) ``` With transformers 4.x, a model that uses no RoPE scaling (Qwen3's `config.json` says `"rope_scaling": null`) returned `None` here, and nothing happened. transformers 5 changed the API: `config.rope_scaling` is now an alias of `rope_parameters` and returns `{"rope_type": "default", "rope_theta": 1000000}`. That dict is truthy, so the JAX port started applying `apply_rope_scaling`, which never checks `rope_type` and uses hard-coded Llama-3 defaults (scale 8, cutoffs at 2k and 8k tokens). Result: 37 of Qwen3's 64 RoPE frequency bands were rewritten, the lowest divided by 8. The model's sense of position was wrong at every token, and worse the farther apart two tokens were, so long documents suffered most. ### Timeline - **2026-06-12** tpu-inference cuts `releases/v0.23.0`; the bug is latent (it needs transformers 5). - **2026-06-26** Google fixes it on `main` (PR #2838, "Get the right rope_scaling values from config"); the fix ships in v0.24.0 and later, never in v0.23.0. - **2026-06-29** Marin `main` migrates to transformers 5 (#6735) while every tpu-inference pin from 06-17 to 08-13 is v0.23.0-based, so `main` is broken for every dense model on the default JAX path. - **2026-08-13 11:39 PT** `main` auto-refreshes the stack to v0.26.0 (#8207) and is fixed, by accident. - **My checkout** tracked `main` as of 05-06 (transformers 4.57.5, tpu-inference 0.18.0 fork) until the parity sync on **2026-08-13 13:54 ET**, which landed 11 commits before #8207. With transformers 4 the config reports `rope_scaling = None` and the scaling branch never runs, so the lpv11 10k extraction (late July to ~Aug 20), the 3,000-WARC llm_pipeline_v1 run and all distillation data gathered by Aug 12 were produced on a correct model. Being behind `main` skipped the broken window entirely. - **after the sync, from the same checkout** (transformers 5.12.1 + the v0.23.0-based `e8809d49` pin): the lpv11 gap-fill (12 re-extracted WARCs, 09-01 to 09-04), WebMainBench 7,809 (09-19), the devset "lpv11 direct" reruns, classifier logprob scoring, and all ReScraper TPU runs (late Sept to 10-12): broken port. Any 10k-extraction worker relaunched after 08-13 13:54 ET would also have picked up the new lock; the tail of that run (~Aug 13-20) should be checked against the job logs. - **2026-10-13** root-caused and confirmed. Reruns on the correct path are in progress. ### Something nice we know (more easily) because of this GitHub issue log **FROM AUGUST 12th THE DAY BEFORE** So 7k WARC files were processed properly. The last 3k may be corrupted by this. All of our distillation data for the cascade came from an uncorrupted version. **I AM RUNNING SOME EXPERIMENTS NOW AND TRYING TO DETERMINE HOW SERIOUSLY THIS IMPACTS RESULTS**
> [!TIP] > A bug impacted RoPE embeddings on vllm-tpu. This only impacted us after August 13th so the damage is somewhat contained. Doing a deeper analysis of what this fully impacts. ---
Updated Ablation Plots
> [!TIP] > Better presentation of our filter and extractor ablations. ---
Investigating Filter Disagreements Artifact: https://claude.ai/artifact/6dJ1HuoXNyofFeJhbXwdbM My general sense: Although I prompted the LLM against keeping docs like this (and on average it drops them) there are edge cases where long lists make it through, and these are not high quality training docs: **ONLY LLM KEEPS** **ONLY CASCADE KEEPS** The cascade has a few of these too: Clear that the LLM noise drops some good docs that the cascade keeps: === Extraction Differences === Less clear why the rule based is better for extraction... If anything I like a lot of the LLM extractions better. Might be the hallucination problem especially for the last 3000 WARC files with the tpu-inference bug. Extractions Viewer: https://claude.ai/artifact/DvebZUJJy3w3647QzArytD
> [!TIP] > Investigated qualitatively why the cascade is better. Some clear cut cases for the filtering, but the LLM extraction really does seem better, so it is a bit odd that the cascade extraction seems so much better on downstream benchmarks after you train the model. ---

comments.body:
## Weekly Sync 10/19 - 10/23 **Agenda:** - Investigation of how RoPE impacted the LLM Data - Deduplication details - Decontamination plan - Release Plan ---
Investigation of how RoPE impacted the LLM Data Last week's worry: the last ~3k WARCs of the lpv11 10k extraction might have run with the vllm-tpu RoPE bug. **They did not. No LLM data we use was affected.** **Why:** the bug lives in tpu-inference's JAX re-implementation of Qwen3. Our Qwen3-8B extractor loads from a `gs://` checkpoint through the runai streamer, and the JAX Qwen3 port has no streaming weight loader, so vLLM's `auto` setting resolves to the PyTorch-via-torchax path, which is correct. **Only models loaded from the HF cache or local disk took the JAX path. In our work that was only ReScraper.** **Verified three ways:** - Code path and old job logs: every Qwen3-8B run used the torchax path (lpv11 10k extraction, gap-fill, WebMainBench 7,809, devset, classifier scoring). - Reruns with the implementation pinned to torchax: devset 99.8% decision agreement; WebMainBench shard 00 F1 .6400 vs .6422; 1k lpv11 pages 626/975 byte-identical, median similarity 0.994 on the rest. - Quality unchanged on the 1k rerun: major hallucinations 1.1% vs 1.6%, within judge noise (51 vs 52 flagged on identical pages); SRS 2.64 vs 2.66. **The 8M hero data runs no LLM at inference time:** it is resiliparse-rs extraction, then a fastText gate, then a ModernBERT classifier. The LLM only produced the distillation labels, and those came from the correct path.
> [!TIP] > False alarm for our data: only ReScraper (loaded from local disk) hit the bug. Every Qwen3-8B extraction ran on the correct path, which logs and reruns confirm. ---
Deduplication details | Stage | Docs | Characters | Tokens (llama3) | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Extracted (8,582,115 WARCs) | 61.21B | 341.8T | ≈80.6T | | After exact dedup | 21.84B | 133.9T | ≈31.6T | | After fuzzy dedup (hero cluster method, c075) | **9.95B** | **72.7T** | **17.15T** | Characters are exact at every stage. The final token count is measured; the first two use the final corpus's 4.239 chars/token. - **17.15T llama3 tokens** (72.7T chars, 26.5 TB). The refit after the 2M run projected 16.9T (15.7–18.9T); the projections made at 500k (21.8–25.0T) were too high. - 64% of extracted records were exact duplicates, confirmed to be the same pages recrawled across crawls. - By source: **CC-MAIN 16.68T**, **CC-NEWS 0.21T** (tagged `CC-NEWS-YYYY-MM`, so it can be mixed separately), **CC-SUPPLEMENTAL 7.8B**. - Random-sample viewer: https://claude.ai/artifact/9Wp8sdhFwC7xmRqz74ddpx
> [!TIP] > Dedup is done: **17.15T tokens** from 8.58M WARCs, in line with the post-2M projection. The hero run used ~25T. ---
Decontamination plan Full walkthrough with examples: https://claude.ai/artifact/FPrunN93nfrApC6j4hcgSN **How Marin's decon works.** Take the test questions and answers from every benchmark we report (the 9 Artificial Analysis benchmarks plus the lm-eval tasks in Marin's eval suite). Split each training doc into paragraphs. If at least half of a paragraph's 13-word runs also appear in the eval text, the doc is removed. Phrases that are common all over the web are ignored, so boilerplate can't trigger a removal. The version the hero run used (v3) adds one more check for short paragraphs (3–12 words), which are too short to contain a 13-word run: a short paragraph that exactly matches a short line from the evals also removes the doc. That check is meant to catch short eval answers, but it also matches ordinary lines like "2 years ago" or "Lana Del Rey". Marin changed this after the hero run (v4, PR #8327, Sept 24): a paragraph now needs at least two different eval phrases in it to count, so a single short line can't remove a doc by itself. **Where we are.** Every doc in the pool has been checked. Picking a rule now just means one ~3 h filter run, then an ~18 h re-tokenize. **Tokens each rule would remove** (estimated from a 24k-doc audit sample): | Rule | Eval set | Docs removed | Tokens removed | |---|---|---:|---:| | v3 (hero run's rule) | hero's + 118 tasks the hero failed to load | ~11M | ~87B (0.5%) | | v3 (hero run's rule) | hero's | ~5M | ~40B (0.23%) | | v4 (Marin `main` today) | hero's + 118 tasks | ~0.46M | ~8B (0.05%) | The two v3 numbers will drop somewhat: I'm re-running the boilerplate count with the hero's sample size (1M docs per crawl; my first pass used ~80k). **Problems with the hero run's decon:** 1. **gsm8k was probably never checked.** 118 of the lm-eval tasks, including gsm8k, truthfulqa, winogrande, boolq and triviaqa, failed to load in the hero's eval set because their old dataset names break with the `datasets` version the hero branch uses. The pipeline skips tasks that fail to load instead of stopping. This is based on the eval set's manifest in us-central2. **Not yet checked against the CoreWeave copy that production actually used.** 2. **The short-line check mostly removes harmless pages.** On our data, ~95% of v3 removals come from a single short line like "2 years ago" or "Mechanism of Action", and none of the 40 I read by hand were contamination. Our extracted text has lots of standalone short lines (96% of docs have one, against 25–77% in Nemotron-CC), so this hits us harder than it hit the hero data. v4 fixes the second problem. On the audit sample it still caught every real overlap we found (SQuAD passages, wikiHow/HellaSwag, MATH problems, paper abstracts) and only let through stray short phrases and two generic LSAT question stems. **Decisions:** 1. **Eval set:** add the 118 tasks the hero missed? 2. **Rule:** v3 (~87B tokens, mostly harmless pages) or v4 (~8B tokens, same real catches)? 3. **ACTION ITEM:** Check with Will about the potential GSM8K gap in decontamination
> [!TIP] > Every doc has been checked against the evals. The hero run's rule (v3) would remove ~87B tokens, mostly harmless pages; Marin's current rule (v4) removes ~8B with the same real catches. The hero run also perhaps checked 117 fewer tasks. ---
Release Plan **Need to run the embedding and scaling ladder**: Reached out to Will to discuss this. I have all my data in `us-central2` ready to run a scaling ladder! Just want to figure out pointers on what to run and if I need to do control against Nemotron or if that has already been run somewhere. **Otherwise after decontamination the data is ready to go!**
> [!TIP] > After decontamination we are ready to release! ---

issues.author: yonromai
issues.body:
Megatron training checkpoints save BF16 model weights alongside FP32 master weights and optimizer state. Rebuilding the BF16 weights on restore could save:

- **Snowball (67B, AdamW): estimated ~939 GB → ~805 GB**, saving ~134 GB per checkpoint (14%).
- **Hero (535B, MuonH): measured 5.36 TB → estimated ~4.29 TB**, saving ~1.07 TB per checkpoint (20%).

[Levanter already saves weights once in FP32 and casts them to BF16 for computation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/332b6bf2fdff80522c3807802edc927274e0a9bc/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L245-L251).

For Megatron, save FP32 master weights, optimizer state, and any model tensors that cannot be reconstructed. Rebuild BF16 weights when loading, while keeping the existing runtime layout. The storage saving and resumed-training equivalence remain untested.

<details>
<summary>Evidence and source pointers</summary>

Sizes were measured from CoreWeave object listings on October 13, 2026, using decimal TB:

- **Hero MuonH checkpoint:** 5,362,025,577,137 bytes at `s3://hero-checkpoints/marin/users/romain/hero-final-860-gpu-01a0e406/muonh-seed-a2/checkpoints/global_step_2/`. Its metadata contains BF16 model tensors and FP32 optimizer master weights.
- **Hero BF16 export:** 1,070,969,346,522 bytes at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-vllm-rl/hero-535b-step144000-bf16-split-v1/`.
- **Snowball BF16 export:** 134,175,089,690 bytes at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/exports/grug/june-67b-a2b/step-42150/hf-bf16-vllm/d819cbc63780bd86/`. Its index records 134,157,765,632 bytes of model tensors.

The savings estimates use the size of one BF16 weight copy. Exact removable bytes have not been measured.

Snowball's total Megatron sizes are estimates, not object-listing measurements. With the [default AdamW configuration](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/c0dbe0f21a31d08b05e071c0344af74969c8055b/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/config/ppo_base_config.yaml#L126-L135), standard checkpoint state uses approximately 14 bytes per parameter: BF16 weights (2), FP32 master weights (4), and two FP32 optimizer moments (8). Omitting BF16 reduces this to 12 bytes. Applied to the measured 134 GB BF16 weight copy, that gives ~939 GB → ~805 GB. Extra checkpoint state, padding, and any duplication can change the actual totals.

Native Levanter checkpoints measured **539 GB for Snowball** and **4.29 TB for Hero** at these paths:

- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step39k-79ebf3/checkpoints/step-42150/`
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-main-step121638/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-144000/`

These are separate training runs with different optimizer recipes, not before/after measurements of a smaller Megatron format.

The [checkpoint writer](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/c0dbe0f21a31d08b05e071c0344af74969c8055b/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/distributed/megatron/megatron_strategy.py#L209-L216) saves model and optimizer state separately. Snowball uses the same machinery.

[NVIDIA's optimizer guide](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/blob/main/docs/user-guide/features/dist_optimizer.md#key-steps) describes casting updated FP32 master weights into BF16 working weights.

Related: [#403 tracks checkpoint save latency](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/issues/403).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design rationale and upstream findings (October 13, 2026)</summary>

**This is a storage optimization, not a demonstrated correctness bug.**

- **Shared backend, not universal behavior.** The inspected full-training Megatron paths in [SkyRL](https://github.com/NovaSky-AI/SkyRL/blob/a1e34dbf21003f66bd7921487fd47db6c154aba2/skyrl/backends/skyrl_train/distributed/megatron/megatron_strategy.py#L346-L358), [verl](https://github.com/verl-project/verl/blob/76e837e0bfcb18b380a66c0ba56ef9f0ac840f09/verl/utils/checkpoint/megatron_checkpoint_manager.py#L1203-L1248), and [NeMo RL](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/RL/blob/9406968a6951ec6f42c13e4d063a32483738977b/nemo_rl/models/policy/workers/megatron_policy_worker.py#L4688-L4786) save model and optimizer state using NVIDIA machinery. Actual contents depend on optimizer precision and configuration.
- **Separate uses are intentional.** Model weights can be loaded without optimizer state for inference or fresh training. FP32 master weights and optimizer state preserve precise training continuation. [Verl's guide](https://verl.readthedocs.io/en/latest/advance/checkpoint.html) explicitly distinguishes resumable checkpoints from deployment-only exports.
- **The original PR states the format choice.** [SkyRL #298](https://github.com/NovaSky-AI/SkyRL/pull/298) adopts Megatron checkpointing for parallel writes and restoration under different sharding. It does not compare saving both weight representations with reconstructing BF16.
- **Compatibility has value.** [NVIDIA's guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/checkpointing.html#limitations) warns that custom formats are not supported by some standard conversion and inference utilities. A compact format would need an adapted loading/export path.

**Search limit:** No inspected original discussion explicitly weighs the extra BF16 storage against reconstruction. That absence does not establish an accidental design, nor does the supported format prove both copies are numerically necessary.

</details>

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`MegatronStrategy.save_checkpoint()` writes the model and optimizer sharded states into one training checkpoint; the issue's metadata shows BF16 model tensors alongside FP32 masters, but the exact mapping and removable bytes still need measurement. Restore requests the model tree before loading the optimizer, and HF export calls that loader with `load_training_state=False`; omitting model tensors at save time alone would break both paths. Open [MarinSkyRL #769](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/769) changes the same save, load, and export files while keeping checkpoint contents unchanged.

**Relevant code**
- [`megatron_strategy.py#L332-L355`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/distributed/megatron/megatron_strategy.py#L332-L355) — builds the saved state tree.
- [`megatron_strategy.py#L426-L483`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/distributed/megatron/megatron_strategy.py#L426-L483) — restores model before optimizer.
- [`checkpoint_exporter.py#L91-L101`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/checkpoint_exporter.py#L91-L101) — loads model without training state.
- [`test_save_load_checkpoint.py#L54-L145`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/tests/gpu/gpu_ci/test_save_load_checkpoint.py#L54-L145) — existing four-GPU continuation test.

# Compact Megatron checkpoint design

The target is a resumable training checkpoint that stores each reconstructible BF16 parameter once, as its FP32 optimizer master. The estimated 14% Snowball and 20% Hero reductions in the issue remain hypotheses until a matched save measures actual bytes.

## Challenges and risks

The optimizer state layout differs between AdamW and MuonH, and not every model tensor necessarily has an FP32 master. A compact checkpoint also has to serve model-only HF export without reading every optimizer moment. Restoring BF16 from a master could expose a save-boundary mismatch, a layout error under resharding, or extra restore memory.

## Design and sequence

1. After #769 lands, inventory model keys, dtypes, shapes, and optimizer-master keys in small Snowball/AdamW and Hero/MuonH checkpoints. Compare each candidate BF16 tensor with the cast of its corresponding FP32 master at the save boundary. Keep every tensor without a verified mapping, including buffers and optimizer-independent model state.
2. Add a versioned compact-format marker and the omitted-key mapping to checkpoint metadata. Apply omission only to full training saves with the required optimizer masters. Existing full checkpoints and explicit model-only checkpoints keep their current layout.
3. For compact restores, load the FP32 masters and retained model tensors, reconstruct BF16 parameters through the Megatron master-to-model copy path, then restore optimizer, scheduler, RNG, and client state. Extend the model-only export loader to read the needed master shards and reconstruct weights without materializing optimizer moments. Preserve the existing runtime tensor layout and report a missing master as an error.
4. Extend the tests on #769's final code. The GPU save/load test should assert omitted keys, exact reconstructed BF16 values, and exact next-step logits for both optimizer sharding modes. Add fresh-process continuation for AdamW and MuonH, legacy full-checkpoint loading, model-only HF export, and a changed-sharding restore where the optimizer format supports it. Compare checkpoint bytes, save pause, restore time, and peak memory against the same model/configuration using the full format before enabling compact saves for production runs.

## Open questions

- Do Snowball AdamW and Hero MuonH expose a stable FP32 master for every BF16 parameter at the checkpoint barrier? The inventory and exact cast comparison decide which keys can be omitted.
- Can the current distributed checkpoint reader project only master shards for HF export? If it cannot, the loader needs a targeted read path before compact checkpoints are usable by export.

Final results and the full ledger: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6076348127 (ledger also at https://gist.github.com/karansag/0ce1a07580bd430bc8c5b890069385b0). ## TL;DR (final, 2026-10-09). ** Given **one expert E** ([open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`)) built from the Snowball student B ([open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab)) by SFT on [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) CruxEval traces, three methods were used to transfer E's gain back into B: * plain SFT on E's traces * SFT on rejection-sampled E traces (RS-SFT) * on-policy distillation from E (OPD). served as `glm-5.3` through the internal glm53 relay, reasoning effort high) | 94.0 | 90.5 | — | — | — | — | | E (expert; B + SFT on GLM traces, step 272; [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`)) | 79.4 | 71.4 | 100% | 92.1 | 92.2 | 35.9 | | Plain SFT on E demos, 400 updates (final; 376.4 full run; +14–15 per HF export | ## Models Student B = [`open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab) (Hugging Face commit; the repo received a later commit on 2026-10-13, so the pin matters). E = B after full SFT on 1,454 execution-correct [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) CruxEval traces (trace collection: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/glm-bench-traces/`) (LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, 272 updates, 32 H100, fresh optimizer state, frozen router biases), export [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`). E keeps B's tokenizer and chat template. E+ (E + 2 epochs at LR 1e-6; 80.2 / 75.1) was built as a separate reference and is not an arm. Every arm starts from B. ## Benchmark CruxEval (800 Python functions; input prediction and output prediction scored separately by executing the assertion). MATH500 was dropped as the target because B already scores 89.8% there; GSM8K and MATH500 are the collapse checks. Teacher gate: B 55.4 / 57.8; GLM 5.3 on the identical 1,600 prompts 94.0 / 90.5; E 79.4 / 71.4 (two-pass mean), passing the gate of B + 10 points on both tasks with no GSM8K drop. ## Frozen evaluator Marin `experiments.evaluation.cli launch` with Evalchemy [`ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8), vLLM on H100x8 (DP8 + EP8), `max_model_len` 32768, `max_gen_toks` 30720, `enable_thinking: true`, reasoning parser `grug`. Configs and pitfalls: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71. Evalchemy's chat client sends no temperature, top_p or seed, and B's `generation_config.json` sets none, so every run samples at vLLM's default (temperature 1.0, unseeded). One pass on 800 problems has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp; selected checkpoints get two passes. **Arms as run (all from B; AdamW LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen; 4 epochs over the 1,600 prompts; one checkpoint per epoch).** - E demos: 8 samples per prompt from E at temperature 1.0, both directions, execution-graded in an isolated container (12,800 samples, 14.6 H100-h, shared by both SFT arms). - Plain SFT: E's first sample per prompt, correct or not (1,600 rows; 1.45M supervised tokens per epoch; batch 16; Levanter, 32 H100). - RS-SFT: first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows; 97 prompts with no correct sample stay in the eval denominator; 1.06M supervised tokens per epoch; Levanter, 32 H100). - OPD: [MarinSkyRL](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL), 4 on-policy rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E as the teacher (sampled reverse KL on chosen tokens, no verifier), 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch; 4 learner + 1 rollout + 1 teacher H100x8 nodes (Megatron). - Selection: the final checkpoint when it is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions, otherwise a second pass on both and the two-pass means decide. Plain SFT selected its final checkpoint (400 updates); RS-SFT (283 of 376) and OPD (75 of 100) selected their epoch-3 checkpoints after their finals dropped on one direction. ## Artifacts Trace browser (GLM, E, E+ traces, side-by-side compare): https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/072c90b0-281e-4692-a4bf-845874c021b1/. OPD W&B: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/skyrl/runs/p3ie2bg7. Selected exports: plain [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Plain-SFT-Step399 @ 3e34be3f](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Plain-SFT-Step399/tree/3e34be3f884ff737f85354b060ea831ce0c90636) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-plain-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-399`), RS-SFT [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-RS-SFT-Step282 @ 073d128c](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-RS-SFT-Step282/tree/073d128cb1e53652126cce37a7cc2c96625d3c80) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-rs-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-282`), OPD [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-OPD-Step75 @ 9d189320](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-OPD-Step75/tree/9d1893207226cf72f701187e1d5260d9fc3c931d) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/karan/skyrl/snowball-opd-cruxeval-e-2/exports/global_step_75/policy`). Eval records: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals//record.json` (every record id is in the final comment's ledger). GPU-hour method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298. ## Not in scope Weight merging (needs RL-trained experts that share B's init; none exist) and transfer from the older Snowball experts (none beats B under the matched eval). ## Decision log - 2026-10-06: matched eval of B and the existing experts (E6, E17a, E18, SWE, Stage-3) on MATH500/GSM8K; none beats B, so no promotion to teacher. - 2026-10-07: MATH500 near ceiling for B → CruxEval chosen; MMLU-Pro (B 44.1) and GPQA-D (B 41.9) measured as fallbacks and not used. - 2026-10-07: full SFT over LoRA for building E; LoRA kept as the fallback if full SFT collapses out-of-domain. - 2026-10-07: rejection-sampled SFT added as a third arm. - 2026-10-08: E frozen at step 272 for every arm; E+ built as a separate reference only. Arms changed from the plan: one sample per prompt for both SFT arms (not up to 4), no LR sweep, 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD. The arms ran in parallel on Iris. - 2026-10-09: RS-SFT and OPD final checkpoints not selected (drops on one direction with paired CI excluding 0); epoch-3 checkpoints selected on two-pass means. comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Teacher training and three transfer arms make this a gated experiment. As of 23:29 UTC, the owner has submitted the W&B-corrected teacher retry; startup, optimizer progress, and export remain unconfirmed ([latest status](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6048938002)). No open PR targets #9920, while the owner is already preparing the recipe on `task/133`; the earlier coding-teacher spike [#9528](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9528) ended without a usable MOPD transfer result.

**Relevant code**
- [`experiments/sft/launcher.py#L494`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L494) — shared SFT specification and training setup
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L150`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L150) — versioned SkyRL experiment and export contract
- [`experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147) — shared evaluation launch path

# Proposed Fix

1. Follow the submitted teacher retry through a completed update, full training, and verified HF exports. Evaluate the planned exports with the frozen CruxEval/GSM8K configuration. Stop the transfer arms unless E clears the stated +10-point gate on both CruxEval directions without a GSM8K drop beyond noise.
2. Pin E, B, prompt IDs, tokenizer/template, grader, evaluator, and one eight-sample-per-prompt teacher generation artifact. Build unfiltered SFT from samples 1–4 and rejection-sampled SFT from up to four execution-correct samples. Record missing-correct-sample prompts, actual supervised tokens, and teacher-generation GPU-hours; a matched prompt set alone does not equalize training tokens.
3. Start OPD from the same B and prompts. Check teacher/student token-score alignment and one update plus export before the full run. Match the planned sweep and student update budget across arms, and record teacher-scoring GPU-hours separately.
4. Evaluate every selected arm twice with the same pinned evaluator on CruxEval input, CruxEval output, and GSM8K. Report each arm's accuracy, `(arm − B) / (E − B)` per direction, run-to-run spread, prompts and tokens consumed, and total GPU-hours. Label gains as transfer on the trained test prompts; this protocol cannot establish held-out generalization.

comments.body:
🤖 Final results: SFT vs rejection-sampled SFT vs on-policy distillation for transferring the CruxEval expert back into B

TL;DR. All three arms recover most or all of the expert's CruxEval gain. Every arm trains on prompts drawn from the same 1,600 the evaluator scores (800 input-prediction and 800 output-prediction problems; plain SFT and OPD use all 1,600, RS-SFT the 1,503 with an execution-correct E sample), so this is transfer on seen prompts. Two-pass means on the selected checkpoints: plain SFT 73.9 / 72.0 (400 updates), RS-SFT 80.8 / 77.9 (283 updates), OPD 79.6 / 75.2 (75 updates); the expert E scores 79.4 / 71.4 and B scores 55.4 / 57.8 (CruxEval input / output, pass@1 on 800 problems each). RS-SFT's two-pass means are 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD's; two passes on one run per arm do not resolve that ordering. Both are above plain SFT by 5.7–6.9 pp on input and 3.2–5.9 pp on output. Training cost: OPD 287 H100-h from allocation to the selected checkpoint (376 for the full 4-epoch run); plain SFT 62 and RS-SFT 57 for their full 4-epoch runs (the RS candidate is update 283 of 376 and was not timed separately). RS-SFT also used ground-truth execution results to pick its demos, which the other arms did not have. No arm dropped below B on GSM8K (B 90.4) or MATH500 (B 89.8); OPD 75 scores 90.4 on MATH500, 1.8 below E, inside MATH500's binomial 95% half-width of about 2.6 pp at n=500. These numbers do not measure generalization to unseen prompts.

Setup (the design doc is linked from the issue body).

- Student B: [`open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab).
- Expert E: B after full SFT on 1,454 [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) CruxEval traces, LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, step 272 (35.9 H100-h); export [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`). E+ (E + 2 epochs at 1e-6, 80.2 / 75.1) is a reference only.
- Evaluator: Evalchemy [ae362881](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8) (corrected 2026-10-13: the revision that actually ran is `ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8`, recorded in every record's `eval_runtime` field; `c131e5ab` was the code constant in `eval_policy.py`, which the launcher did not use. The scorer and sampling settings are the ones at ae362881 throughout, so no number changes.), vLLM H100x8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap, thinking enabled, unseeded sampling at vLLM's default temperature 1.0 (the lm-eval chat client sends no sampling parameters). One pass has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp at n=800 (p≈0.55) and 3.0 pp at p≈0.75. Paired deltas use a problem-resampling bootstrap conditional on the sampled completions. Gist of all evaluator configs: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71.
- Matched AdamW hyperparameters across arms, in different implementations (Levanter for the SFT arms, Megatron for OPD): LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen (E froze it too; all exports verified to carry B's 26 router-bias tensors).
- Plain SFT: B + 4 epochs on E's first sample per prompt (1,600 rows, unfiltered), batch 16, 32 H100. 1,452,363 supervised tokens per epoch.
- RS-SFT: all 12,800 E samples (k=8) execution-graded in an isolated container; first correct sample per prompt kept. 1,503 of 1,600 prompts covered (774 input / 729 output); the 97 uncovered prompts stay in the eval denominator. 4 epochs, 376 updates. 1,056,479 supervised tokens per epoch.
- OPD: MarinSkyRL, B samples 4 rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E scores them (sampled reverse KL on the chosen tokens, coefficient 1.0, reward replaced by the distillation signal, no verifier). 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch, 4 epochs. 4 learner nodes (PP2 × EP8) + 1 rollout node + 1 teacher node, all H100x8.
- Selection procedure used (the rule 'prefer the final checkpoint when similar or better on both directions' was agreed before the final checkpoints were scored; the operational reading of similar as 'paired 95% CI includes 0' was fixed while applying it): if the final checkpoint is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions on the first pass, select it; otherwise run a second pass on both checkpoints and choose on the two-pass means. GSM8K and MATH500 run on the selected checkpoint and on any terminal checkpoint that lost the selection.

Results. CruxEval pass@1 (%), input / output. "Gap closed" is the gain over B divided by E's two-pass gain over B (24.06 pp input, 13.63 pp output). GSM8K (flexible-extract, 0-shot) and MATH500 are single pass for every model.

| Model | Input | Output | Gap closed | GSM8K | MATH500 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B | 55.4 | 57.8 | 0 | 90.4 | 89.8 |
| E (CruxEval 2-pass mean) | 79.4 | 71.4 | 100% | 92.1 | 92.2 |
| GLM 5.3 (teacher of E) | 94.0 | 90.5 | — | — | — |
| Plain SFT, 400 updates (2-pass mean) | 73.9 | 72.0 | 77% / 104% | 94.0 | 92.6 |
| RS-SFT, 283 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 80.8 | 77.9 | 106% / 148% | 93.5 | 93.6 |
| OPD, 75 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 79.6 | 75.2 | 101% / 128% | 92.5 | 90.4 |

Learning curves (single pass per checkpoint; the training trajectory, not the selection basis):

| Arm | Epoch 1 | Epoch 2 | Epoch 3 | Epoch 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plain SFT (101/201/301/400 updates) | 69.6 / 67.5 | 73.5 / 69.9 | 69.4 / 71.8 | 74.8 / 71.3 |
| RS-SFT (95/189/283/376 updates) | 75.5 / 72.0 | 82.0 / 75.8 | 81.4 / 77.1 | 77.0 / 76.5 |
| OPD (25/50/75/100 updates) | 74.9 / 68.9 | 81.8 / 75.8 | 79.0 / 76.8 | 80.9 / 72.3 |

Selection. Plain SFT's final checkpoint was similar or better than its epoch-3 checkpoint on both directions (+5.4 / −0.5 pp), so it was selected and repeated (second pass 73.1 / 72.8). RS-SFT's final checkpoint was 4.4 pp below epoch 3 on input, and OPD's final checkpoint was 4.5 pp below epoch 3 on output, each with a paired CI excluding 0. Both arms got a second pass on their last two checkpoints. RS-SFT: 376 updates 76.1 / 76.2 against 283 updates 80.8 / 77.9 (two-pass means); the final is lower on both directions, so 283 was selected. OPD: 100 updates 79.875 / 72.0 against 75 updates 79.625 / 75.19; input differs by 0.25 pp and the final is 3.19 pp lower on output, so 75 was selected. The terminal checkpoints are reported in the curve table, not as the method result. The second passes reuse the same runs, so the four pass pairings per arm are one comparison, not four. Same-checkpoint pass pairs moved by up to 3.1 pp (OPD 75 output: 76.75 on pass 1, 73.6 on pass 2, paired CI [−6.0, −0.25]), so the conditional problem-bootstrap intervals do not capture all generation variability; two repeats are too few to estimate it. The final-checkpoint drops are therefore suggestive, not established.

Paired comparisons at the selected checkpoints (pass 1 vs pass 1; 95% bootstrap CI): RS-SFT 283 vs OPD 75: +2.4 [−1.0, +5.8] input / +0.4 [−2.5, +3.3] output on pass 1, and 0.0 [−3.4, +3.3] / +5.0 [+2.0, +8.0] on pass 2. RS-SFT 283 vs plain 400: +6.6 [+3.1, +10.1] / +5.9 [+2.8, +9.3] (pass 2: +7.1 / +5.9). OPD 75 vs plain 400: +4.3 [+0.9, +7.9] / +5.5 [+2.3, +8.8] (pass 2: +7.1 / +0.9 [−2.3, +4.0]). Against E (pass 1): RS-SFT 283 +2.0 [−1.5, +5.5] / +6.9 [+3.8, +10.1]; OPD 75 −0.4 [−3.8, +3.0] / +6.5 [+3.5, +9.5]; plain 400 −4.6 [−8.4, −1.0] / +1.0 [−2.4, +4.5]. Pass-1 and pass-2 pairings share the training runs; they are two draws of the evaluator, not two experiments.

Response shape: B leaves no final answer after the thinking block in 1,110 of 1,600 CruxEval responses; E in about 90. The same count was not made for the three arms, so part of each arm's gain may be this shape change. The 97 prompts with no execution-correct E sample among 8 (26 input, 71 output) score low for every model. Correct/n on pass 1 and pass 2: B 1/26, 1/71; E 2/26, 1/71 and 1/26, 4/71; plain 400 0/26, 3/71 and 0/26, 4/71; RS-SFT 283 4/26, 8/71 and 4/26, 9/71; OPD 75 3/26, 6/71 and 2/26, 2/71. The slice was selected by E failing all 8 samples on these prompts, so E's low score is selection-induced. RS-SFT saw no demos for these prompts. Comparing different methods on 97 selected prompts does not identify the effect of omitting them, so these are counts only.

Cost (H100-hours, Iris task-runtime accounting). Training figures are full-run costs for 4 epochs and include in-gang startup, native saves and exports; they exclude CPU preprocessing, demo generation and evals. The selected RS-SFT checkpoint is update 283 of 376 and the selected OPD checkpoint is update 75 of 100; costs are not pro-rated to the candidate. OPD's allocation-to-checkpoint figure comes from the run's log timestamps and ends at the checkpoint request, so it excludes the native save; plain SFT's 61.6 runs through its final HF export and job teardown. The two selected-cost endpoints are therefore not identical.

| Arm | Training (full 4-epoch run) | Demo generation | Exports | Allocation to selected checkpoint |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E (expert) | 35.9 for 3 epochs (+15.3 in aborted attempts) | GLM traces via relay, no GPU-h on our side | in-gang | — |
| Plain SFT | 61.6 | shares the one k=8 E collection (14.6 measured once for all 12,800 demos, plus a 0.7 pilot; plain used 1 of the 8 samples, and no standalone 1-sample generation run was timed) | in-gang | 61.6 (final checkpoint selected) |
| RS-SFT | 57.4 | the same k=8 E collection (14.6, counted once for both SFT arms) + CPU execution grading | in-gang | full run 57.4; update 283 was not timed separately |
| OPD | 376.4 (6 nodes × 7h50m) | none (on-policy) | 58.8 (4 export-only jobs, 14–15 each) | 286.9 from allocation start to the update-75 checkpoint request (before the native save completes), plus its 14.2 export job |

OPD also spent 73.5 H100-h on smoke tests, debugging and the export path and 4.6 on a startup failure (missing W&B key) before the full run. These training-only figures are not the experiment total; the ledger adds evaluation (about 3.3 per CruxEval pass), failed-eval overhead, E and E+ training, and the reference runs. OPD per-update wall time was 4–5 min (256 sampled responses, 30,720-token cap) against about 17 s per SFT update; one prompt epoch is 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD and 1 demo for SFT, so epochs are matched on prompts, not on tokens or compute. One CruxEval pass costs about 3.3 H100-h; the ledger lists every eval run. Failed eval groups (serve preemption with a stale endpoint in the eval runner, and one preflight disconnect; see below) cost about 11 H100-h.

Confidence. The gains over B are large relative to noise (the lower 95% bound of every arm's paired gain over B is at least 9.8 pp). Between arms, the measured two-pass means put RS-SFT 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD and both 3–7 pp above plain SFT; each arm is one training run with no LR sweep, same-checkpoint pass pairs moved 0.5–3.1 pp on the six repeated checkpoints, and two repeats do not estimate run-to-run variance, so the RS-SFT vs OPD ordering is unresolved and the gap to plain SFT is the better-supported difference. The last-checkpoint drops in RS-SFT (input) and OPD (output) are each supported by two passes but one training run; see the selection paragraph for the statistical limits.

Deviations from the plan in the issue body.

- Plain SFT used one sample per prompt (E's sample 0, 1,600 rows), and RS-SFT used the first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows), instead of up to 4 samples per prompt. Uncovered prompts stayed in the eval denominator.
- No LR or epoch sweep was run for any arm; every arm used LR 1e-6 and 4 epochs, with per-epoch checkpoints as the only sweep.
- OPD used 4 rollouts per prompt, so its prompt epochs are not token- or compute-matched to the SFT arms.
- GSM8K and MATH500 are both reported as collapse checks (the plan named GSM8K only).

Material failures and fixes.

- Levanter could not HF-export from an S3 reference checkpoint; fixed by plumbing `hf_save_reference_code=False`.
- MarinSkyRL accepted teachers only as HF repo ids; added staging of the teacher from S3. The export-only job's config inherited the run's distillation objective, which requires a teacher the export job does not start, so the export failed at config validation; the fix drops the distillation block from the export config. Learner nodes ran out of host memory at checkpoint save with 512 GB; the full run reserved 1024 GB.
- MarinSkyRL does not convert checkpoints to HF format during training; it writes a small export request per checkpoint, and the conversion is a separate 4-node export-only job (about 14–15 H100-h each).
- The Marin eval runner keeps the serve address it first resolved. When the serve job is preempted and re-registers on another host, the eval loops on connection errors until its timeout. Two RS eval groups were lost this way and relaunched as fresh groups; no partial outputs were reused. Not fixed yet.
- Evalchemy sends no temperature or seed, so every run samples at vLLM's default. One GSM8K run failed Evalchemy's preflight request 9 s after the serve registered (server disconnected); relaunched alone, it passed.
- GPQA-D (41.9%, needs an HF token and a 28,672-token generation cap) and MMLU-Pro (44.1%) were measured on B while choosing the benchmark, as fallbacks in case CruxEval failed the teacher gate; they were not used further.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖

## Weight deltas against the student

A reader asked what the weight changes behind these transfers look like. Table and method below; numbers are percentages.

| Model (vs student B) | ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ all, % | attention % | expert MLPs % | shared expert % | router % | LM head % | weights changed, % | cos(Δ, Δ_expert) all | attention | expert MLPs | LM head |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expert E (CruxEval SFT, LR 1e-5, 3 ep) | 0.036 | 0.65 | 0.047 | 0.069 | 0.17 | 0.13 | 13.7 | — | — | — | — |
| Plain SFT step 399 | 0.123 | 0.30 | 0.27 | 0.31 | 0.022 | 0.41 | 41.2 | 0.05 | 0.08 | 0.05 | 0.68 |
| RS-SFT step 282 | 0.094 | 0.24 | 0.21 | 0.25 | 0.015 | 0.34 | 34.5 | 0.06 | 0.09 | 0.07 | 0.71 |
| OPD update 75 | 0.035 | 0.12 | 0.077 | 0.12 | 0.006 | 0.060 | 20.3 | 0.08 | 0.12 | 0.12 | −0.32 |

Reading:
- Everything is a small perturbation: no checkpoint moves more than 0.13% of B's weight norm overall, and the largest component change is the expert's attention at 0.65%.
- The expert (LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, 1,454 rows) concentrates its change in attention, the router and the LM head and leaves the MoE expert MLPs almost untouched (0.047%, 13% of weights changed). The two SFT transfer arms (LR 1e-6, 4 epochs, 1,500–1,600 rows of the expert's text) do the opposite: they move the expert MLPs 4–6× more than the expert did and touch 35–41% of all weights. OPD moves least of the three arms (0.035% overall, comparable to the expert) and touches 20%.
- Direction: none of the arms re-creates the expert's weight change. The cosines between an arm's delta and E's delta are 0.05–0.12 in attention and the expert MLPs (random directions in this dimension give ≈0). The one shared direction is the LM head, where plain SFT and RS-SFT align with E (cosine 0.68 and 0.71) while OPD moves the LM head the opposite way (−0.32). Recovering the expert's CruxEval score therefore does not require copying its weights; three different weight changes produce it.
- RS-SFT changes the weights less than plain SFT (0.094% vs 0.123% overall) while scoring higher; it trains on fewer, verifier-correct rows.

Method: every tensor of each checkpoint was compared with the student B (open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5) in float32 after widening the bf16 exports; ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ is the relative Frobenius norm over all 67.1 B weights or over one component (attention q/k/v/o and attention gates; the 26 layers' fused MoE expert MLPs, 65.4 B weights; shared experts; router weights and biases; embeddings; LM head), 'weights changed' is the share of scalars whose bf16 value differs from B's, and cos(Δ, Δ_expert) is the cosine between the checkpoint's delta and the expert's delta over the same weights. Embeddings and norms are omitted from the table (relative change ≤ 0.01% everywhere). Caveat: the exports are bf16, so training-time changes below half a bf16 ulp of a weight are invisible; magnitudes and 'weights changed' are lower bounds, and the cosines are computed only on what survived rounding. Script `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_stats.py` (eval worktree); per-tensor results at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/review/wdelta-<model>.json`, all summaries in `wdelta-all-summaries.json`.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Weight-delta direction for this experiment: does the OPD update point the same way as the expert update? Same method as the #9984 follow-up.

## Method

Deltas against the student B (`Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ fdc3c3c5) for expert E (step 272) and the three selected checkpoints: OPD update 75, plain SFT step 399, RS-SFT step 282. Per component: the Frobenius norm of each delta (absolute and relative to B), cosine with E's delta, sign agreement on weights changed in both, and subspace overlap. Overlap is the share of a delta's energy inside E's top-k singular directions per matrix, with k holding 50% of E's energy, compared with a random k-dim subspace and with E's delta permuted within each matrix. E's norms reproduce the earlier weight-delta table exactly. Script: `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_subspace.py` on branch `task/239` (711ba609ae).

## Result

All weights, against E:

| Delta | ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ | weights changed | cos vs E | sign agree | overlap (random) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expert E | 0.0366% | 13.7% | — | — | — |
| OPD update 75 | 0.0355% | 20.3% | 0.079 | 0.598 | 0.203 (0.101) |
| RS-SFT step 282 | 0.0938% | 34.5% | 0.058 | 0.581 | 0.196 (0.108) |
| Plain SFT step 399 | 0.1236% | 41.2% | 0.045 | 0.562 | 0.184 (0.108) |

Overlap with E's half-energy subspace, as a multiple of the random null:

| Component | OPD 75 | RS-SFT 282 | plain SFT 399 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attention | 3.9× | 3.0× | 2.7× |
| Expert MLPs | 1.9× | 1.7× | 1.6× |
| Shared experts | 4.0× | 2.6× | 2.2× |
| Router | 3.7× | 2.2× | 2.1× |
| LM head | 391× | 710× | 686× |

## Reading

- **Same pattern as #9984, and stronger.** OPD shares direction with E more than either SFT arm in attention, expert MLPs, shared experts and over all weights. It is also more aligned than the MOPD update was there (all-weights cosine 0.079 vs 0.049).
- **Size.** OPD moves the weights about as much as E did (0.036% of ‖B‖). The SFT arms move them 2.6–3.4× more, mostly in the expert MLPs (0.20–0.27% vs E's 0.05%).
- **Router.** OPD leaves the router almost untouched (0.006% of its norm, against E's 0.17%). Its router cosine with E equals the SFT arms' (0.15 vs 0.14–0.15); only its sign agreement and overlap are higher.
- **LM head.** The SFT arms align strongly with E (cosine 0.68–0.71). OPD moves inside the same few top directions but with the opposite sign (cosine −0.32, sign agreement 0.26). MOPD showed the same flip in #9984 (−0.14), so it repeats across both experiments.
- **Small shared part.** 0.6% of OPD's update energy lies along E's delta, and 20% sits inside E's half-energy subspace against 10% at random. The transfer is mostly a different weight change that reaches the same behaviour.

## Limits

Correlational geometry only, with no ablation, so no causal claim about the scores. OPD 75 is the selected mid-run checkpoint, not the final update 100. The SFT arms train on E's own samples in one domain, which raises their alignment with E. bf16 exports hide changes below half an ulp, so every measure covers only what survived rounding.

🤖 Efficiency view: CruxEval score against GPU-hours and trained tokens, per checkpoint.

| Arm, checkpoint (updates) | H100-h | trained tokens | input / output |
|---|---|---|---|
| B (start) | 0 | 0 | 55.4 / 57.75 |
| Plain SFT 101 / 201 / 301 / 400 | 30.2 / 45.6 / 61.0 / 76.2 | 1.5 / 2.9 / 4.4 / 5.8M | 69.6 / 67.5; 73.5 / 69.9; 69.4 / 71.75; 74.75 / 71.25 |
| RS-SFT 95 / 189 / 283 / 376 | 29.1 / 43.5 / 57.8 / 72.0 | 1.1 / 2.1 / 3.2 / 4.2M | 75.5 / 72.0; 82.0 / 75.75; 81.4 / 77.1; 77.0 / 76.5 |
| OPD 25 / 50 / 75 / 100 | 108.5 / 203.3 / 296.5 / 391.5 | 8.8 / 14.2 / 20.2 / 26.2M | 74.9 / 68.9; 81.75 / 75.75; 79.0 / 76.75; 80.9 / 72.25 |
| E (expert, reference) | 35.9 | 1.8M | 79.4 / 71.4 (two-pass mean) |

How the numbers are built:
- **H100-hours.** Each arm's measured training-gang allocation, pro-rated by updates.
- **SFT arms.** Each carries the 14.6 H100-h of the E demo collection from step 0.
- **OPD.** Each checkpoint carries its own export job, about 15 H100-h. Measured allocation-to-checkpoint for OPD, as a cross-check: 118.8 / 197.8 / 286.9 / 375.7 H100-h.
- **Trained tokens.** Loss-bearing tokens, counted each time they are trained on: SFT from the row manifests × epochs, OPD from the run's per-update scored tokens.
- **Excluded.** Evaluations, building E, and failed attempts.

Reading:
- **Cost to reach E's level.** RS-SFT passes E on both directions at update 189 (43.5 H100-h). OPD gets there at update 50 (203.3 H100-h), about 4.7× more GPU time.
- **Matched GPU-hours.** Both SFT runs ended (72 and 76 H100-h) before OPD's first checkpoint (108.5). At the SFT arms' final cost, a straight line from B to OPD update 25 puts OPD at about 68–69 / 65. That is an interpolation between two measured points, not a measurement.
- **Trained tokens.** OPD trains on 4–6× more tokens than the SFT arms, because it trains on its own, longer samples.

Caveats:
- This is not a matched-compute experiment: different optimizers, batch geometry and verifier access (RS uses execution correctness).
- Single passes unless marked; one pass is about ±3.5 pp.
- OPD's W&B history logged 99 of its 100 updates, so the final token count misses one update.

🤖
# Research

This is a gated two-domain experiment: the canonical MMLU-Pro data is prepared, but E₂ training awaits approval, and all four transfer arms need the resulting checkpoint. [#9920](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920) supplies the B/E baseline and single-expert recipes; [#9974](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974) already implements the checkpoint-merging tools and remains under review. The repository's named evaluation suite does not include working MMLU-Pro or CruxEval tasks, so the frozen Evalchemy configuration from #9920 must be used for comparable scores.

**Relevant code**
- [`SFTSpec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L494) — shared SFT recipe and checkpoint source
- [`SkyRLSpec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L150) — versioned rollout and model inputs
- [`evaluation/cli.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147) — explicit Evalchemy config launch
- [`evaluation/evals.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/evals.py#L297) — named-suite task limitation

# Proposed Fix

1. After approval, train E₂ on the pinned canonical subset with E's #9920 recipe. Export it, evaluate B/E/E₂ on both target domains and the collapse checks, and apply the stated MMLU-Pro paired-gain and GSM8K gates. Stop the transfer arms if E₂ fails.
2. If E₂ passes, pin its k=8 demo collection and construct the two mixed SFT datasets from the same 3,206 prompts. Record rejection-sampling coverage and supervised token counts. Smoke the domain-routed MOPD setup, including teacher score alignment, one update, and HF export, before the four-epoch run.
3. Run MOPD, mixed SFT, and mixed SFT-RS from B with the issue's fixed optimizer and epoch budget. Use #9974 for the B/E/E₂ coefficient sweep and TIES/DARE-TIES after its tools are ready; verify checkpoint tensor alignment and complete exports.
4. Score each selected arm on CruxEval, MMLU-Pro (full set, training subset, held-out groups), GSM8K, GPQA-D, and MATH500 with the frozen evaluator. Report paired intervals, the issue's checkpoint-selection rule, verifier access for SFT-RS, and H100-hours in one final issue update. The trained MMLU-Pro and CruxEval prompts must be labeled as seen-prompt results.
