🤖 **Final report: two experts into one student (MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS, merging)**

## Summary

E_2 reached 66.4% on the MMLU-Pro subset used for its fine-tuning (B 44.5%) and 64.0% on the remaining docs (B 44.1%). Its CruxEval output score was 4.9 percentage points below B in one pass. Its IFEval instruction-strict point estimate was also below B (80.2% versus 81.1%), with an interval spanning zero; the other reported probe point estimates were above B. At the selected finals, mixed SFT-RS step-727 exceeds MOPD step-100 on the MMLU-Pro subset by 4.0 pp [1.6, 6.3]; the held-out difference is unresolved (+0.4 [−0.5, 1.4]). MOPD exceeds RS on CruxEval input by 4.9 pp [1.6, 8.1]; the output difference is unresolved. RS-727 and MOPD-100 are the selected finals of their arms (RS-727 similar to 546, MOPD-100 similar to 50 on every target). They use unequal compute, token budgets and verifier access. Plain-SFT step-803 was selected on two-pass means. The RS arm's demo selector used a different answer-extraction rule from the evaluator (quantified under Caveats). Weight merging at half strength scores above B in both domains with no training (CruxEval input 76.5, output 67.6; MMLU-Pro subset 63.2), below the trained arms on CruxEval output; the full-strength task-arithmetic merge shows a large regression on valid GSM8K (50.0) and GPQA-D (30.0) evaluations with unusually long outputs. Training-gang allocations: RS-SFT 93.6 H100-h, MOPD 557.9 (2 epochs, 7 nodes; plus 28.3 of export-only jobs). Evaluation serve allocation across the 82 eval groups: 1,752.6 H100-h, of which 894.5 in 31 groups with no successful eval child (details under Costs).

## Setup (unchanged from #9920 except where stated)

B = [`open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab). E = #9920's CruxEval expert (step-272; [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`)). E_2 ([open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MMLUPro-Expert-E2-Step254 @ acb97183](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MMLUPro-Expert-E2-Step254/tree/acb97183af633533df4f4f63d83adc1e0a7a9748) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task157-e2/checkpoints/karan/e2-mmlupro-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.09.1/hf/step-254`)) = B + full SFT on [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) MMLU-Pro traces with E's exact recipe (AdamH 0.9/0.95, LR 1e-5, 3% warmup then cosine, 3 epochs, fresh optimizer, frozen router bias, 32 H100), 1,359 usable traces over a seeded category-proportional draw of whole question-text groups (1,589 questions = 1,606 docs); the other 10,426 docs are held out from this fine-tuning and used as an additional probe (prior exposure of either split during B's own training is not ruled out; both primary targets are test-exposed). Labels: the GLM collection had keyed the dataset by question text, so 190 docs carried a wrong gold; every doc was re-joined to TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro test @ `b189ec76` by exact question + ordered options (artifacts and SHA-256 at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/mmlupro-canonical-v2/`, independently verified against the pinned source and captured prompts; verification artifact `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/task162-candidate-verification-v4/`). Transfer arms start from B with matched AdamW hyperparameters (LR 1e-6, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, gradient clip 1.0) and frozen router bias, implemented in Levanter for SFT and Megatron for MOPD. The shared evaluation universe has 3,206 prompts (1,600 CruxEval + 1,606 MMLU-Pro). Plain SFT trains four epochs on 3,206 sample-zero demonstrations; RS-SFT trains four epochs on 2,903 covered prompts. MOPD runs two epochs with four rollouts per sampled prompt and domain-routed teachers (100 optimizer updates of 64 prompts; 50 per epoch). These budgets are not token- or compute-matched. MOPD = MarinSkyRL on-policy distillation with two pinned teachers, CruxEval prompts scored by E and MMLU-Pro prompts by E_2 (sampled reverse KL, 4 rollouts per prompt, 1:1 route mix). Mixed SFT = one demo per prompt (E's and E_2's sample 0 from k=8 pools). Mixed SFT-RS = the first sample per prompt in index order that is execution-correct (CruxEval) or accepted by the implemented answer selector (MMLU-Pro) from the same k=8 pools (1,503 + 1,400 covered prompts; uncovered prompts stay in every denominator). Merges = #9974 tools, B anchor, E and E_2 donors: task arithmetic at a = b = 0.5 and a = b = 1.0, and TIES (density 0.5, a = b = 1.0); CPU only.

## Frozen evaluator

Evalchemy [`ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8) (recorded in every record's `eval_runtime`; the `c131e5ab` label in earlier text was an unused code constant and has been corrected in #9920), vLLM H100x8 DP8+EP8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap (28,672 for GPQA-D), thinking on, unseeded sampling at temperature 1.0. MMLU-Pro runs score all 12,032 docs; subset and held-out numbers are sliced from the record's active FineStore snapshot against the canonical gold; intervals resample question-text groups for MMLU-Pro (subset 1,589, held-out 10,212) and problems within each CruxEval direction (800), conditional on the observed sampled completions; they do not estimate generation or training run-to-run variability. At ae362881, MMLU-Pro extraction uses final content when available, falls back to reasoning for REASONING_ONLY responses, and returns no answer for truncated reasoning-only responses; it applies `final_response_text`, then the three answer-letter regexes, and uppercases the result. Exact replay reproduced native predictions on all 12,032 rows of each of B-220c, E_2-254, RS-727 and MOPD-100. The broader matrix has uniform runtime-revision metadata; it was not replayed in full. The stored normalized output is not always the scorer input (the scorer saw the parser-split final content), so re-grading must start from the native completions. All comparisons are paired on the same docs.

## Results, MMLU-Pro

(Single pass per checkpoint; subset % / held-out % / all %; Δ = paired vs B on the subset, pp with 95% group bootstrap; B 44.46 / 44.05 / 44.11; E 60.34 / 59.76 / 59.84; E_2 66.44 / 63.97 / 64.30).

## Results, CruxEval and probes

## Paired deltas (pp, 95% bootstrap)

All plain-803-versus-other-model intervals below use its pass 1; both passes are shown in the tables, and selection uses their mean. CruxEval vs B (in / out): MOPD-100 +26.75 [+23.0, +30.5] / +18.6 [+15.0, +22.25]; RS-727 +21.9 [+17.9, +25.75] / +19.5 [+15.75, +23.1]; plain-803 +20.0 [+16.0, +24.0] / +13.75 [+9.9, +17.5]; TA-0.5 +21.1 / +9.9; TIES +17.4 / +10.4. The following CruxEval-versus-E deltas use E's first CruxEval pass (635/800 input, 562/800 output), not the two-pass E mean displayed in the table; plain-803 deltas here use its first pass, and both plain passes are reported together for selection. CruxEval vs E: MOPD-100 +2.75 [−0.5, +5.9] / +6.1 [+2.9, +9.4]; RS-727 −2.1 [−5.6, +1.5] / +7.0 [+3.75, +10.4]; plain-803 −4.0 [−7.75, −0.4] / +1.25 [−2.0, +4.6]; TA-0.5 −2.9 / −2.6; TIES −6.6 / −2.1. The pass-to-pass swings at fixed weights (603 CruxEval input 79.25 → 75.4; 803 MMLU-Pro subset 62.39 → 61.71) are the run-to-run measurements this experiment has; pass-1 intervals do not include them. MOPD: step-50 has two valid CruxEval records, 641/585 from the first group (`20261011-035349`, whose MMLU-Pro and GSM8K evals failed) and 644/608 from the retry group (`20261013-023108`, which produced all three records); no rule fixed before scoring chose between them, and the retry record was used as the selection input because its group is the one that completed. Step-100 vs step-50 (paired, single pass each, retry record): MMLU-Pro subset −0.81 [−2.99, +1.55], CruxEval +1.62 [−1.50, +4.75] / +0.38 [−2.62, +3.38] → similar on every target → step-100 selected; the held-out probe favours step-50 by 1.2 pp [−2.08, −0.36], reported as context. Sensitivity with both step-50 CruxEval passes (step-100 single pass vs the per-problem two-pass mean of step-50, 80.31 / 74.56): +1.81 [−0.94, +4.50] / +1.81 [−1.00, +4.56]; same decision. Merges: single artifacts, no selection.

## Reading the result

(1) At RS-727 and MOPD-100, both domains improve over B. Relative to the specialists, MOPD's MMLU-Pro subset difference from E_2 is −2.24 pp [−4.47, +0.06], while RS's is +1.74 pp with an interval spanning zero. Intervals spanning zero do not establish preservation or equivalence. Both checkpoints have higher CruxEval output scores than E's first pass; their input differences from E are unresolved. Paired changes versus B on each split: MOPD-100 +19.7 pp on the subset and +20.3 on the held-out docs; RS-727 +23.7 and +20.7. (2) RS-SFT and MOPD differ by domain: RS higher on the MMLU-Pro subset, MOPD higher on CruxEval input, output unresolved. RS-SFT had ground-truth verifier access, 8 teacher samples per prompt and an unequal token budget; MOPD had on-policy samples scored by the teachers. Neither is a matched control for the other. (3) Plain mixed SFT recovers less than either (MMLU-Pro −5.8 pp vs RS; CruxEval below E on input). (4) Merging recovers CruxEval input (76.5 at a = b = 0.5) and most of MMLU-Pro (63.2) with no training, but its CruxEval output (67.6) is 2.6 pp below E's first pass (70.25), 3.8 below E's two-pass mean (71.4), 8.8 below MOPD-100 (76.4), 9.65 below RS-727 (77.25) and 3.9 below plain-803's first pass (71.5); TIES output (68.1) sits 0.5 pp above TA-0.5 on each of those comparisons; at full strength (a = b = 1.0) the merge shows a large regression on valid GSM8K (50.0) and GPQA-D (30.0) evaluations with unusually long outputs (median 85–95k characters), so it was withheld from the rest of the matrix. (5) Probes on the two finals (single pass each; 0 infrastructure-error rows; MATH500 median output 2,496 and 1,525 characters): RS-727 MATH500 92.4, GPQA-D 57.6, IFEval instruction-strict 78.3 (below B with the interval excluding 0: −2.76 [−5.21, −0.24]; loose −0.36 [−2.66, +2.03]); MOPD-100 MATH500 90.0, GPQA-D 47.5, IFEval 80.0 (−1.08 [−3.59, +1.21] vs B). RS-727's GPQA-D score is above every other model in this matrix (B 41.9, E 44.8, E_2 47.6, MOPD-100 47.5, merges 47.1–47.3); it is one evaluation with three generations for each of 198 questions and is reported with its paired interval, not interpreted.

## Caveats

One pass per checkpoint except the explicitly reported repeats; plain 603/803 selection uses per-item two-pass means. Intervals are unadjusted for multiple comparisons and checkpoint selection; additional-probe findings are exploratory. Targets are 800 problems per CruxEval direction and 1,606 docs; intervals resample question-text groups for MMLU-Pro and problems within each CruxEval direction, conditional on the observed sampled completions, and do not estimate generation or training run-to-run variability (E's two CruxEval passes differed by 0.1 / 2.25 pp in #9920). The MMLU-Pro subset was the fine-tuning set for E_2 and the training prompt set for every arm; the 10,426 held-out docs are an additional probe, reported and never used for selection. RS demo selector mismatch: the k=8 demo grader implemented the older first-match-anywhere extractor on the whole text, while the evaluator grades the final answer after the think block; under the evaluator's rule 14 of the 1,400 selected RS MMLU-Pro demos (1.0%) are wrong, 15 more prompts would have been covered and 1 lost, and 45 prompts would have used a different sample. The RS arm is reported as trained; no corrected run was made. Record provenance: two records (B MMLU-Pro and MOPD-100 MMLU-Pro) had a retried eval attempt that left a second full sample stream; all numbers here come from each record's pinned active FineStore manifest (HEAD), with the native writer taken from the active source-blob provenance (normalized sample rows can carry null correctness); superseded attempts are kept as overhead and evidence, not as independent repeats (an earlier reading of the first stream gave B 43.90 and MOPD-100 65.32 on the subset and has been superseded). Three merge MATH500 records from 2026-10-10 are invalid (Evalchemy `AgentTimeoutError` in 500/500, 455/500 and 300/500 rows) and were rerun for TA-0.5 and TIES; TA-1.0 was not rerun.

**Costs (H100-hours = GPUs × Iris task or attempt duration; method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298; every figure labelled by what it includes).** Training-gang allocations (image pull, load, steps, in-gang checkpoint/HF export and teardown; queue time excluded): E_2 60.6 (3 epochs, 32 H100). Mixed SFT-RS 93.57 (728 updates, 32 H100). Mixed SFT 107.83, plus 14.21 for a first attempt evicted by Kueue after 16 updates and relaunched from B. MOPD 557.9 for the 2-epoch run (100 optimizer updates, 7 × H100x8; the launch plan said ≈102, the sampler yielded 50 full windows per epoch; the W&B run `skyrl/snowball-mopd2-cruxeval-mmlupro-2ep` logged 99 steps and is marked `crashed`; coordinator logs record 100 updates and the terminal export at global_step 100 succeeded), plus 28.3 in two separate export-only jobs (step-50 13.8, step-100 14.5), which the SFT figures include in-gang; allocation to the step-50 checkpoint ≈ 317 and to step-100 ≈ 531 from timestamps (full run, not pro-rated). E_2 k=8 demo pool 8.91 (counted once, shared by both SFT arms; #9920's CruxEval pool is reused and its cost stays in #9920). Merges: CPU only (33, 28 and 68 min). Excluded from every total: GLM trace generation, E's construction (#9920), CPU preparation and audit jobs, the MOPD smoke run (≈60.6, reported in the design ledger). Evaluation serve allocation (serve attempt `started_at`→`finished_at` × 8 H100; queue time and CPU eval tasks excluded; two sweeps, 2026-10-13 05:20 and 11:40 UTC, 82 groups): 1,752.6 H100-h. Of this, 858.2 belongs to 51 groups with at least one successful eval child, including groups with invalid or superseded records; 894.5 belongs to 31 groups with no successful eval child. Per evaluated model (record / no-record): B 121.7 / 0; E 46.2 / 0; E_2 167.5 / 284.9; mixed plain 111.7 / 0; mixed RS 73.3 / 13.6; MOPD 112.0 / 0 (the step-50 retry alone 72.4: its MMLU-Pro eval ran 8 h 41 min without errors); merge TA-0.5 94.4 / 231.6; merge TA-1.0 79.9 / 241.6; merge TIES 51.6 / 122.7. Eight serves ran 13.8–14.6 h (110–117 H100-h each): six in the no-record bucket (`20261010-043736` E_2-85 MMLU-Pro, `20261010-030122` and `…030230` TA-1.0, `20261010-042000` and `…042104` TA-0.5, `20261010-042136` TIES; 689.4 together) and two in the record bucket (B's MMLU-Pro group `20261007-172014-…-9225`, 116.9, whose MMLU-Pro eval ran two attempts while its GPQA-D eval failed; E_2-85's `20261010-003548`, 110.3). Several of these groups have documented stale-endpoint failures after a serve preemption (#10030; its fix #10033 was not applied to this frozen evaluator), and B's group is documented as an eval retry after `PodDeleted`; the totals include all serve allocation regardless of cause, and the per-group attribution is only as complete as the overhead ledger's entries. These are infrastructure allocation costs, not inference-compute estimates. For scale, the #9984 training-gang allocations listed above sum to 834.1 H100-h (E_2 60.6 + RS 93.57 + plain 122.04 + MOPD 557.9), plus 28.3 of MOPD export-only jobs and 8.91 for the demo pool.

🤖

## Weight deltas against the student

A reader asked what the weight changes behind these transfers look like. Table and method below; numbers are percentages; cosines are given against E and against E₂.

| Model (vs student B) | ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ all, % | attention % | expert MLPs % | shared expert % | router % | LM head % | weights changed, % | cos(Δ, Δ_expert) all | attention | expert MLPs | LM head |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expert E (CruxEval) | 0.036 | 0.65 | 0.047 | 0.069 | 0.17 | 0.13 | 13.7 | — | — | — | — |
| Expert E₂ (MMLU-Pro) | 0.035 | 0.64 | 0.043 | 0.067 | 0.15 | 0.11 | 12.9 | 0.21 vs E | 0.37 | 0.06 | 0.38 |
| Mixed plain SFT step 803 | 0.180 | 0.40 | 0.40 | 0.42 | 0.033 | 0.53 | 56.3 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.06 / 0.06 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.40 / 0.50 |
| Mixed RS-SFT step 727 | 0.171 | 0.38 | 0.38 | 0.40 | 0.030 | 0.49 | 54.7 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.06 / 0.06 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.42 / 0.51 |
| MOPD update 100 | 0.045 | 0.13 | 0.099 | 0.12 | 0.008 | 0.084 | 25.2 | 0.05 / 0.05 | 0.11 / 0.13 | 0.07 / 0.07 | −0.14 / −0.15 |
| Merge TA a = b = 0.5 | 0.031 | 0.53 | 0.041 | 0.064 | 0.13 | 0.11 | 12.1 | 0.71 / 0.69 | 0.82 / 0.82 | 0.60 / 0.56 | 0.78 / 0.71 |
| Merge TIES d = 0.5 | 0.043 | 0.73 | 0.057 | 0.084 | 0.19 | 0.14 | 17.2 | 0.73 / 0.69 | 0.75 / 0.73 | 0.73 / 0.65 | 0.84 / 0.69 |

Reading:
- The two experts are built the same way and look the same: 0.035–0.036% of B's norm overall, change concentrated in attention (0.65%), router (0.15–0.17%) and LM head, expert MLPs nearly untouched, 13% of weights changed. Their deltas share a direction (cosine 0.21 overall, 0.37 in attention, 0.38 at the LM head) while their expert-MLP changes are nearly independent (0.06), consistent with a common change in how the model answers (both experts start using their reasoning block on far more prompts) on top of domain-specific MLP changes.
- The mixed SFT arms move the weights most (0.17–0.18% overall, 55–56% of weights changed, expert MLPs 0.38–0.40%), 5× more than the experts whose text they train on, and in a direction almost orthogonal to both experts' deltas (cosine ≈0.02 overall and in the expert MLPs; 0.06 in attention). Only the LM head aligns (0.40–0.51).
- MOPD moves the weights a quarter as much as the SFT arms (0.045% overall, 25% of weights changed), again nearly orthogonal to the experts (0.05–0.13), with the LM head moving against both experts (−0.14 / −0.15). It recovers both experts' scores anyway.
- The merges are, by construction, the experts' deltas: TA 0.5 is their average (cosine 0.69–0.71 with each, magnitude 0.031%), TIES keeps the larger of the two per weight (0.043%, attention 0.73%). They sit far from where the trained arms end up (cosine between merge and arm deltas not computed here).
- Net: four different weight changes, differing in size by 5× and nearly orthogonal in direction, all land within a few points of the experts on both domains. The transfer is not a recovery of the expert's parameters; it is a re-learning of the behaviour from a different starting direction, which is also why the arms' off-domain scores (GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA-D, IFEval) do not simply track the experts'.

Method: every tensor of each checkpoint was compared with the student B (open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5) in float32 after widening the bf16 exports; ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ is the relative Frobenius norm over all 67.1 B weights or over one component (attention q/k/v/o and attention gates; the 26 layers' fused MoE expert MLPs, 65.4 B weights; shared experts; router weights and biases; embeddings; LM head), 'weights changed' is the share of scalars whose bf16 value differs from B's, and cos(Δ, Δ_expert) is the cosine between the checkpoint's delta and the expert's delta over the same weights (two values = vs E / vs E₂). Embeddings and norms are omitted from the table (relative change ≤ 0.01% everywhere). Caveat: the exports are bf16, so training-time changes below half a bf16 ulp of a weight are invisible; magnitudes and 'weights changed' are lower bounds, and the cosines are computed only on what survived rounding. Script `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_stats.py` (eval worktree); per-tensor results at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/review/wdelta-<model>.json`, all summaries in `wdelta-all-summaries.json`.

🤖 Follow-up on the delta-direction question: is the MOPD update "nearly orthogonal" to the expert update, or aligned beyond chance?

## Method

Deltas against the student B (`Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ fdc3c3c5) for expert E (CruxEval, step 272), expert E₂ (MMLU-Pro, step 254), the MOPD update (step 100) and the two mixed SFT arms (plain step 803, RS step 727). Three measures per component: cosine, sign agreement on weights changed in both, and subspace overlap, the share of a delta's energy inside the reference delta's top-k singular directions per matrix (k holding 50% of the reference energy), against two nulls: a random k-dim subspace and the reference delta with entries permuted within each matrix. The run reproduces the cosines posted above exactly. Script: `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_subspace.py` on branch `task/239` (4c99d4d9a4).

## Result

Overlap with E's half-energy subspace, as a multiple of the random null:

| Component | E₂ (peer expert) | MOPD | plain SFT | RS-SFT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Attention | 3.4× | 3.5× | 2.4× | 2.4× |
| Expert MLPs | 1.5× | 1.6× | 1.3× | 1.3× |
| Shared experts | 3.9× | 3.4× | 1.7× | 1.8× |
| Router | 2.0× | 2.8× | 1.7× | 1.6× |
| LM head | 295× | 198× | 397× | 407× |

Cosine and sign agreement with E, all weights: E₂ 0.21 / 0.55; MOPD 0.049 / 0.56; plain SFT 0.021 / 0.53; RS-SFT 0.023 / 0.53. In attention MOPD reaches 0.10 / 0.68 against E₂'s 0.38 / 0.71.

## Reading

- Cosine 0.05 over 6.7e10 weights is about 12,000 chance SDs (1/√n = 3.9e-6), so "beyond chance" is a weak bar. The informative controls are the SFT arms (same student, same prompts, same expert texts) and the peer expert.
- Against those controls, MOPD shares direction with the experts more than the SFT arms do, in every component except the LM head, and relative to the random null it sits close to the peer expert in attention and expert MLPs. The permuted null equals the random null everywhere, so the excess comes from the experts' dominant singular directions, not from their entry distribution.
- The shared part is small in energy: 0.24% of MOPD's update lies along E's delta, and 16% inside E's half-energy subspace against 10% for a random subspace. The posted conclusion stands: the transfer is mostly a different weight change that reaches the same behaviour.
- The LM head reverses the pattern: the SFT arms align strongly with the experts there (cos 0.40 to 0.51), while MOPD moves inside the same narrow top directions with the opposite sign (cos −0.14, sign agreement 0.39).
- None of the deltas is rank-1: participation ratios are 20 to 90 directions per matrix. The experts' attention deltas are the most concentrated (top-10 directions hold 80% of their energy); MOPD's is more spread (39%), the SFT arms' more still (24%).

## Limits

Correlational geometry only; no ablation, so no causal claim about the recovered scores. Cross-step self-consistency of the MOPD direction could not be measured because only step 100 exists. The bf16 exports hide changes below half an ulp, so every measure covers only what survived rounding.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
The agent above put some numbers together for "how orthogonal" the task vectors really are for each experiment arm. This is related to @penfever 's [comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6201304545) about how the Frobenius norm of the task vector for MOPD is significantly smaller than SFT's.

However, I realized something else that I put in the experiment setup but forgot about: **The MOPD arm's batch size was effectively 16x higher than the SFT arm's with the same LR and fewer steps** . This might explain the whole difference. Specifically, they were "prompt matched", with each epoch seeing 3200 unique prompts / epoch. Specifically:

* SFT had 16 demonstration rows / step
  *  x 200 steps / epoch x 4 epochs = 12800 rollouts
  *  LR 1e-6
* MOPD had 64 prompts x 4 student rollouts / step x 50 steps / epoch x 2 epochs = 3200 prompts
  * x 50 steps / epoch x 2 epochs = 25600 rollouts 
  * LR 1e-6

As for why, at the time:
* We had known SFT runs on Snowball that used a 1e-6 LR, and I think even after doing sweeps in #10213 , that seems to be a good LR for this class of experiments
* We had existing M/OPD experiments under the proof-of-life experiments that used the 256 rollouts + 1e-6 LR
* MOPD needed more rollouts / batch to keep it from being as rollout-constrained
* MOPD by construction would see more unique sequences / epoch anyways if they started with the same dataset. 

Either way, we can do an experiment increasing MOPD LR to 4e-6, computed by sqrt(MOPD batch  / SFT batch) ( 1e-6) = 4 * 1e-6.

We'll also run for 4 epochs. This will give us a better sense of whether MOPD was under-stepped. 

Another difference I should note that won't change: MOPD is running using Megatron (our SkyRL setup), SFT is using Levanter

How the numbers are built:
- **H100-hours.** Each arm's measured training-gang allocation, pro-rated by updates.
- **SFT arms.** Each carries both demo pools from step 0: E's (14.6 H100-h, reused from #9920) and E₂'s (8.9).
- **MOPD.** Each checkpoint carries its export job (about 14 H100-h). Measured allocation-to-checkpoint for MOPD, as a cross-check: ≈317 / ≈531 H100-h.
- **Trained tokens.** As in #9920: SFT from the row manifests × epochs, MOPD from per-update scored tokens.
- **Excluded.** Evaluations, building the experts, and the evicted plain attempt (14.2 H100-h).

Reading:
- **The arms reach different targets.** RS-SFT reaches E₂'s MMLU-Pro subset level at update 546 (93.7 H100-h); MOPD never does (best 65.0). MOPD reaches E's CruxEval input level at update 50 (292.8 H100-h); neither SFT arm does (best 78.75 / 79.25).

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Support expert-block weight synchronization when policy training and vLLM inference share GPUs (`trainer.placement.colocate_all=true`). The current restriction prevents this transport from being used in colocated runs; those runs must use another supported transport or allocate separate inference GPUs.

The restriction remains on main at [`3a8e8a72681011012ebb59c0c1ed34688ad6fdea`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/3a8e8a72681011012ebb59c0c1ed34688ad6fdea):

- [`validate_expert_block_transport`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/3a8e8a72681011012ebb59c0c1ed34688ad6fdea/marinskyrl/inference_placement.py#L16-L63) explicitly rejects `colocate_all=true` for `generator.weight_sync_transport=expert_block`.
- [The inference-engine factory](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/3a8e8a72681011012ebb59c0c1ed34688ad6fdea/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/inference_engines/ray_wrapped_inference_engine.py#L594-L602) excludes hybrid/shared-GPU and sleeping engines from verified receiver placement, then rejects expert-block synchronization without those placements.

This is a confirmed implementation restriction from source inspection, not evidence that GPU colocation is fundamentally incompatible with expert-block transfer. No new GPU experiment was run for this issue. [Marin #10333](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10333) adds an early launcher rejection for the existing restriction; it does not implement support.

Done when:

- At least one documented colocated MoE Megatron/vLLM configuration can complete training, expert-block synchronization, and generation across repeated updates. An initial subset of parallelism configurations is sufficient.
- Receiver placement checks account for shared physical GPUs and worker lifecycle. Sleep/offload modes may remain unsupported initially if explicitly rejected; any supported mode needs transition coverage.
- GPU tests compare transferred weights and fixed-input logits against a fresh vLLM load of the same updated checkpoint, with documented numerical tolerances, and detect stale or misrouted weights.
- Non-colocated transfer remains covered, unsupported combinations fail before GPU allocation, and the documented support matrix and Marin launcher guard agree with the implemented support.


Transferred from https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/issues/1033.
<!-- skyrl-migration: issue=I_kwDOSx5uL88AAAABYjOPIA -->

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The vendored SkyRL config rejects `expert_block` with `colocate_all=true`, and the engine factory omits shared-GPU workers from verified receiver placement. The colocated update path wakes weights and syncs without setting the generation-paused state required by `ExpertBlockSync.sync()`; startup also puts engines to sleep before `prepare()` collects receiver inventories. These are implementation barriers, not evidence that shared GPUs cannot transfer the blocks; no colocated GPU run has validated the path.

**Relevant code**
- [Transport validation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ea93941256996206691eef58f29e8b0fa7fa5060/vendor/skyrl/marinskyrl/inference_placement.py#L16-L63) — rejects colocation before launch.
- [Engine placement gate](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ea93941256996206691eef58f29e8b0fa7fa5060/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/inference_engines/ray_wrapped_inference_engine.py#L594-L602) — excludes hybrid and sleeping engines.
- [Engine startup](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ea93941256996206691eef58f29e8b0fa7fa5060/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/inference_engines/ray_wrapped_inference_engine.py#L973-L1025) — reports placement or sleeps, then records receivers.
- [Expert-block driver](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ea93941256996206691eef58f29e8b0fa7fa5060/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/weight_sync/expert_block/driver.py#L151-L203) — prepares receivers and requires paused generation.
- [Colocated update](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ea93941256996206691eef58f29e8b0fa7fa5060/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/trainer.py#L1185-L1217) — wakes, syncs, offloads, then wakes KV cache.

# Design

Enable one bounded colocated configuration first: a single-node Megatron MoE policy with TP=ETP=1 and EP=4, one local vLLM engine with TP=PP=1 and DP=EP=4 on the same four GPUs, NCCL expert-block transport, and vLLM sleep level 1. Keep other parallelism and sleep/offload combinations rejected before GPU allocation. This needs a four-GPU model small enough to leave room for the weight-wake/transfer phase; memory fit and communicator survival are GPU acceptance criteria, not assumptions.

## Challenges and risks

The current verified-placement path builds receiver evidence from dedicated inference placement groups, while colocation uses the trainer's shared group. Sleeping can also discard receiver tensors or NCCL state. A successful first transfer would not establish that later updates reach the right expert ranks or that the receiver survives another train/sleep/wake cycle.

## Implementation

1. Extend placement reporting to the shared placement group. Match each receiver's reported host, GPU UUID, DP/EP rank, and bundle to the actual allocation; allow its GPU UUID to match a trainer rank while still requiring distinct receiver GPUs and unique receiver ranks. Recheck after an actor restart or placement change.
2. Define the supported lifecycle in the trainer: pause and drain generation at the rollout boundary, sleep engines for training, wake receiver weights after training, prepare or rebuild expert-block groups while receivers are live, transfer and verify the current version, release policy memory, wake KV cache, then resume generation. Reconcile startup `prepare()` with the initial sleep barrier and tear down or rebuild groups if sleep invalidates them. Fail the update without resuming generation when placement or version verification fails.
3. Gate only the tested configuration in `validate_expert_block_transport` and the Marin launcher. Coordinate with [#10333](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10333), which adds the current early rejection, and reuse the non-colocated GPU harness from [#10377](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10377) after it lands. Update the support matrix and an exact runnable config with the same constraints.

## Testing

Add CPU tests for shared-group placement, duplicate/misrouted receiver identity, unsupported config rejection before engine creation, and pause/wake failure behavior. On four GPUs, run at least two training updates with a tiny MoE model; after each transfer compare selected dense and per-expert tensors plus fixed-input logits to a fresh vLLM load of that update's checkpoint. Record and justify numerical tolerances, change different expert blocks between updates to expose stale or swapped weights, and generate after each wake. Retain the non-colocated transfer test and run the launch guard against both supported and rejected configs.

## Open question

Does level-1 sleep free enough GPU memory while preserving the receiver and NCCL groups for the target four-GPU layout? If the probe fails, keep colocation rejected while implementing an explicit level-2 wake/rebuild path and repeat the same GPU gate before enabling it.

issues.body:
Add support for Harbor's host-side Claude Code adapter in the shared task rollout path. The controller should run on the host while its task tools operate in the sandbox.

Current main (`2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950`) routes task rollouts through RolloutEngine. Its [agent adapter](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_runtime.py) requires `BaseInstalledAgent` and rejects host-side Harbor agents. Host-side means the controller runs in the rollout-worker process or a host subprocess while task commands execute in a sandbox. Harbor already provides [ClaudeCodeLocal](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/aee476676983dfa62f5d824538193302ef46e3f9/src/harbor/agents/local/claude_code.py), selected by `name: claude-code` and `mode: local`. It derives from `BaseAgent` and is rejected by the current adapter.

Done when:

- Document and validate the local-mode configuration, client version, supported model endpoint, and sandbox tool routing. Reuse Harbor's adapter and establish which operations remain on the host.
- Demonstrate whether the client can use the trainable policy through the supported protocol bridge. For on-policy RL, retain exact served tokens and behavior log probabilities and verify their alignment with training inputs.
- Reject unsupported client/backend/objective combinations before allocating a full run. A fixed external Claude model used to collect teacher trajectories must be labeled separately; it is not an on-policy rollout of the trainable model.
- Test concurrent-trial isolation, credential boundaries, timeout and error classification, cancellation, verifier execution, and cleanup of host processes and containers.
- For a supported trainable-policy configuration, complete a live multi-turn smoke through verification, an optimizer update, and synchronized evaluation. Preserve reproducible configs and traces, exclude credentials, and review client-supplied instructions before publication.

Endpoint compatibility and training-evidence support require validation; this request does not assert that selecting local mode alone makes Claude Code usable for on-policy RL. If the client cannot support the required trainable-policy endpoint, record that blocker with evidence; teacher-only collection does not complete this integration request.

comments.body:
🤖 Open design question shared by marin-community/marin#10387, marin-community/marin#10386, and marin-community/marin#10385: can the agent implementations remain in Harbor, with MarinSkyRL collecting the training evidence through an adapter? Is there a concrete operational constraint that requires porting them into Marin?

Please compare two ownership models before choosing an implementation:

- Harbor owns the full trial: agent controller, environment lifecycle, retries, and verification. MarinSkyRL supplies policy inference and captures training evidence.
- RolloutEngine owns the trial: its adapter runs Harbor's agent controller and propagates cancellation to it, while Marin manages environment lifecycle and verification.

For either option, establish how the integration retains exact model requests, sampled tokens, behavior log probabilities, tool observations, and verifier outcomes. Assign explicit owners for inference-request retries, tool-operation retries, whole-trial retries, cancellation, and cleanup, without duplicate handling of the same operation. Preserve original Harbor errors and diagnostics when mapping outcomes to MarinSkyRL's training decisions: include, exclude, or fail.

Keeping the implementations and, where practical, the full trial lifecycle in Harbor may avoid duplicating its operational behavior. This remains an architectural question, not a decided requirement or a claim that the current adapter supports it. What would prevent that arrangement, and what tests would establish that Marin's tracking and training interfaces can observe it correctly?

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

Current MarinSkyRL has a Harbor-owned full-trial path for setup, verification, and cleanup, but its training runner requires `BaseInstalledAgent`; Harbor's `ClaudeCodeLocal` derives from `BaseAgent` and cannot enter it. Harbor exposes an Anthropic Messages translation route, while the local adapter inherits the host environment and launches a host subprocess; the reviewed code does not establish trainable-policy routing, per-trial request correlation, or cleanup of that subprocess on cancellation. Marin pins separate Harbor and MarinSkyRL revisions, so a validated integration must update those pins and its reproducible run config.

**Relevant code**
- [MarinSkyRL `agent_runtime.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_runtime.py#L150-L213) — Harbor-owned trial path.
- [MarinSkyRL `harbor_trial_session.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/harbor_trial_session.py#L49-L64) — installed-agent gate and session correlation.
- [Harbor `claude_code.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/e96b6dcca1513e97e43523eaa971a85c68fcedae/src/harbor/agents/local/claude_code.py#L97-L222) — host CLI, inherited environment, cleanup.
- [Harbor `native_routes.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/e96b6dcca1513e97e43523eaa971a85c68fcedae/src/harbor/literal/native_routes.py#L173-L217) — Messages and token-count routes.
- [Marin `external_dependencies.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/external_dependencies.py#L64-L79) — runtime pins.

# Design

Use the existing Harbor-owned full-trial path. Harbor owns the agent process, sandbox, verifier, whole-trial retry, and cleanup; MarinSkyRL owns policy inference, exact model-turn evidence, and training inclusion decisions. The RolloutEngine-owned borrowed-machine path would require duplicating Harbor's environment and verifier lifecycle. This choice can be shared with the related host-agent requests in #10386 and #10387. No open PR for this adapter was found in the Marin or MarinSkyRL searches.

## Challenges

The Claude CLI must speak the bridge's supported Messages protocol and route every policy request through it. A successful Harbor trial alone cannot establish that the recorded tokens, log probabilities, and training masks match the policy's actual turns.

## Costs / Risks

The rollout worker would need a pinned host CLI. Host credentials, CLI session files, and task-supplied instructions require explicit isolation and review before traces are published.

## Implementation

1. **Prove the protocol first.** Pin a Claude Code CLI version and run its local mode against Harbor's `/v1/messages` and `/v1/messages/count_tokens` bridge with a trainable-policy server. Check model naming, streaming, tool calls, compaction, and that every model request reaches that server. Compare the server's exact prompt/completion token IDs and behavior log probabilities with the recorded turns and training projection, including masks after tool observations. If any required endpoint or evidence is unavailable, reject on-policy configuration before a full run and record the failing request and trace. Label fixed external-model collection as teacher data.
2. **Wire only a proven configuration.** Give each local trial an explicit model endpoint, model name, and scoped capability credential. Correlate its requests at its dedicated proxy, since the CLI does not currently provide the installed-agent correlation header. Admit `ClaudeCodeLocal` to the Harbor-owned trial path while keeping the borrowed-machine path restricted to installed agents. Validate the client version, backend, objective, and supported request modes at launch.
3. **Close lifecycle and credential gaps.** Pass the host process only the required runtime variables and trial-scoped credentials; keep task tools inside the sandbox. On timeout or cancellation, terminate and reap the CLI process, then close the proxy and Harbor environment. Preserve Harbor's original error and verifier details when choosing include, exclude, or fail. Bound client and bridge inference-request retries; let Harbor own whole-trial retries, with no second retry of the same trial in RolloutEngine.

## Testing

Exercise two concurrent trials, tool routing, credential separation, endpoint failure, timeout, cancellation, verifier execution, retry classification, and cleanup. Then run a bounded multi-turn Daytona smoke through verification, a non-skipped optimizer update, and evaluation after weight synchronization. Save exact pins, config, token/log-probability alignment checks, and sanitized traces; review client-supplied instructions before publication. Update Marin's pins and documentation only after the protocol and smoke gates pass.

## Open Questions

Can a pinned Claude Code CLI use the Messages bridge without changing model-visible requests or losing the evidence required for the chosen RL objective? This decides whether on-policy support is feasible; local mode alone does not.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

At the issue's pinned MarinSkyRL revision, `InstalledAgentRuntime` constructs the Harbor agent but rejects it unless it is a `BaseInstalledAgent`; Terminus-Kira inherits Terminus-2's host-side `BaseAgent`, so the trial stops before setup. The existing worker already supplies a Daytona machine and a correlated model endpoint that records served token IDs and log probabilities. [#10045](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10045) covers the installed-agent foundation, and [#10326](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10326) identifies a separate risk of losing earlier training turns after a history reset; neither establishes Terminus-Kira support.

**Relevant code**
- [`agent_runtime.py#L149-L168`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_runtime.py#L149-L168) — installed-agent rejection and execution.
- [`agent_backend.py#L53-L103`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_backend.py#L53-L103) — correlated requests and served evidence.
- [`task_worker.py#L622-L643`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/d361d939926a0308a0892f25adbbe851e709de34/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_worker.py#L622-L643) — agent runtime and Daytona factory.
- [`terminus_kira.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/aee476676983dfa62f5d824538193302ef46e3f9/src/harbor/agents/terminus_kira/terminus_kira.py) — native tools over Terminus-2.
- [`task_projections.py#L205-L267`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_projections.py#L205-L267) — training disposition and masks.

# Terminus-Kira host-agent design

Run Harbor's Terminus-Kira controller in the rollout worker against the existing correlated policy endpoint and an engine-owned Daytona task machine. Keep Harbor's prompts, native tool loop, terminal behavior, and context recovery in Harbor. This shares the host-agent path with [Terminus-2 #10387](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10387) and leaves installed agents on their current path.

## Ownership choice

A Harbor-owned full trial would reuse its retries and verifier, but would require a second bridge for exact model turns and training projection and would duplicate RolloutEngine's machine, grading, and cancellation contracts. Use RolloutEngine as the attempt owner because the installed-agent path already owns those boundaries. Harbor owns the controller's semantic tool loop and context handling; a borrowed environment forwards commands and file transfers to the engine-owned machine without starting or deleting it.

## Design

1. Add a host-agent execution path beside `run_installed_agent` in MarinSkyRL. Validate `terminus-kira` and `terminus-2` as host agents, construct them through Harbor's factory, inject the trial correlation header into each host-side LiteLLM request, and run their `setup()` and `run()` against `BorrowedMachineEnvironment`. Keep one configuration shape for the agent identity, Daytona backend, model endpoint, and setup/run/cleanup deadlines. Do not port the agents into Marin.
2. Route every host-agent chat request through `AgentInferenceBackend` and `ModelTurn`. Preserve the full native `tool_calls` message and tool observations in the next request. Use the engine's served prompt IDs, sampled completion IDs, and behavior log probabilities as canonical training evidence; derive loss masks only over sampled assistant tokens. Reject missing or misaligned token/logprob evidence and unsupported history rewrites before projection, including the [#10326](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10326) multi-conversation case. Harbor trajectory files remain diagnostics, not a source for reconstructed training tokens.
3. Start with a declared text-only mode and `enable_summarize: false`. Disable or reject Kira's `image_read` action in that mode and fail on image content before model inference or projection. Add image mode only after a separate test proves image-part serialization and all generated-token offsets through the serving endpoint and projector; do not silently strip image parts.
4. Give each operation one retry owner: the serving bridge must deduplicate a retried inference request by stable request ID or fail without a second sample; the borrowed machine's transport handles transient Daytona command failures, while Harbor decides whether a completed tool error warrants another action. The worker/orchestrator owns whole-attempt retries and maps original Harbor/Daytona errors to train, exclude, or fail without changing verifier outcomes. RolloutEngine owns the attempt deadline and verifier; cancellation stops the host agent and endpoint, records partial evidence, and releases the Daytona machine.

## Costs and risks

The host path needs cross-repository changes in MarinSkyRL and possibly Harbor to suppress `image_read` and expose stable request IDs. Terminus-2 context recovery can change prompt history, so text-only support must reject such attempts until every sampled action can be retained and attributed. No open Marin PR targets #10386 or Terminus-Kira by title; check current MarinSkyRL PRs and pins before implementation, since this triage session has read access only to `marin-community/marin` on GitHub.

## Testing and completion

First, run a local multi-turn fixture with `execute_commands`, `task_complete`, malformed native-tool arguments, a changed history, and an attempted `image_read`; compare served token IDs, log probabilities, masks, observations, and verifier outcomes at the final projection boundary. Exercise setup failure, inference timeout and retry, Daytona command failure, agent timeout, cancellation, upload failure, and machine cleanup, asserting one outcome and retained diagnostics per attempt. Then run a version-pinned Daytona RL smoke with at least two tool turns through verification, one optimizer update, weight synchronization, and evaluation; attach the non-secret config and durable model, trajectory, and verifier artifact links here.

## Open questions

- Can Harbor's current LiteLLM request path carry a stable request ID through retries without resampling? Probe this before enabling on-policy training.
- Does Kira's native-tool response preserve the exact served completion token span when the provider returns tool calls and reasoning fields? Reject the mode if the answer is no.

issues.body:
Allow RL runs to select Harbor's Terminus-2 controller, retaining its prompts, terminal interaction, context management, and grading inputs.

Current main (`2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950`) routes task rollouts through RolloutEngine. Its [agent adapter](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_runtime.py) requires `BaseInstalledAgent` and rejects host-side Harbor agents. comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

At MarinSkyRL main (82396a73), both the installed-agent runner and full Harbor trial runner require BaseInstalledAgent; Harbor's Terminus2 derives from BaseAgent, so selection fails before its first model turn. The full-trial path already lets Harbor run setup, verification, and cleanup while a correlation-keyed bridge sends model requests through RolloutEngine. Terminus-2's default summarization can leave its rollout details incomplete, and [#10326](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10326) reports that a history reset can discard earlier trainable actions.

**Relevant code**
- [agent_runtime.py, lines 150–275](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_runtime.py#L150-L275) — full trial and installed-agent gate
- [harbor_trial_session.py, lines 38–114](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/harbor_trial_session.py#L38-L114) — trial grade and model session
- [agent_backend.py, lines 31–116](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_backend.py#L31-L116) — correlation and served token data
- [terminus_2.py, lines 316–445](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/e96b6dcca1513e97e43523eaa971a85c68fcedae/src/harbor/agents/terminus_2/terminus_2.py#L316-L445) — host agent and context options
- [task_projections.py, lines 238–352](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_projections.py#L238-L352) — training rows and masks

# Terminus-2 shared rollout plan

## Design

1. Extend the existing full Harbor trial route in agent_runtime.py and harbor_trial_session.py to accept a host-side BaseAgent. Keep Terminus-2 in Harbor. Use Trial.create and Trial.run so Harbor continues to own the controller, Daytona environment, verifier, attempt deadlines, cancellation, and sandbox cleanup. Give each host trial a local inference URL and unique correlation header; installed agents keep their current leased endpoint. Reject a model request without an active trial correlation ID.
2. Add a checked-in Terminus-2 RL recipe with a trainable policy, Daytona snapshot mapping, verifier, and evaluation settings. Validate the supported mode before allocating training workers: text chat completions through LiteLLM, exact token capture and requested behavior log probabilities, no Responses API, and summarization disabled for the first release. A context overflow must stop that attempt as nontrainable. Summarization can be enabled only after its rewritten prompts and all generated actions can be represented without loss; configuration that requests it before then must fail preflight.
3. Use served Prompt/ModelTurn records as the training source of truth. Before a trainable smoke, land a strict append-only guard for [#10326](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10326): transport metadata and generation-budget changes must not reset the trace, while genuine non-prefix rewrites fail closed. Check every turn's prompt IDs, completion IDs, finite aligned log probabilities, and loss mask through the chosen training projection. A last-segment-only sample must never receive the whole-trial reward.
4. Keep retry ownership singular. Harbor's controller handles tool operations and its model client handles inference-request retries; the bridge must replay an identical accepted request without generating another action. MarinSkyRL's TaskWorker owns whole-trial retry/backoff, while Harbor Trial owns verification and cleanup on success, timeout, error, or cancellation. Preserve the original Harbor exception and trial URI in the grading result. Missing or invalid verifier scores and infrastructure failures must follow the configured nontraining/error policy, even if the agent produced turns.

## Validation

Add focused CPU tests for a two-turn host trial, per-trial request isolation, duplicate inference requests, token/log-probability alignment into both training projections, a changed prompt, context overflow, cancellation and cleanup, verifier failure, and trial retry classification. Then run one live Daytona smoke with a trainable policy and GRPO objective: at least two terminal turns, verifier result, trajectory conversion, one optimizer update, inference-weight synchronization, and evaluation. Attach the pinned recipe, model and verifier traces, trial URI, and training/evaluation results to this issue.

## Coordination and open question

Searches of open PRs in Marin and MarinSkyRL found no Terminus-2 host-agent implementation. [MarinSkyRL #1030](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/1030) changes nearby rollout evidence and failure handling; reuse its final contracts. [#10386](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10386) can share the host-agent bridge but needs separate native-tool and multimodal validation. For a later summarization-capable mode, should every segment receive the whole-trial reward, or should summary-only actions be excluded from the loss? Decide this before enabling summarization.

issues.author: yonromai
issues.body:
The 4K RL snapshot was checked through 28 September 2026, 11:45 a.m. Pacific. Long-context performance-only probes were checked on 29 September. Comments are the dated experiment log. Expand C1–C2 and P1–P4 for run IDs, configurations, and evidence.

## At a glance

- **4K correctness passes** on H100 and GB200 with recorded expert routes replayed during Megatron scoring. Native routing fails the numerical gate.
- **Hero learns GSM8K** on both: held-out accuracy rises by 4.6 percentage points on H100 and 5.5 on GB200 after 64 updates. Full optimizer restore at step 32 and continuation pass on both. This is one training seed per accelerator.
- **65K training capacity passed separately:** full Hero completed 65,536-token Megatron updates and exact checkpoint continuation on 256 H100s and 64 GB200s. This used synthetic data and fresh AdamW, not long-context RL or vLLM serving. See C2.
- **Beyond 4K:** Hero served 256K requests with short outputs on H100 and GB200. Sustained long-response throughput and long-context RL correctness remain unmeasured. See P4.
- **Fleet sizing is still open.** A 48-learner + 8-server GB200 run now passes, but it does not establish the best fleet or resolve slow online response supply.
- **Qualified RL scope:** BF16, TP1, non-eager batch-invariant vLLM, at most 4,096 total tokens, grouped async RL, fresh MuonH/AdamH/Adam, frozen query-balancing bias, and staleness at most one. The >4K probes do not qualify longer-context RL, FP8, another task, or a released wheel.

Sources: [numerical decision](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6299979623) and [step-64 audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6299981395).

## Correctness and learning

| Hardware | Ratio outliers / tokens | GSM8K correct, version 0 → 64 | Step-32 restore → 64 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| H100 | 6 / 50,059 (0.012%) | 563 → 610 / 1,024 (+4.59 points) | Passed |
| GB200 | 5 / 54,090 (0.009%) | 569 → 625 / 1,024 (+5.47 points) | Passed |

Gate: fewer than 0.1% of sampled-token trainer/serving probability ratios outside [0.8, 1.2], with the **same token** scored by both. See C1 for the separate runs, uncertainty intervals, and reward limits.

## Measured performance

The three rates count different tokens: learner-only **prompt + response**, serving-only **generated decode**, and whole-RL **accepted, loss-masked response**.

### Learner-only

Each update uses the same 116,351-token bank. Rates exclude serving, scoring, and checkpointing.

| Model | Hardware | Learner GPUs | Seconds/update | Sequence tok/s/GPU |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Hero | H100 | 96 | 19.97 | 60.7 |
| Snowball | H100 | 32 | 5.57 | 653 |
| Hero | GB200 | 48 | 60.36 | 40.2 |
| Snowball | GB200 | 16 | 10.45 | 696 |

These are efficient **tested** layouts, not proven minimum fleets or measured MFU. Hero on 64 GB200s reduces update time to 52.13 s but uses 15.1% more GPU-seconds than 48. See P1.

### Serving-only

The clients continuously supply a forced-length 4K GSM8K bank to non-eager vLLM. Decode rates are aggregate, not per GPU.

| Model | Hardware | Serving GPUs | Clients | Decode tok/s | KV preemptions |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Hero | H100 | 32 | 1,280 | 5,243 | 120 |
| Hero | H100 | 32 | 1,536 | 5,690 | 448 |
| Hero | GB200 | 16 | 1,024 | 3,492 | 0 |
| Snowball | H100 | 8 | 4,096 | 32,967 | 0 |

GB200 is near its configured running-sequence cap, not a measured hardware maximum. Raising the H100 cap from 64 to 128 sequences at 1,536 clients improved **whole-bank** completion rate by 16%, while supplied decode fell 2%; an online RL check is pending. A Snowball GB200 curve is missing. See P2.

### Whole asynchronous RL

Rates include response wait, scoring, training, and weight publication. The denominator includes **all learner and serving GPUs**; first-update, evaluation, and checkpoint time are excluded.

| Model | Hardware | Learner GPUs | Serving GPUs | Warm window | Accepted response tok/s | Response wait |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Hero | H100 | 128 | 32 | 4 cycles | 1,781 | 14.9% |
| Hero | GB200 | 48 | 16 | 29 updates | 73.6 | 57.9% |
| Hero | GB200 | 48 | 8 | 4 updates | 75.5 | 50.2% |
| Snowball | H100 | 32 | 8 | 2 updates | 5,743 | 0.38 s/update |

The GB200 48+8 run passed. On matched step numbers, it delivered 75.46 accepted tok/s versus 76.58 for 48+16, or 12.6% more tokens per GPU-second. Its responses were 15.8% shorter, so this does **not** prove that fewer servers improve throughput. Different batches and response lengths also prevent a Snowball-to-Hero speed ratio. See P3.

## Still open

- **Feed the GB200 learner:** A staleness-two admission-window diagnostic is running. The earlier 48+16 run spent 57.9% of warm time waiting for responses and 28.3% publishing weights. More generation workers alone did not lift the 32-group admission cap.
- **Finish serving sizing:** The disposable >4K probes establish fit and short-output rates. Sustained long-response generation, online RL throughput, and an efficient fleet at each longer length remain unmeasured. The permanent export and qualified RL path still have a 4,096-position bound. See P4.
- **Price the numerical choice:** On fixed H100 tokens and weights, route replay cut ratio outliers from 114 to 5 of 50,962, while adding 24.1% to the scoring timer. Its whole-RL cost is unmeasured. See the [matched TIM comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6299980536).
- **Package the tested code:** [#799](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/799) pins wheels that do not yet include the qualified [vLLM #77](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/77) and [#78](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/78) changes.
- **Optional FA4 serving follow-up:** [vLLM #81](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/issues/81) tracks batch-invariant FA4 and its Hero GB200 throughput value. Current 4K qualification stays on FA2; no Hero FA4 gain is established.

<details>
<summary>C1 — numerical, learning, and restore runs</summary>

All use the permanent step-144000 BF16 [serving export](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6299979623), GSM8K with eight responses per group, a 4,096-token combined cap, and source vLLM revision `25f0fc1aae71cccb6da65046cff13145512a6946`. Fresh RL uses MuonH/AdamH/Adam at 1e-6; resume restores the RL optimizer. The fixed-weight score check uses the same response tokens, positions, and captured expert routes. The strict `#### number` reward was independently recomputed from all 12,288 retained evaluation responses, but can reject mathematically correct answers in another format. The paired 95% intervals for the held-out gains are +2.54 to +6.64 points on H100 and +3.61 to +7.32 on GB200; they reflect question sampling, not training-seed variation. One training seed per accelerator was tested.

**H100 learning:** 128 learners + 24 servers; PP16/EP8/CP2. Iris `/romain/hero-learning-h100-01a0dca4-a6`; SkyRL source `ff03e83baa0624144cdeb9944b72f96813468045`. Reward manifest: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-learning-01a0dca4/analysis/h100-step64-rewards-20260927/manifest.json`.

**GB200 learning:** 48 learners + 16 servers; PP12/EP4/CP4. Iris `/romain/hero-learning-gb200-01a0dca4-a3`; SkyRL source `d9c9997ea13c314fd2ddd2c698b8d2d50320e2a0`. Reward manifest: `s3://hero-checkpoints/marin/users/romain/hero-learning-01a0dca4/analysis/gb200-final64-20260927/manifest.json`.

The H100 6/50,059 numerical check in the opening table comes from the separate `/romain/hero-integrated-h100-01a0dca4-a8` run (source `3d455ebf648fb3a58764f20afa5923a7afffa0c5`), not the H100 a6 learning continuation. The GB200 check comes from a3. Both learning rows are TP1. Each restored the step-32 full optimizer checkpoint and continued to step 64 with executed-route checks, sampled weight readbacks, finite rewards and optimizer samples, frozen biases, and staleness at most one. Maximum observed PPO clipping on the continuations was 0.04438% H100 and 0.17554% GB200. The [final audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6299981395) reports limits: sampled state checks are not full-byte checkpoint checksums; repeated same-checkpoint evaluations changed three answers per platform. The earlier [AdamW/eager baseline](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6299979409) is historical and does not define this decision.

</details>

<details>
<summary>C2 — 65K Megatron training capacity, not long-context RL</summary>

The step-108000 full-Hero BF16 export completed repeated synthetic AdamW updates at 65,536 tokens on both accelerators. Each run saved and restored model plus fresh optimizer state and reproduced its next update bit for bit. Both used context parallelism 4, activation recomputation, and CPU optimizer offload. This does **not** test the step-144000 RL checkpoint, MuonH/AdamH/Adam at 65K, long-context answer quality, vLLM generation, or end-to-end RL throughput.

| Hardware | GPUs / hosts | 32K → 65K peak PyTorch GPU allocation | 65K steady update time | Iris run |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| H100 | 256 / 32 | 38.34 → 63.15 GiB | 42.46 / 41.78 s | `/romain/hero-megatron-full-h100-01a0bca4-a10` |
| GB200 | 64 / 16 | 138.26 → 154.02 GiB | 22.65 / 22.74 s | `/romain/hero-megatron-full-gb200-01a0bca4-a6` |

The peaks exclude GPU allocations outside PyTorch and the two hardware layouts use different sharding and optimizer-offload fractions; do not read them as a controlled H100-versus-GB200 memory ratio. The [training report and exact configurations](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/e3f5fff039f9b965d3f014584f8abd34164c0381/docs/grug-megatron-training.md#full-hero-capacity) identify the immutable reports at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-megatron-01a0bca4/full-h100-a10/report.json` and `.../full-gb200-a6/report.json` (source revisions `d386f521` and `7dc88a2b`).

</details>

<details>
<summary>P1 — fixed-bank learner runs and throughput denominator</summary>

All rows use BF16, TP1, the same 128-sequence bank: 19,327 prompt plus 97,024 response tokens, 116,351 unpadded sequence tokens, maximum combined length 4,041. Bank SHA-256: `6d97026e4235babacdfe1d04d4e53d9e7deef4c68e1c96a6be73a12ced09c896`. Rates divide that bank by the median of three later warm training updates and all learner GPUs; scoring, serving, and checkpointing are excluded. Hero uses fresh MuonH/AdamH/Adam, Snowball AdamW. Useful active FLOP/s estimates exclude recomputation, communication, optimizer, and much elementwise work; they are **not measured MFU**.

| Model / hardware | Learner GPUs | PP | EP | CP | Iris run |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Hero H100 | 96 | 24 | 4 | 1 | `/romain/hero-learner-h100-96g-01a0dca4-a2` |
| Snowball H100 | 32 | 2 | 8 | 1 | `/romain/snowball-learner-h100-32g-01a0dca4-a1` |
| Hero GB200 | 48 | 12 | 4 | 4 | `/romain/hero-gb200-learner-48g-01a0e406-a1` |
| Snowball GB200 | 16 | 2 | 8 | 1 | `/romain/gb200-snowball-learner-16g-01a0e406-a1` |

H100 source revisions: Hero `80907a6de65c49cee29ca3b13c2fee27d2a05556`, Snowball `fa7059545a8a6ec62456fda3bdb9ce05dae103f8`. Their run outputs are under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-learning-01a0dca4/`. A later H100 Hero 96-GPU control without the profiler measured 20.25 s/update and 59.9 sequence tok/s/GPU, close to the cited point. Both GB200 runs use source `ca91727c765e6f79399b8844b195108cc78a6ee1`; outputs are under `s3://hero-checkpoints/marin/users/romain/hero-perf-01a0e406/`. Matching the bank does not match model, optimizer, or parallel layout. Hero 64 GB200 learners shorten this update to 52.13 s but increase GPU-seconds/update by 15.1% versus 48.

</details>

<details>
<summary>P2 — supplied serving protocol and run IDs</summary>

The 1,024-row GSM8K bank fixes prompt and forced-response lengths (combined 244–4,041, mean 916); SHA-256 `b15aeac7c3eb714fe45fc6b8e274342ad26f00970d84f2b7985b42c422b4e905`. At least four full client waves run at the cited points. Native token-counter deltas come from a supplied window before the final drain. These are BF16, TP1, non-eager, batch-invariant vLLM probes with prefix caching off. They measure server capacity, not accepted online RL tokens.

| Model / hardware | Serving GPUs | Clients | EP | Sequence cap | Batched-token cap | Iris run |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Hero H100 | 32 | 1,280–1,536 | 32 | 64 | 512 | `/romain/hero-h100-serve-32g-knee-01a0e406-a1` |
| Hero GB200 | 16 | 1,024 | 16 | 64 | 512 | `/romain/hero-gb200-serve-16g-01a0e406-a2` |
| Snowball H100 | 8 | 4,096 | 8 | 1,024 | 4,096 | Raw S3 report below |

Hero H100 source `9ffb4919322b4bd67cb51b05c98332f506e644c1`; raw report `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-perf-01a0e406/h100-serve-32g-knee-a1/analysis/report-3093ac5959d84e2f2be00fd0e5d657481e184bd53b9b392e8e364f997d159dab.json`. Hero GB200 source `ca91727c765e6f79399b8844b195108cc78a6ee1`; output `s3://hero-checkpoints/marin/users/romain/hero-perf-01a0e406/gb200-serve-16g-a2/`. Snowball H100 source `b8c37cc90111795c3cccb355b0de163796280b8f`; raw report `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-learning-01a0dca4/snowball-capacity-h100-a8/analysis/report-bb47d02f3c5f23179dbcf6b58aa58939f6aeb837e31ba0abe875d40df2f1e761.json`.

The same-node H100 cap-128 control is `/romain/hero-h100-serve-32g-highseq-01a0e406-a1`; output `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-perf-01a0e406/h100-serve-32g-highseq-a1/`, raw report SHA-256 `e4ce600daaadc3f03d1768c68d14b7fe336f7267b5463e9bbfc8dd23416f7bec`. At 1,536 clients, supplied decode was 5,577 versus 5,690 tok/s with cap 64; whole-bank rate was 3,694 versus 3,183 tok/s. The latter is a finite-bank gain, not a supplied-throughput plateau. The GB200 1,024-client point hit the configured sequence cap before KV capacity.

</details>

<details>
<summary>P3 — whole async RL protocol, comparisons, and remaining evidence</summary>

Each group asks for eight completions. Generation overlaps learner updates. The reported rate is accepted loss-masked response tokens divided by complete ordinary warm-cycle wall time, including response wait, scoring, training, and weight publication. Evaluations and checkpoint steps are excluded. These rows do **not** use the same batch or realized response lengths, so their rates cannot be treated as a model-only speed ratio.

| Model / hardware | Groups/update | Group workers | Window | Iris run |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| Hero H100 128+32 | 512 | 1,024 | Updates 2–5 | `/romain/hero-integrated-h100-01a0dca4-a8` |
| Hero GB200 48+16 | 16 | 32 | 29 ordinary updates | `/romain/hero-learning-gb200-01a0dca4-a3` |
| Hero GB200 48+8 | 16 | 32 | Updates 34–37 | `/romain/hero-gb200-feed-48p8s-01a0e406-a2` |
| Snowball H100 32+8 | 256 | 512 | Updates 2–3 | `/romain/snowball-integrated-h100-01a0dca4-a3` |

Hero H100 source `3d455ebf648fb3a58764f20afa5923a7afffa0c5`, report SHA-256 `3adca5d0673b0f9c4d8ba5b571a4618a769d3c464aa1ef3c113534a99fba96c6`. Hero GB200 48+16 source `d9c9997ea13c314fd2ddd2c698b8d2d50320e2a0`, report SHA-256 `e7e6e7cc6b8d8938e21cd6700f426ee7ca1815d6a864151dcc8aed04277c079a`; its [step-64 manifest](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6299981395) and Iris job provide state checks.

The first GB200 48+8 attempt failed before an update. Its identity-only retry passed 14/14 Iris tasks, fixed-weight checks and four warm updates. Source `9ffb4919322b4bd67cb51b05c98332f506e644c1`; final report SHA-256 `3e6955ccddf02e4a1fcdffa6eae35c875bf95971cf1f42fe78363f7f8bcba31c`; output `s3://hero-checkpoints/marin/users/romain/hero-perf-01a0e406/gb200-feed-48p8s-a2/`. Its same-numbered 48+16 comparison is a workload-sensitive sizing point, not an optimizer learning curve. Doubling GB200 group workers from 32 to 64 did not lift the 32-group admission ceiling at batch 16 and staleness one. The online server had low sustained running/KV load; long group tails and publication remain live hypotheses, not proven kernel limits.

Retain these cited object-store prefixes and the C1 manifests during experimental-storage cleanup. The raw reports and Iris jobs are the audit trail; a local agent-session path alone is not a team-retrievable citation. Related Snowball numerical findings are in [marin #7554](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7554).

</details>


<details>
<summary>P4 — longer-context serving probes and capacity limits (29 September)</summary>

The step-144000 BF16 weights ran in non-eager vLLM with HF, vLLM, and rotary position limits raised together in disposable configurations. The permanent export and qualified RL path remain at 4,096 tokens. GSM8K prompts were repeated to reach the requested combined lengths (input bank SHA-256 `6b83c65a4faf7418c9cc28035225978fb1a164cabe7fd4e30f87be4b76f7cd35`; vLLM revision `25f0fc1aae71cccb6da65046cff13145512a6946`). Each bank used one-token outputs to measure finite-bank prefill plus request overhead; selected 64-token continuations also passed at 64K, 128K, and 256K. These runs do not test answer quality beyond 4K, sustained long-response decoding, or whole-RL throughput.

| Combined length | H100 prompt tokens/s/GPU | GB200 prompt tokens/s/GPU |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 64K | 329 on 32 GPUs | 530 on 16 GPUs |
| 128K | 268 on 32 GPUs | 506 on 16 GPUs |
| 256K | 159 on 64 GPUs, PP2 | 371 on 16 GPUs |

The H100 32-GPU layout had about 208K KV slots per engine, insufficient for one 256K request; 64 GPUs with PP2 passed. The GB200 16-GPU layout had about 1.13M slots per engine and passed 256K at 16 clients; a separate 32-client one-token bank also passed. The table's H100 256K layout differs from its 64K/128K layout. These rates cannot be scaled into the 32K-rollout rack/day estimate. The 65K synthetic trainer result is in C2. 128K/256K trainer layouts are extrapolations only; their same-layout memory projections exceed physical HBM.

Audit trail:

- H100 64K/128K: Iris `/romain/hero-h100-long-32g-128k-01a0e406-a1`; source `1e0f0571d1a5e2162c3296b2e38a5d9d8abed6b9`; output `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-perf-01a0e406/h100-long-32g-128k-a1/`; raw report SHA-256 `4d98a3c024438dc84a2dc971fd4fede729ece41d2097d0a272b03aba4a505788`.
- H100 256K: Iris `/romain/hero-h100-long-64g-256k-pp2-01a0e406-a2`; source `784895246e2a892d1850d6c024a043f20f920654`; output `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-perf-01a0e406/h100-long-64g-256k-pp2-a2/`; raw report SHA-256 `f66944e7c639c95f20c094a62acbc3116e07edd98fa2f2a56e973f0741104e92`.
- GB200 64K–256K: Iris `/romain/hero-gb200-long-16g-256k-01a0e406-a1`; source `0e4aacd8fa83fbf224318962d302f63bc5ce85e9`; output `s3://hero-checkpoints/marin/users/romain/hero-perf-01a0e406/gb200-long-16g-256k-a1/`; raw report SHA-256 `fcedf2cc1aa6dacf9eefec047f555b5e4d6c67cc58e91aec848efc80268ced5c`.

</details>

🤖 **Hero 4K Megatron update (2026-09-23).** At the pinned step-108000 BF16 export, full Hero scored four prespecified H100 GSM8K captures on the same token IDs, positions, masks, and captured 48-layer routes: **15,831 response tokens**. Full-prefix `abs(log p_Megatron − log p_vLLM)` was mean **0.010696**, p99 **0.060486**, max **0.528999**. The importance ratio had **2/15,831 below 0.8**, none above 1.2; actual PPO clipping was zero under the probe’s *synthetic alternating* advantage signs. Real advantages and learning quality are unproven because all 32 saved GSM8K continuations hit the 4K cap without an exact final-answer line.

The 128-H100 retry succeeded 16/16. On one 4K backward/update, captured-route hit and executed-set match were both **1.0**, native ordered/set mismatch **0.318/0.100**, router gradient norm **0.135**, and update time **118.9 s**. All per-token Megatron scores in three route modes reproduced exactly across two independent runs. The zero trainer log ratio compares Megatron with its own rescored old-action values; it is not serving parity. No causal SkyRL defect or code fix was identified. The two largest rank-0 outliers are response indices **1,532/2,672** (prediction positions **1,661/2,801**) for the serving-path trace.

Report, raw per-token scores, resolved config, and exact producer scripts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-megatron-4k-01a0bca4/h100-128-a2/` (`report.json` SHA256 `8e17cdac1348d2ce997e0a6eec3f17df26ed3537d971575c1ef1f7bedd0a4320`). The 64-GB200 transfer check was deferred: only 48 GB200 were free cluster-wide at the final check. The larger correctness sample and sustained end-to-end RL timing in this issue remain open.
