comments.body:
🤖 GLM-5.3 completed the September 25 BixBench-Verified-50 run using merged Harbor main and Pi: **39 correct, 7 incorrect, 4 ungraded**. Accuracy among graded tasks is **84.78% (39/46)**; coverage is **92% (46/50)**. The four ungraded outcomes cannot all be attributed to the model. [EvalDash run](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/glm53-bixbench-verified50-pi-main-20260925-150940).

The run used [Marin a795b1d](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a795b1d4306c71b1f4fc52cdcac2b5b1f0ed70d4), [Harbor 21e0ea6](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/tree/21e0ea6a0cc1a0b617aebd86988ea93e1795f84a), and [task snapshot 674c37c](https://github.com/gonzalobenegas/harbor-datasets/tree/674c37ca8b2e537d36a1886f6cba99f2c6bdaa2f/datasets/bixbench-verified-50). There was one fresh attempt per question, up to 16 concurrent trials, Pi 0.87.0, 32,768 tokens of total context, an 8,192-token per-response limit, an 8,192-token compaction reserve, and setup/agent/verifier limits of 360/1,800/300 seconds. Daytona storage was explicitly set to 10 GiB. Grading used decimal-precision-v1 and Together GPT-OSS-120B. Exact served weights revision was unavailable.

Pi was configured with `thinking=medium` and `thinking_format=chat-template`. The [provider registration](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/21e0ea6a0cc1a0b617aebd86988ea93e1795f84a/src/harbor/agents/installed/pi.py) disables `supportsReasoningEffort` and sends `enable_thinking`; “medium” therefore does not establish a provider-enforced medium reasoning budget. This applies the Pi runtime/budget settings from [#9409](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9409) to Verified-50; it is a different benchmark from that policy's 205-task BixBench CLI corrections set. The earlier Terminus-2 result also used different agent and time budgets, so the aggregate difference is not a controlled model comparison.

| Tasks | Saved evidence | Attribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bix-30-q3`, `bix-53-q2` | Pi ended with `stopReason: length` after approximately 5m10s and 6m18s. The verifier explicitly reported that `/workspace/answer.txt` was absent. | Incomplete agent output under the response budget, combined with Pi/Harbor termination handling. No evidence of a judge service failure. |
| `bix-31-q2`, `bix-49-q4` | Both agents reached 30 minutes while a tool was still running; the last commands ran `notebook.py` and `deseq2_analysis.R`, respectively. Both subsequent verifiers timed out at 300 seconds. No answer or verifier-output artifact was recovered. | Agent time-budget exhaustion followed by verifier failures. Saved evidence does not establish why the computations took so long or where verification stalled. |

Source inspection and an offline replay on October 9 narrowed the harness behavior:

- [Pi 0.87.0's loop](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono/blob/16787ad5b2dc748047f314ca1bfe7708f30f54f3/packages/agent/src/agent-loop.ts#L244-L319) can end after a length-limited response with no tool calls and no continuation. Harbor's pinned Pi validator only rejects a final `error`. Feeding that exact validator a synthetic `length` event returned exit 0; an `error` control returned exit 1. Thus a truncated response can reach verification as a normal agent exit. This reproduces the validator behavior, not the biological computation or model generation.
- [Daytona cancellation cleanup](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/21e0ea6a0cc1a0b617aebd86988ea93e1795f84a/src/harbor/environments/daytona/environment.py#L1860-L1907) cancels local polling and runs `pkill -9 -f opencode`. Pi does not pass a remote execution timeout in its run command. That leaves a concrete gap in stopping Pi and its children before shared-sandbox verification. Continued processes could interfere with verification; this is a plausible contributor, not a demonstrated cause of these two verifier timeouts. Missing verifier logs alone do not prove the grader never started, because Harbor downloads those logs after the exec completes.
- [Trial exception recording](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/21e0ea6a0cc1a0b617aebd86988ea93e1795f84a/src/harbor/trial/trial.py#L430-L452) deliberately lets the later exception replace the earlier one. A final `VerifierTimeoutError` therefore does not exclude an earlier agent timeout.
- The [Verified-50 grader](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/21e0ea6a0cc1a0b617aebd86988ea93e1795f84a/adapters/bixbench-verified-50/src/bixbench_verified50/template/tests/llm_judge.py#L76-L85) deliberately returns without reward when no answer exists. This is the pinned missing-submission convention, not a newly established grading bug. #9409 also does not automatically assign zero to Harbor agent errors. No grades were changed.

The saved launch configuration allowed up to 10 retries for an explicit infrastructure-exception list, but omitted `VerifierTimeoutError` and `RewardFileNotFoundError`. Consequently those failures were not automatically retried, despite #9409 classifying verifier timeouts as retryable infrastructure errors. This is a launch-policy mismatch for the two verifier timeouts.

The September 25 artifact inspection and sandbox inventory found no recoverable answer/workspace for verifier-only replay. No solver or judge calls were made during this diagnosis, and no verifier retry could be executed faithfully. On October 9 the old diagnostic job was no longer available through Iris and this VM lacked direct CoreWeave storage credentials; the new findings above come from the pinned source and offline validator replay, combined with the previously recorded artifact inspection.

Next: validate generic Pi process-tree cancellation and verifier isolation with a bounded harness reproduction, record response truncation explicitly, and decide the intended continuation behavior within the existing budget. Retain verifier logs and answer artifacts even on failure. Those checks should precede any fresh four-task solver retry. The biological causes of the long computations remain unresolved; [harbor#192](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/issues/192) already tracks Verified-50 source/runtime concerns, including a separate earlier R failure.

comments.author: gonzalobenegas
comments.body:
🤖 Snowball v0.1 was unreliable at completing the agent workflow in this BiomniBench-DA configuration: **38 of 50 tasks ended without a nonempty report at either required path**. The mean benchmark score was **4.24/100**. This result combines submission failures with low rubric scores on the submitted work; it does not isolate biology knowledge from agent execution or model–harness integration. The trace audit found no evidence of a general report-collection defect, but does not establish that the serving and agent configuration was appropriate for this checkpoint.

[EvalDash run](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/20261020-144256-open-athena-Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14-biomnibench-da-pi-volume-free50-e8bf). The displayed metric averages rubric points and missing-submission zeros; it is not accuracy. This run uses five input variants and substitutes MiniMax for the dataset's original judge. The adapter scorer also applies signed rubric penalties and validates complete criterion coverage; the released scorer parses unsigned points. Comparisons with published results require matching these choices. No reference model was evaluated under this same protocol. This is supplementary to the Snowball v0.1 release evaluations in [#10197](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197); their benchmark set and aggregate are unchanged.

| Final submission state | Tasks |
| --- | ---: |
| Both nonempty reports preserved and rubric-graded | 5 |
| One nonempty report preserved and rubric-graded | 7 |
| Neither report nonempty at the required paths; native zero | 38 |
| Total | 50 |

A missing submission means neither `/app/trace.md` nor `/app/answer.txt` contained text beyond whitespace at verification time. It does not establish that the model did no analysis or lacked a biological answer: some traces contain attempted analyses, simulated execution, or reports written elsewhere.

The score decomposes into **24% submission coverage × 17.67/100 mean score among the 12 submitted tasks = 4.24/100 overall** (conditional mean rounded). Only five tasks supplied both reports. The 12-task mean describes a selected subset under this judge and scorer; it does not estimate how the other 38 would score after fixing submission. Submission failures account for 38 zeros, while the submitted work also received low rubric scores.

Structured events from the selected final-attempt Pi logs for all 50 logical tasks were audited, with detailed inspection of the examples below. The table assigns each missing-submission task once: the four specific submission failures take precedence; the remaining 34 are grouped by termination. Filename checks use executed tool arguments and do not by themselves prove that no indirect write was attempted.

| Observed termination or submission failure | Tasks |
| --- | ---: |
| Normal model stop; no executed tool argument contained `trace.md` or `answer.txt` | 22 |
| Per-response output limit reached before submission | 11 |
| Agent timeout at 30 minutes | 1 |
| Both reports written under `/app/analysis/` instead of `/app/` | 1 |
| Empty `answer.txt` and no `trace.md` | 1 |
| Malformed write arguments rejected by the tool | 1 |
| Analysis script failed before writing reports | 1 |
| Total | 38 |

These are observations from the saved events, not 38 independently established checkpoint defects. Ten of the 11 output-limit cases generated thousands of repetitions of “Now.” All 11 consumed the configured 16,384 output tokens. Pi then ended without another solver turn; this termination behavior contributes to missing submissions under the evaluated protocol. The [earlier Verified-50 investigation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6086246928) documents the same Pi behavior with length-limited responses.

Examples distinguish execution from text that only describes execution:

- `da-26-2` executed zero tools but generated a simulated terminal transcript. Other cases emitted terminal-control JSON or incomplete tool-call markup as ordinary assistant text.
- `da-10-1` received successful write confirmations for `/app/analysis/trace.md` and `/app/analysis/answer.txt`. The prompt and verifier require `/app/trace.md` and `/app/answer.txt`.
- `da-17-5` streamed malformed JSON for a report write. Replaying the saved argument deltas through Pi 0.87.0 and its exact `partial-json` 0.1.7 dependency reproduced the parsed `{ "path": "/app/trace.md" }` argument and missing-content validation failure. A valid multiline-JSON control parsed correctly.

All 50 initial prompts contained the required absolute output paths. Reports from 12 tasks were preserved and rubric-graded; three successful direct writes were also compared byte-for-byte with their archived verifier files and matched. Native per-task rewards, the sealed 50-row sample archive, and the canonical/EvalDash mean agree. Missing submissions receive zero before any judge call, so those 38 zeros do not depend on MiniMax's rubric judgments. No scores were repaired and no new model calls were made during the audit.

An independent review recomputed the 212 total points, mean, coverage, and failure counts from the saved task records. The audit bundle referenced below contains the per-task summaries, inspected trace details, parser replay, and audit scripts.

The evidence implicates several stages of execution. Repetition is an observed generation failure; Pi ending after a length-limited response is a harness behavior that can prevent a later submission. Invalid tool formats could reflect checkpoint behavior or a serving/interface mismatch. Successful report collection on other tasks argues against a general collection defect, but does not resolve those integration questions. The audit cannot attribute all 38 failures to the checkpoint or determine whether the weakness is biology-specific.

The next useful comparisons would be a reference model on the identical protocol and a small controlled Snowball diagnostic capturing raw model tokens, API requests/responses, and executed tools. The former would test whether this setup permits another model to complete the tasks; the latter would help separate checkpoint, template/parser, sampling, and serving effects. Pi events retain API text and argument deltas, but the inspected artifacts do not contain pre-parser model token captures. Neither comparison has been run; no diagnostic GPU rerun has been launched.

<details>
<summary>Protocol and reproducibility</summary>

- Model: [open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14/tree/6783e9743478bd25a9ce03ab3460e84d6a9814b0), revision `6783e9743478bd25a9ce03ab3460e84d6a9814b0` (v0.1).
- Dataset: [phylobio/BiomniBench-DA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/phylobio/BiomniBench-DA/tree/e1c8ca5e11a620087bc48d97888eb69176a1f235), revision `e1c8ca5e11a620087bc48d97888eb69176a1f235`; all 50 public tasks, no held-out tasks. The `derived-input-v1` variant uses 45 native-input tasks and five existing input variants: `da-1-3`/`da-1-4` omit an unused counts matrix; `da-17-1`/`da-17-3`/`da-17-5` use the previously pinned all-cell raw-count H5AD, omitting normalized expression and embeddings. Questions, required outputs, and rubrics are unchanged.
- Runtime: [Marin 75a5690](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/75a5690b0ff2e1510d73e576649e3e059f06da9a), [Harbor 016dd78](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/tree/016dd78b301b621ee4089f2da5776ebe80236820), Pi 0.87.0. BixBench execution settings from [policy #10197](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197): 65,536 total-context tokens, 16,384 output tokens per response, 32,768 compaction reserve; 360/1,800/300-second setup/agent/verifier limits; 16 concurrent trials. Daytona used at most 8 GiB RAM and 10 GiB disk, with no volumes.
- Serving: Snowball on 8 H100s, TP=1/DP=8 with expert parallelism and the native chat template; Hermes tool parser, no reasoning parser, `thinking_format=chat-template`. Judge served by a separate eight-H100 Iris job: [MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8/tree/c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba), revision `c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba`, TP=8; temperature 0, 8,192 output tokens, native rubric levels, scores divided by 100 for Marin's reward metric. This replaces the dataset's original judge configuration.
- There were 50 logical trials and 52 physical solver attempts. Two verifier timeouts triggered the policy's automatic infrastructure retries; both failed attempts and their replacements retain separately readable result records and Pi logs. The separate preliminary pilot is excluded. The evaluator succeeded, both serving jobs terminated, and the final Daytona inventory found no sandboxes belonging to this run or its preflight.

It contains `launch_full.py`, the task/input manifest, and exact configurations. The campaign was placed under `experiments/evaluation/campaigns/biomnibench-da-volume-free50-20261020/` in the pinned Marin workspace. Execution used the canonical `prepare_evaluation_batch` and `run_evaluation_batch` functions in the same CPU orchestrator after remote staging and sandbox preflight. The submitted entry point was:

  ```bash
  python -c 'import runpy; runpy.run_path("experiments/evaluation/campaigns/biomnibench-da-volume-free50-20261020/launch_full.py", run_name="__main__")'
  ```
- Original task outcomes, verifier files and Pi logs remain under the run's `results/harbor_jobs/harbor_prepared_tasks_6dd0c97fd4c6/` prefix. Each logical trial's `result.json` identifies its selected physical `trial_uri`; the native log is `<trial_uri>/agent/pi.txt`. EvalDash samples currently have no automatic Pi trajectory links, although native logs are readable through its artifact endpoint.
- Audit bundle: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261020-144256-open-athena-Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14-biomnibench-da-pi-volume-free50-e8bf/provenance/submission-audit-20261020.tar.gz`, SHA-256 `971d8dd7f17d04f114605dcd7933415cdda2c2caae513bf645551f0a46a02d03` (953,187 bytes). Upload and readback hashes match. It covers selected final attempts for all 50 logical tasks, plus result/log readback for both failed retry attempts and their replacements; it does not classify every event from all 52 attempts.

</details>

comments.author: gonzalobenegas
comments.body:
🤖 Snowball v0.1’s official BixBench result is **19/205 = 9.27%**, reported as **9.3%** in the [release results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10283). A saved-trace audit shows that missing submissions account for most failed tasks.

| Final outcome | Tasks |
| --- | ---: |
| Missing `/workspace/answer.txt`; automatic zero | 156 |
| Empty answer sent to judge; rejected | 1 |
| Nonempty answer rejected by judge | 29 |
| Answer accepted by judge | 19 |
| **Total** | **205** |

All 205 tasks received scores, but only **48 contained nonempty submitted answers**. Full scoring coverage should therefore not be interpreted as full submission coverage.

Among the 156 missing-file cases, **141 had a final assistant event with `stopReason=stop`** and **15 had `stopReason=length`**. Here, `stop` is Pi’s normal-end status for the model response, distinct from `length`; it does not establish that the agent completed the task or wrote the required file. Pi 1.3.0 also maps a null provider finish reason to `stop`, so the status alone does not prove an intentional completion decision. Across the run, 22 selected traces contained no tool-execution-start events; inspected examples generated tool-call markup or simulated terminal output as ordinary assistant text (for example, [`bix-28-q6`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-28-q6.jsonl)). All initial prompts specified the required answer path. These observations overlap: the 22 tasks are not an additional failure category.

The [public trace examples](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples) open in Hugging Face’s Agent Trace Viewer. Seven BixBench examples and four BFCL follow-up examples include their original logs and verifier output. Because this Harbor run used Pi with `--no-session`, the viewer copies minimally adapt completed event messages into Pi session entries; message content is unchanged, and compaction events are labeled import annotations.

The traces show several distinct problems:

- **Missing submissions (three examples):** [`bix-10-q1`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-10-q1.jsonl) performed an analysis and stated an odds ratio in chat, but never created the required answer file. The [verifier log](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/verifier/bix-10-q1.txt) records the missing file. Its computed odds ratio, approximately **1.169**, also falls outside the [pinned reference range of 1.50–1.54](https://github.com/penfever/harbor-datasets/blob/454d04b5427fd90de78d7bec9dfe57561a21ff03/datasets/bixbench-cli-marin-corrections-1/bix-10-q1/tests/ground_truth.json). Writing that value would have fixed submission completeness, but not the reference mismatch; the underlying analysis has not been independently recomputed. Two further missing-file examples illustrate different behaviors: [`bix-28-q6`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-28-q6.jsonl) ended with `stop` after generating an entire simulated execution transcript inside one assistant text response, with zero executed tool calls. It supplied its own shell observations and numerical result, then showed code supposedly writing `0.1258380127877238` to `/workspace/answer.txt` and a simulated `cat` confirming it. None of those operations ran: this was simulated execution and submission, not merely omission of the save instruction, and the numerical result has no verified execution behind it; [`bix-13-q2`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-13-q2.jsonl) executed 18 tool calls but ended in repetitive generation with `length`, also without an answer file. Their verifier logs confirm the missing files ([bix-28-q6](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/verifier/bix-28-q6.txt), [bix-13-q2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/verifier/bix-13-q2.txt)).
- **Repetition and length limits:** 11 of the 15 length-stop cases contained over 1,000 occurrences of “Now” in one response (for example, [`bix-13-q2`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-13-q2.jsonl)). Fourteen ended with a response reporting 16,384 output tokens. In the remaining case, [`bix-30-q5`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-30-q5.jsonl), the final response reported 65,535 input tokens and one output token; its trace also records failed compaction and failed context-overflow recovery. These counts describe the final response, not the entire task trajectory.
- **Analysis errors:** [`bix-35-q3`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-35-q3.jsonl) used the BUSCO `Score` column as an evolutionary rate despite the question specifying PhyKIT `evo_rate`. [`bix-27-q2`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-27-q2.jsonl) reported 7,992 accumulated classifications across 50 iterations for a question asking how many samples were consistently classified.
- **Grading concern:** [`bix-8-q5`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-8-q5.jsonl) submitted `8.10e-194` and received zero against a reference of `p < 2.2e-16`. The [verifier log](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/verifier/bix-8-q5.txt) preserves the submitted answer, reference, and rejection. The submitted value satisfies that inequality. This merits adjudication, although the underlying analysis has not been independently recomputed.

Compaction errors appeared in **29 tasks**, including some that eventually submitted answers; these observations overlap with the categories above. Across all 205 final trials, compaction count showed little association with a missing answer file (Pearson r = 0.052; Spearman ρ = −0.005). Missing-file rates were **94/122 (77.0%) without compaction** and **62/83 (74.7%) with at least one compaction event** (two-sided Fisher p = 0.74). Tasks with a compaction error had 24/29 missing files, versus 132/176 without an error (82.8% versus 75.0%; Fisher p = 0.48). Counts include successful and failed compaction-end events; using only successful events also gave little association (Pearson r = 0.035). These are unadjusted observational comparisons: task difficulty and trajectory length may affect both compaction and outcomes, so they neither establish causation nor rule out harm in individual traces.

This audit examined structured events from all 205 selected final trajectories, with detailed inspection of the examples above. The run had 211 physical attempts: six verifier-timeout attempts preceded replacements. The final per-task rewards match the sealed sample archive. An independent review reproduced the outcome and event counts from the saved records and traces, and verified all 205 unique task IDs, logical trial IDs, and rewards against the sealed sample shard. Neither audit independently recomputed the biological analyses. No grades changed and no solver or judge calls were made.

Missing submissions also occurred in the same checkpoint’s **BFCL parity evaluation**: **55/123 final trials (44.7%)** explicitly failed because `/app/result.json` was absent. This BFCL evaluation required a JSON description of the selected benchmark function call(s) in `/app/result.json`, written using Pi’s actual tools. The remaining outcomes were 42 accepted submissions, 25 rejected submissions, and one JSON parsing error; the parsing error is not counted as a confirmed empty answer. These counts come from the [saved BFCL result records](s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261019-104642-open-athena-Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14-bfclparity-pi-e8cb/results/) identified in the [release archive map](https://gist.github.com/penfever/b7deea3a2eaec1642a56c0d67ba1e41a#file-trace_archive_source_prefixes-json). BFCL used **Pi 0.87.0**, versus **Pi 1.3.0** here. A follow-up inspected four missing-file traces: the lexicographically first missing trial in each of the irrelevance, multiple, parallel, and simple-python categories. This selection illustrates mechanisms; it does not estimate their prevalence among the 55 missing submissions.

All four inspected BFCL traces ended with `stop`, had no compaction events, and failed the file-existence check despite an explicit instruction to execute a write to `/app/result.json`:

- [`bfcl-multiple-170`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bfcl-multiple-170.jsonl) selected `soccer_stat.get_player_stats` for Ronaldo’s 2019–2020 season and emitted the proposed JSON in chat, with zero tool executions. The content follows the requested player and season, but was not submitted or regraded.
- [`bfcl-parallel-147`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bfcl-parallel-147.jsonl) described three `light_travel_time` calls and considered both `echo` and heredoc commands for writing the file, but executed neither. It ended with JSON in chat and zero tool executions. Recognizing the write requirement did not translate into executing it.
- [`bfcl-irrelevance-103`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bfcl-irrelevance-103.jsonl) made six real tool calls to inspect the environment, then said it would write the result but only emitted JSON in chat. It also selected `weather_forecast.get` for a current-time question; the described weather function does not meet that request, so the prompt’s no-applicable-function branch calls for `[]`. This is a function-selection mistake in addition to a submission failure.
- [`bfcl-simple-python-161`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bfcl-simple-python-161.jsonl) attempted to invoke `crime_statute_lookup` as a live agent tool and received `Tool crime_statute_lookup not found`. The task required writing a JSON description of the call. After six actual shell calls, it stopped without writing the file; its final text contained a `<tool_response>` imitation of the earlier Python-version output, not another tool execution. The seven execution-start events include the rejected unknown-tool dispatch.

These examples extend the evidence for general instruction-following and tool-use problems beyond biology: leaving answers in chat, describing writes without executing them, and confusing benchmark function descriptions with live agent tools. None of these four reproduces the complete fabricated execution and successful-file-write transcript in `bix-28-q6`. The final tool-response imitation in `bfcl-simple-python-161` is a narrower resemblance. Different Pi versions and the small purposive sample prevent attributing all missing submissions to one mechanism. Original logs and verifier outputs accompany each linked HF trace; no BFCL answers were regraded.

The terminal suites provide additional examples: OpenThoughts-TBLite reported missing `answer.txt` in five trials across two tasks, and Terminal-Bench reported missing `result.txt` in three trials across two tasks. These are confirmed subsets, not overall failure rates; both suites used Terminus-2 and repeated each task three times. Conversely, all 200 DS-1000 trials had nonempty saved code submissions. Missing files, wrong submitted answers, and agent timeouts should therefore remain separate outcomes when comparing these evaluations.

The evaluated configuration used **Smartie Step14, `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3`, Pi 1.3.0, and MiniMax-M3-MXFP8 judging**. A substantial part of the observed failure burden concerns general tool execution and answer submission, limiting what the overall score tells us about biological reasoning. In particular, the simulated execution in [`bix-28-q6`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-28-q6.jsonl) provides evidence of a tool-use failure, not an executed biological analysis whose correctness can be assessed. The BFCL trace inspection demonstrates related submission and tool-use failures beyond biology, while leaving the frequency and shared cause of each mechanism unresolved. Question-specific concerns also remain: the wrong evolutionary-rate column and classification-count interpretation are analysis errors, and the odds-ratio result disagrees with the pinned reference. Writing the missing answer file would not resolve that disagreement; the underlying analysis has not been independently recomputed. The evidence does not isolate checkpoint behavior from serving, tool parsing, or harness behavior; a controlled diagnostic should test those boundaries before interpreting this score as a measure of biological reasoning alone.

comments.author: gonzalobenegas
comments.body:
🤖 GLM-5.3 completes the BiomniBench-DA reporting workflow much more often than Snowball v0.1 under the same task and agent policy. The first-attempt comparison already establishes this difference without crediting infrastructure retries. The shared harness also exhibits verifier failures, so this experiment does not establish that every Snowball failure originates in the checkpoint.

The reference run ended with an infrastructure failure after the judge and then evaluator were preempted. It retained scores for 43/50 tasks: 41 rubric-graded submissions with both reports, one confirmed missing-submission zero, and one setup-failure zero. Seven tasks remain unresolved. The mean over the 43 scored tasks is **74.56/100**; it is not a complete 50-task score. Allowing each unresolved grade to range from 0 to 100 gives an all-50 range of 64.12–78.12. Both Iris jobs are terminal and a full Daytona inventory found zero owned sandboxes remaining.

The baseline is the [Snowball v0.1 run and trace audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6297505720). Both runs use the same 50 public tasks, inputs, Harbor/Pi revisions, context and output budgets, time limits, retry policy, MiniMax judge, and signed rubric scorer. GLM uses its supported serving interface; Snowball used its own serving and tool parser. The GLM service did not report an exact weights revision, and sampling/serving defaults were not independently matched. This is a comparison of the two model-serving systems under a shared evaluation setup.

| First attempt, all 50 tasks | Snowball v0.1 | GLM-5.3 |
|---|---:|---:|
| At least one nonempty report retained | 12 | 35 |
| Both `trace.md` and `answer.txt` retained | 5 | 35 |
| Confirmed missing submission | 36 | 1 |
| Submission unverified after verifier failure | 2 | 14 |
| Native rewards available | 48 | 34 |
| Sum of available scores, in points | 212 | 2,623 |
| All-50 mean allowing each unavailable score to range from 0 to 100 | 4.24–8.24 | 52.46–84.46 |

These ranges bound the effect of unavailable grades; they are not confidence intervals. Even assigning every unavailable GLM grade zero and every unavailable Snowball grade 100 leaves a large gap. GLM retained reports on 23 of the 36 tasks where Snowball's first attempt had a confirmed missing submission.

“Unverified” means the verifier did not retain the reports and did not produce a missing-submission verdict. It does not establish whether files existed in the sandbox. The GLM first attempts include two judge failures with both reports retained, in addition to the 14 cases with unverified submissions.

The traces reveal three distinct problems:

- GLM's confirmed missing submission, `da-3-5`, performed 27 tool calls before an empty assistant response with normal `stop` and one output token. No executed tool arguments mentioned either required report filename. This was not an observed context/output-limit stop. Without raw pre-parser output, its origin cannot be assigned to the checkpoint alone.
- Two first attempts retained both reports but received `{}` from MiniMax. The strict rubric parser rejected the response, producing a verifier runtime error. These are judge failures, not missing submissions.
- All 14 first-attempt verifier timeouts followed the 1,800-second agent limit and the 300-second verifier limit. Seven of their traces were inspected in detail: all seven lacked `agent_end`, and four had pending tool calls. This exposes a timeout/cancellation or verification problem requiring separate diagnosis. The policy retries the whole solver after a verifier timeout, so final scores must be accompanied by the first-attempt results.

A later retry also failed while installing Pi because GitHub DNS resolution failed, before GLM ran. The current error taxonomy assigns that attempt a zero. The canonical record must preserve that classification, but the analysis must identify its infrastructure origin.

The MiniMax judge worker was subsequently preempted. Automatic Harbor recovery preserved all 43 scored results but removed the seven unscored logical trial directories before waiting for the judge to recover. The complete first-attempt audit had already been read back and saved at 20:12 UTC, along with detailed summaries of seven timeout traces. Those saved summaries support the first-attempt table, but the removed native traces can no longer be independently replayed from their original locations. Replacement attempts numbered `000` must not be mistaken for original first attempts. Harbor briefly resumed the seven tasks before the evaluator was itself preempted with `WorkloadEvictedDueToPreempted`. [Incident and evidence-retention limitations](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/805).

The evidence supports a substantial difference in task completion and output delivery between the two model-serving systems. It does not isolate Snowball's checkpoint from its serving integration, establish a general biology knowledge deficit, or certify the harness as error-free.

The terminal audit checked all 43 retained outcomes, their report files, and 42 readable Pi traces; the setup failure has no Pi trajectory. It also verified that the 43 scores and selected attempt paths were unchanged across judge recovery. No manual regrading or score imputation was performed.

The full reference run ID is `20261020-182620-glm-5.3-biomnibench-da-pi-volume-free50-4bc2`. The evaluator was preempted before publishing a canonical record, and EvalDash's API returns `404 unknown run_id`; there is no working full-run EvalDash link. Root Iris job: `/exedev/glm53-biomnibench-reference50-20261020-181225`. The first-attempt audit was preserved outside the mutable trial tree in the run's `provenance/preemption-audit-20261020.tar.gz`, with verified SHA-256 `6ff863d4f8fda3604e6f9a9218302bde1f143385055d3c716c2db8513ea9fc51`.

The terminal audit bundle is `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261020-182620-glm-5.3-biomnibench-da-pi-volume-free50-4bc2/provenance/partial-final-audit-20261020.tar.gz`: 68 files, 1,806,043 bytes, verified readback SHA-256 `e2254e1c888317c1ee80d63d0c89f310579b156bc98c94f6a5fa4d908d630d97`. It contains the per-task audits, saved first-attempt comparison, terminal readback, cleanup proof, and comparison plot. Deleted raw traces are not reconstructed.

Reproduction uses Marin `75a5690b0ff2e1510d73e576649e3e059f06da9a`, Harbor `016dd78b301b621ee4089f2da5776ebe80236820`, Pi `0.87.0`, and dataset revision `e1c8ca5e11a620087bc48d97888eb69176a1f235`. Budgets are 65,536 context tokens, 16,384 output tokens, a 32,768-token compaction reserve, 360/1,800/300-second setup/agent/verifier limits, and concurrency 16. Each sandbox has 8 GiB RAM and 10 GiB disk, with no Daytona volume. The same five input variants from the Snowball run are retained. A separate one-task pilot scored 82/100 and is excluded from the 50-task comparison. This supplementary evaluation is excluded from the release aggregate and uses a signed scorer that differs from the benchmark's released unsigned parser.

issues.title: Track biology evals

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
Add small structural evals for basic agent behavior. The [BixBench trace audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6300963037) found answers left in chat instead of the required file, and simulated tool execution with no actual tool calls. The audit does not isolate model behavior from serving, tool parsing, or harness behavior.

Cover four checks:

- Required-file submission: when instructed to write an answer to a path, verify that a nonempty file exists in the actual task environment. An answer in chat or a claimed write does not pass.
- Actual tool execution: verify a real tool invocation and its execution status for tasks that need one. Tool-call markup, invented tool responses, or a narrated shell session do not pass. Distinguish missing/invalid invocations, executor failures/timeouts, and successful execution.
- Thinking disabled: verify the emitted response respects the supported `thinking=false` setting. Define the prohibited reasoning-channel output or delimiters under the pinned template; this checks observable output, not internal reasoning. Keep extraction/serving errors distinguishable from model violations.
- URL loading: when a task explicitly requires information at a supplied URL and a retrieval tool is available, verify an actual retrieval attempt. Record tool/network failures separately from failure to attempt retrieval.

Done when:

- Each check has minimal tasks and positive/negative grader fixtures, including narrated execution and missing-file cases.
- Results separate protocol compliance, submission completeness, and answer correctness. Passing the structural check alone must not imply a correct answer.
- Traces retain the request settings, raw response, parsed tool calls, execution events, and checked artifacts needed to locate failures.

Scope is evaluation additions; training interventions are separate.

Related: #10060 (output-contract validation), #10061 (tool-protocol syntax and localized supervision).

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The [BixBench audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6300963037) found 156/205 tasks without the required answer file and a trace that narrated shell execution with no tool event; the evidence does not isolate model output from parsing or execution. Harbor keeps a trajectory but maps verifier reward to one `correct` value, leaving no separate protocol, submission, and answer labels. The duplicate preflight found no PR for these four checks; [#10045](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10045) covers BFCL training and syntax diagnostics.

**Relevant code**
- [`trial_driver.py#L316-L352`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py#L316-L352) — validates one Harbor dataset and agent.
- [`runner.py#L126-L145`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L126-L145) — reads trial result and trajectory path.
- [`runner.py#L172-L189`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L172-L189) — equates reward with `correct`.
- [`eval.py#L111-L141`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py#L111-L141) — sample and metric contract.
- [`eval.py#L288-L342`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py#L288-L342) — flattened trajectory fields.

# Design: agent protocol probes

Add a versioned four-task diagnostic through the evaluation launcher. Pin the model revision, chat template, tool schema/parser, agent/runtime revision, request settings, and task content. Use Harbor's existing local dataset path for sandbox checks; use a dedicated single-turn request to the same served endpoint for `thinking=false`, so the grader can inspect the exact request and response independently of an agent's final message.

1. **Required file.** Ask for a short known answer in `/workspace/answer.txt`. The verifier reads that path in the task environment after the agent stops and records existence, byte count, and content hash. Score file presence separately from matching the known answer; chat text or a claimed write cannot satisfy presence.
2. **Tool execution.** Ask the agent to obtain a per-trial nonce with an exposed shell tool. Record the raw generated response before tool parsing, parsed calls, dispatch/start/end events, and exit status. Label missing or invalid invocation, executor error/timeout, and successful execution separately. A narrated shell session, tool-call markup in ordinary text, or invented tool response must fail the execution check.
3. **Thinking disabled.** Send `enable_thinking=false` only for a pinned template that supports it. Define forbidden reasoning fields and template delimiters for that template; inspect the raw HTTP response and parsed message. An unsupported setting, server error, or extraction failure gets its own status, never a model-violation label. This measures emitted output only.
4. **URL loading.** Supply a task-local HTTP URL serving a per-trial nonce and make a retrieval tool available. Score a request observed by that endpoint or an executor-recorded retrieval attempt. Record no attempt, retrieval/network failure, and successful retrieval separately; compare the answer to the nonce independently. The local endpoint avoids public-site availability as a source of false failures.

Store one versioned evidence bundle per trial with request settings, raw response, parsed calls, execution events, URL access log, and checked file metadata. Archive it alongside the existing raw trajectory through `EvaluationStore`; link it from the sample's grading detail. Export `protocol_compliance`, `submission_completeness`, and `answer_correctness` as distinct numeric metrics; keep `not_evaluable` and its reason in grading detail when a prerequisite failed. Keep `EvalSample.correct` for answer correctness when assessed, and report each rate with its denominator; a structural pass alone cannot raise answer accuracy.

## Validation

Write grader fixtures before implementation. Include positive cases for all four checks: file submission, executed tool call, no emitted reasoning, and successful URL retrieval. Negative cases cover missing and empty files; answer only in chat; a fully narrated fake tool transcript; malformed call; dispatch failure and timeout; URL answer without retrieval and retrieval failure; reasoning-field and delimiter leaks; and a serving/extraction error. Assert both the label and the retained evidence for every fixture. Run the checked-in Harbor config through preflight and one capped end-to-end diagnostic suite covering all four checks on the pinned reference setup before using model comparisons. Keep [#10060](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10060) and [#10061](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10061) separate: they cover general output contracts and tool-call syntax/training.

## Open question

Do the pinned Pi/Harbor/vLLM versions expose the pre-parser generated text and executor lifecycle? The current archive records parsed tool calls and observations, but does not establish those boundaries. If either is unavailable, add capture there before grading that failure class, and mark earlier traces `not_evaluable`.

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The [design comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10393#issuecomment-6302257478) covers the cause: Harbor maps verifier reward to a single `correct`, and ATIF trajectories record parsed tool calls and observations but no executor lifecycle or pre-parser text. No open PR covers these checks.

- [`runner.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py) — one reward per trial.
- [`trajectory.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trajectory.py) — the trajectory archive the evidence bundle sits beside.
- [`eval.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py) — `EvalSample`, `Grading.detail`, and `EvaluationStore.add_artifact`.

# Proposed Fix

This PR adds the grader layer in `marin.evaluation.protocol_probes`: a versioned evidence bundle, one typed spec and grader per check, the four minimal tasks, archiving that stores the bundle and links it from the sample, and denominator-aware rates for `protocol_compliance`, `submission_completeness`, and `answer_correctness`. Fixtures cover every positive and negative case listed in the design. When a prerequisite is missing, such as no captured executor lifecycle, the result is `not_evaluable` and never a model violation. A follow-up will connect the tasks to Harbor runs and the served endpoint once the capture question is settled.

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body: 🤖 Opened #10399 with the grader layer: evidence bundle, the four checks with separate protocol, submission, and answer results, the minimal tasks, and fixtures for every case in the design. Running the probes through Harbor waits on capturing executor lifecycle and pre-parser text, which current ATIF trajectories lack.

issues.author: davidlundgren
issues.body: Snowball checkpoints from the Antidoom RLVR1 lineage onward often write several consecutive think blocks in one assistant message. The blocks are near-duplicates with nothing between them, for example: ``` <|start_think|>We need to see the files first. Let's list them and examine content.<|end_think|><|start_think|>We need to inspect the files to understand the corrections. Let's list and view them.<|end_think|><|start_think|>We need to see the content. Let's run ls to see files.<|end_think|><|start_think|>I'll list the files in the workspace.<|end_think|> ``` The `grug` reasoning parser moves only the first block into `reasoning`. It splits at the first `<|start_think|>` and the first `<|end_think|>` ([`basic_parsers.py:157`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/3a054c458ca8a32609ba2bc578c4d9b93eabb395/vllm/reasoning/basic_parsers.py#L157), inherited by [`grug_reasoning_parser.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/3a054c458ca8a32609ba2bc578c4d9b93eabb395/vllm/reasoning/grug_reasoning_parser.py)). Later blocks stay in `content` with raw think tags, so users and LLM judges see them. Tool calls after the blocks still parse. The same conversations also show long thinking-only loops that hit the token limit with an empty reply, for example `\n\nNow.` repeated 7,986 times. Reproduce: 1. Open case `108de5fc` in the [Smartie step 14 vs Qwen 3.6 comparison](https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/25f504c6-c6fb-4e14-8401-07dd8e6fbfba/v/28/?run=smartie-rl-step14-vs-qwen36-20261019-v3-final4#108de5fc029a4b65adb39205bdae818e). 2. Round 0, first assistant message: the reply text contains four stacked think blocks before the `ls` tool call. 3. Rounds 2 and 3: the turns end at `finish_reason=length` with no reply. Expected: at most one think block per assistant message, as rendered by `MARIN_CHAT_TEMPLATE` (`lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/chat_template.py:108`). Rate by checkpoint: 150 random completed ShellSim cases per run from the same comparison applet, counting Snowball assistant messages whose `content` or `reasoning` still contains a think tag after parsing. | Checkpoint | Parser | Cases with leftover tags | Messages with leftover tags | |---|---|---:|---:| | Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21-dr-doom | grug_optional | 0/150 | 0/4,859 | | Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02 | grug_optional | 32/150 | 40/2,148 | | Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02 | grug | 47/150 | 94/2,688 | | Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-NUPA-BFCL-Shared100-2026.10.09 | grug | 146/150 | 294/1,757 | | Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign3-DARE-Linear-02-2026.10.12 | grug | 42/150 | 63/2,699 | | Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14 | grug | 127/150 | 410/2,666 | | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (reference) | qwen3 | 0/150 | 0/2,742 | Observations: - The behavior first appears at Antidoom RLVR1 step 12. Antidoom RLVR1 started from an Antidoom FTPO/DAPO step-45 export, which has no run in the applet and was not measured. The plain 09.21 SFT checkpoint and Smartie's initializer (Merge-Campaign2-DARE-TIES-02) also have no runs. - SFT data: a sample of 7 rendered SFT sources on `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rendered/sft/` (nemotron-terminal, agenttrove, openthoughts-agent-sft-100k, gpt-oss-rollouts, glm-5.2-kernelgym-rollouts, coderforge, massive_function_calling; 178k assistant turns) has no turn with more than one think block. These sources are about 10% of the 09.21 SFT tokens. `nemotron_sft_v3`, `open_swe_traces`, and `penfever-traces` were not checked. - `grug_optional` does not hide the pattern: the same Antidoom checkpoint shows leftover tags under both parsers. - Hypothesis, not tested: FTPO de-looping penalizes exact repeated token spans. A policy can avoid that penalty by closing and reopening thinking with paraphrased text, which matches the near-duplicate blocks. Related: #10305 (Smartie RLVR), #9691 (Dr. Doom de-looping). ￼ ￼￼ ￼ ￼ ￼

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The reported raw generations contain consecutive think blocks; the Smartie step-14 sample has leftover tags in 127/150 cases, versus 0/150 for the Dr. Doom SFT control. The Marin template renders at most one think block per assistant message, while the pinned vLLM parser extracts only the first block, exposing later blocks in `content`. The exact-periodic-suffix loop detector cannot establish whether paraphrased blocks were penalized; the first bad training stage and the proposed FTPO cause remain unverified.

**Relevant code**
- [`chat_template.py#L105-L114`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/036702ca09e1498893582ce1ec6e8e2f04c1bcff/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/chat_template.py#L105-L114) — renders one reasoning span.
- [`basic_parsers.py#L157`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/3a054c458ca8a32609ba2bc578c4d9b93eabb395/vllm/reasoning/basic_parsers.py#L157) — extracts the first span.
- [`trajectory_reward_shaping.py#L262-L294`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/036702ca09e1498893582ce1ec6e8e2f04c1bcff/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/trajectory_runners/trajectory_reward_shaping.py#L262-L294) — detects exact periodic tails.
- [`ftpo.py#L190-L205`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/036702ca09e1498893582ce1ec6e8e2f04c1bcff/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/ftpo.py#L190-L205) — selects that boundary for FTPO.

# Proposed Fix

1. Run the same fixed ShellSim prompts and generation settings on the Dr. Doom SFT control, the Antidoom step-45 parent if retained, RLVR1 step 12, the Campaign-2 initializer, and Smartie step 14. Save raw token output and parsed messages; report repeated-block, leaked-tag, empty `finish_reason=length`, and task-success rates per checkpoint to locate the first regression.
2. In `marin-community/vllm`, make the Grug reasoning parser consume adjacent balanced think blocks into `reasoning` while preserving reply text and tool calls. Cover full and streaming responses, including incomplete blocks, with parser regression tests; release that serving fix separately.
3. Once the onset is known, inspect the unsampled SFT sources and the responsible training stage, then test a structural training signal for one reasoning span and a completed reply. Re-run the matched cohort before selecting a checkpoint: target 0/150 cases with repeated raw blocks or leaked tags, zero empty length-truncated replies, and no regression in task success. A parser fix alone cannot repair the thinking-only loops.

No open Marin PR matched #10400 or this parser symptom during the duplicate-work check.

issues.title: [snowball] Antidoom-lineage checkpoints emit stacked think blocks into replies

spillover_issues.author: davidlundgren
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Three matched mixed-domain RLVR runs from the Grug Datakit SFT (October 5) test whether a share of [PivotRL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21383) pivots improves SWE-bench Verified and OpenThoughts-TBLite without hurting the other domains, and whether pivot selection matters: RLVR alone, RLVR with selected SWE and Terminal pivots at 20% of prompts, and RLVR with random SWE and Terminal turns at the same share. Two optional arms move the selected share to 10% and 30%. Every arm stops at 12 steps. Status: all three arms trained 12 steps at seed 42 and were evaluated at steps 4, 8 and 12; [results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10214#issuecomment-6305992938). B is the only arm above the SFT on SWE-bench Verified (+8.8 points at steps 4 and 8, p=.0001; +4.8 at step 12), C never transfers, and every arm drifts on Math500 and MMLU-Pro by step 12, B least. A seed-43 replicate is training.

## Hypothesis

Pivots that the SFT policy's own pass rates select (#9933), rewarded by #9933's deterministic verifiers, improve SWE-bench Verified and OpenThoughts-TBLite at 20% of prompts while broad holdout accuracy stays within noise. Random SWE and Terminal turns at the same share help less. Training pivots alone has been hard to stabilize; mixing them into broad RLVR keeps the rest of the policy anchored.

## Setup

- **Start:** [open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05), a pure SFT checkpoint. #9933 measured its SWE and Terminal pass rates on this policy, so the selections apply unchanged, and the RLVR data is unseen.
- **RLVR data:** [Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3-2026-09-30) (84,403 train / 94 validation rows; 24% single-step tool use, 14% instruction following, 9% code, 13% math, no SWE or Terminal rows). Any SWE or terminal change between arms is therefore attributable to the added turns.
- **Recipe:** the #9735 reference/KL arm (frozen reference, KL 0.01, sequence-mean loss, entropy 0.001, router replay), 512 prompts × 16 samples per step, at most 12 steps, the same seed in every arm. SFT starts in #9735 collapsed after 12 to 20 steps. Asynchronous rollouts with staleness up to 2, TIS correction, a 102,400-token request window with 49,152 tokens per turn, and thinking on, as #9933 measured the pivots' pass rates.
- **RLVR blend as trained:** 63,590 of RLVR1's rows. MarinSkyRL now runs every Nemotron Ultra row as a task session, and code generation, NeMo tool use, NVARC inductive and Lean sessions execute in a Docker task machine that Iris task pods cannot start, so every arm omits those four agents (about 20% of RLVR1, including #9735's code domain). Rows containing a blank text message, which task conversations reject, are dropped too (3,991 RLVR, 59 Terminal). Validation keeps 67 of RLVR1's 94 rows.
- **Pivot prompts:** the runtime drops earlier assistant turns' reasoning from pivot prompts, which #9933's pass-rate measurement kept.
- **Pivots:** #9933's long-format SWE and Terminal candidates, selected at λ = 0.65 (1 to 10 passes of 16) from the pooled K = 16 pass rates already measured on this policy (`users/dml/pivotrl/{swe,terminal}/pass-rates/grug-67b-a2b-datakit-sft-262k-20261005+seed-1@2026.10.09`). That selects 25,792 of 72,434 scored SWE turns under `nemo` and 6,999 of 36,107 Terminal turns.
- **Reward:** `nemotron_ultra` grades pivot rows through MarinSkyRL#992 with #9933's verifiers: NeMo Gym argument comparison (`nemo`) for SWE and Terminus-2 keystroke similarity without a judge (`string_90`) for Terminal. #10000 uses the same graders. Pivot replies are capped at 4,096 tokens, the cap the pass rates were sampled at.

## Arms

| Arm | Data |
| --- | --- |
| A | RLVR1 |
| B | RLVR1, with selected pivots replacing 20% of prompts |
| C | RLVR1, with random SWE and Terminal candidate turns replacing 20% of prompts |
| B-10, B-30 (optional) | As B, at 10% and 30% |

The batch stays at 512 prompts, so added turns displace RLVR prompts. Each step carries 102 added turns, 51 SWE and 51 Terminal, because the two benchmarks weigh equally in the decision rules; MarinSkyRL's domain-weighted sampling fills every batch to these counts from route-tagged pools and draws each pool uniformly. RLVR rows come first and their pool is shuffled first, so with one seed B's and C's RLVR prompts are a prefix of A's draw order. Twelve steps use 612 of each pool (25,792 SWE and 6,999 Terminal pivots), so no turn repeats.

### Why 20%

Only groups with mixed outcomes produce a gradient, and RLVR1 groups already mostly do: `reward/informative_group_fraction` was 0.79 at the first step from the Datakit SFT (Datakit v4, #9735) and fell to about 0.55 by step 12. Resampling the stored K = 16 pass rates, 88% of selected SWE pivots and 81% of selected Terminal pivots come back mixed, against 58% and 24% of random candidate turns. Pivots' share of the gradient is therefore only 1.1 to 1.5 times their share of prompts, and C carries about half of B's pivot signal at the same share.

Pivot-only RL on this SFT, with the same policy learning rate (4e-6) and gradient clip, bounds the dose. One update of 64 SWE pivot groups raised SWE-bench Verified from 26.0% to 29.4% (146 vs 129 of 496 matched tasks, against a historical base run) with AIME24 unchanged; five updates raised held-out pivot accuracy from 0.29 to 0.38. Forty Terminal updates cost 36 points on AIME24 and 9 to 10 on GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and Math500, and ninety SWE updates collapsed agentic behavior (1 of 248 SWE-bench Verified trials solved, 0 of 190 TBLite) while held-out pivot accuracy kept rising.

Counting a mixed step as its pivot gradient share of a pivot-only update, with RLVR1's informative fraction averaging about 0.68 over the first 12 steps, a first-order approximation that ignores RLVR and KL counteracting drift:

| *p* | Pivot prompts per step | Pivot gradient share | Equivalent pivot-only updates by step 12 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10% | 51 | ~12% | ~1.5 |
| 20% | 102 | ~24% | ~2.9 |
| 30% | 154 | ~35% | ~4.2 |

With at most 12 steps, 10% delivers about one pivot-only update, the dose that gained about 3 points on SWE, below what the benchmarks resolve. 20% places the dose in the middle of the range where pivot-only training helped, about 14 times below where it did damage, with RLVR still about three quarters of the gradient. B-10 and B-30 bracket it.

## Measurements

- At steps 0, 4, 8 and 12: pass rate on #9933's held-out validation turns graded in process, broad holdout pass@1 and normalized verifier score, and per-domain reward.
- Per step and per source (RLVR, SWE, Terminal): informative group count and mean response length, so B and C are compared by delivered pivot signal and any pull toward shorter RLVR answers shows up early. Pivot replies are capped at 4,096 tokens, the cap their pass rates were sampled at, through each pivot row's request; the sequence-mean loss weights them like full RLVR answers.
- At step 0 and each arm's step 4, 8 and 12 checkpoints: full SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks, mini-swe-agent 2.1.0) and OpenThoughts-TBLite (Terminus 2), three runs each, compared per task between arms, plus AIME24, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and Math500, the benchmarks pivot-only training hurt.
- Checkpoints are selected by the broad holdout and pivot validation, never by the benchmarks. A paired comparison on 500 SWE tasks has a standard error of about 2 points; on 100 tasks it is about 4.4, too wide for the effects expected here.

## Decision rules

- B beats A on SWE-bench Verified or OpenThoughts-TBLite by more than two paired standard errors, with the broad holdout and the four reasoning benchmarks within noise: pivots help in mixed RLVR. Next, test RL-then-merge against the Campaign 3 merge recipe (#9975).
- B ≈ C: selection does not matter at this share; random turns are enough. B > C partly reflects C's smaller pivot signal, so the logged informative group counts qualify the comparison.
- B beats A on pivot validation only: the verifier reward does not transfer to the benchmarks. Revisit the reward component (`exact`) or the generation cap.
- An arm collapses: report its best checkpoint before the collapse and compare arms only at matched steps.

## Prerequisites

1. Per-agent `pivot_reward`, declared among the Nemotron Ultra session settings: MarinSkyRL#992.
2. Selection artifacts at λ = 0.65 from #9933's stored K = 16 pass rates: built, 25,792 SWE and 6,999 Terminal pivots.
3. Arm datasets: #10215 builds RLVR1 (`open-athena/Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3-2026-09-30@600262dd`) alone, with the selected pivots, and with every scored candidate turn, each row tagged with its route. Rows move from the retired `skyrl_gym` route to `task_session`, which MarinSkyRL grades Nemotron Ultra rows on since its #879. Validation in every arm is RLVR1's 94 rows plus #9933's 508 held-out SWE and 503 Terminal turns.
4. A two-step smoke run of B on 6 nodes (64 prompts with B's composition, 32K window) confirming that every agent's rows load and grade.

## Links

- PivotRL candidates, pass rates and selection: #9933; SFT baselines on the same pivots: #10000; TaskSpec versions of the candidates: #10181
- Prior broad-domain RLVR: #9359, #9735
- Paper: [PivotRL (arXiv 2603.21383)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21383)

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body:
🤖 Results for the three arms at steps 4, 8 and 12, paired per item against the October 5 Datakit SFT (REF). One run per arm at seed 42. Training runs: [A](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/1u013rdm), [B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/e01zoz2k), [C](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/zblphp52). A12's SWE-bench job is still retrying verifier timeouts, so that one cell is provisional; the rest of the 54 evaluations are final.

Selected pivots are the only treatment that moves SWE-bench Verified, the effect is present at step 4, and random turns at the same share do not transfer. Every arm erodes Math500 and MMLU-Pro by step 12; B erodes least. Step 8 is the checkpoint to report.

## SWE-bench Verified

Strict scoring: a trial with no verifier result counts as unsolved, each cell is one complete 500-task run, and p-values are exact McNemar tests on the discordant pairs.

| Step | REF | A | B | C | B vs A | B vs C | B vs REF |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | .260 | .288 | .348 | .232 | +6.0, p=.004 | +11.6, p<.0001 | +8.8, p=.0001 |
| 8 | .260 | .256 | .348 | .248 | +9.2, p<.0001 | +10.0, p<.0001 | +8.8, p=.0001 |
| 12 | .260 | .272 (provisional) | .308 | .244 | +3.6, p=.07 | +6.4, p=.002 | +4.8, p=.025 |

A and C never differ from REF (every |Δ| ≤ 2.8 points, p ≥ .14). B newly solves 22 to 23% of the tasks REF fails, against 10 to 15% for A and C, and keeps about 70% of REF's solved tasks. B12 vs B8 is −4.0 (p=.054).

## Other benchmarks

Δ vs REF in points. GPQA-Diamond averages 3 trials per question and AIME24 10, tested with a paired sign-flip permutation test; Math500 and MMLU-Pro use exact McNemar; OT-TBLite counts a task solved when at least 2 of 3 trials score 1. Starred cells have p<.05.

| Step | Arm | GPQA-D | MMLU-Pro | Math500 | AIME24 | OT-TBLite |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | A | +3.9 | +0.9 ★ | 0.0 | −3.3 | +2.0 |
| 4 | B | +6.4 ★ | +0.6 | −0.8 | −0.7 | +3.0 |
| 4 | C | +7.6 ★ | 0.0 | −0.8 | −1.7 | 0.0 |
| 8 | A | +6.2 ★ | +0.8 ★ | −0.2 | +1.0 | −5.0 |
| 8 | B | +7.4 ★ | +0.4 | 0.0 | −3.0 | −2.0 |
| 8 | C | +6.1 ★ | +0.4 | −1.0 | 0.0 | −4.0 |
| 12 | A | +5.7 ★ | −1.6 ★ | −7.6 ★ | −4.0 | −4.0 |
| 12 | B | +6.6 ★ | −1.1 ★ | −2.2 (p=.052) | 0.0 | −3.0 |
| 12 | C | +4.5 ★ | −3.4 ★ | −7.8 ★ | −0.3 | −3.0 |

REF accuracies: GPQA-Diamond .635 (n=198), MMLU-Pro .780 (n=12032), Math500 .968 (n=500), AIME24 .830 (n=30), OT-TBLite .16 (n=100). At step 12 B beats A by +5.4 and C by +5.6 on Math500 (both p<.0001) and C by +2.3 on MMLU-Pro (p<.0001). No arm differs from another on GPQA-Diamond or AIME24 at any step, and TBLite with 100 tasks cannot resolve differences under about 9 points.

## Reading

Random turns are the control that makes the SWE-bench result interpretable. C uses the same turn sources, verifiers and share as B, and on the held-out pivot turns it learns the pivot task as fast as B: SWE pivot pass@1 rises from .24 to .42 in both arms and Terminal from .15 to .23, while A stays at .23. Only the selected turns transfer to the benchmark. Random turns also carry less signal, as the plan anticipated: informative-group fraction 0.59 against 0.67 for A and B, and pivot rewards about half of B's.

The GPQA gain of 4 to 8 points in every arm from step 4 comes from the RLVR mix.

The step-12 losses are on hard multi-step items. On Math500, levels 1 to 3 move within 3 points in every arm; level 4 drops 7.8 (A), 2.3 (B) and 8.6 (C) points and level 5 drops 17.2, 4.5 and 15.7. On MMLU-Pro, which is decoded greedily, the losses sit in engineering, chemistry, physics and math; B12 is flat on engineering where A12 is −5.8 and C12 −7.7. The lost Math500 answers run 4.3 times the length of REF's answer to the same question and 34 of A12's 42 end in an extracted wrong answer rather than a truncation. The share of Math500 responses over 100K characters is 0.4% for REF, 4.8% for A4, 8.2% for B12, 11.0% for C12 and 12.4% for A12.

The training curves carry the same signature. Policy entropy rises every step (A 0.83 to 2.76, B to 1.95, C to 2.18) and KL to the frozen reference climbs with no plateau (A .071, B .063, C .086 at step 12), so the 0.01 KL coefficient does not hold the policy. The arm that drifts least degrades least. The in-distribution holdout improves monotonically in every arm (A .21 to .40), so it cannot see the drift; the reference/KL run in #9735 shows the same entropy rise (1.0 to 2.2 by step 10) and had only that holdout. Length stops stay under 9% throughout training and are not the cause.

A's agentic behaviour drifts the same way. Its replies on the pivot validation turns grow 1.5 to 2 times by step 12, A8 overflows the 73K-token context in 17% of SWE-bench tasks (every non-zero agent exit in A8 and A12 is a context-window overflow), and in the A12 eval the median model call took 17 s against 3.6 s for the other runs: 171 of 500 trials hit the 30-minute agent budget, 122 of them then timing out in the verifier. Harbor retries verifier timeouts as infrastructure errors, and the retries have moved A12 from .244 to .272 so far.

## Decision rules

The first rule, B above A on SWE-bench Verified by more than two paired standard errors with the reasoning benchmarks within noise, holds at steps 4 and 8 (SE about 2 points; B−A +6.0 and +9.2). At step 12 no arm has the reasoning benchmarks within noise. The second rule, B ≈ C, fails at every step by 6 to 12 points, and the logged informative-group counts attribute part of that to C's weaker signal. Confidence is limited by one seed per arm; the B effects are 3 to 5 standard errors on SWE-bench, and isolated p<.05 cells such as B8 vs A8 on AIME24 (−4.0, p=.04) are what a hundred comparisons produce.

## What it took

- Layout: 16 H100 nodes per arm, 10 policy nodes with the colocated reference and 12 inference engines at DP4/EP4 on the other 6; 11 to 16 hours per 12-step run.
- Runtime: MarinSkyRL branch `dml/mixed-rlvr-runtime` at bfef1308, seven commits over the fork's main at 563658e5: verifyit pivot graders for the Nemotron pivot rows, per-agent `pivot_reward`, the SWE pivot agent name, null message fields in Parquet prompts, request tools passed as chat tools, and a retry for vLLM engine gangs that die during startup. marin-community/MarinSkyRL#992 carries the first six. The fork was archived on 2026-10-20, so these need porting into `vendor/skyrl` once the verifyit graders from #10215 are published.
- Evaluation: the October 5 verified paired-eval stack (`held/eval-october17-verified` at f9990d36) plus fixes on branch `dml/eval-october17-verified-pivot-mixed-rlvr`: a localhost relay that reports the Iris proxy's 404 during an inference-server reschedule as 503 for ten minutes so Evalchemy retries; Daytona verifier thread limits, because native test libraries sized their pools to the host and exhausted the 300 s verifier timeout; mini-swe-agent pinned to litellm 1.105.1 after an MCP import regression; a 24 h placement budget that treats Kueue's SchedulingGated state as unplaced; the Run:ai streamer load format for staged HF exports; `--cluster-config` so evaluations submit as the openathena.ai login after the contractor service account's default budget demoted jobs to batch band; and an export barrier that waits for the HF export job and verifies its shards before evaluating.
- Scoring: strict first-trial SWE-bench with the fullest run per arm and step; TBLite majority of 3 trials; repeated-trial benchmarks averaged per question.

## Next

- Final A12 SWE-bench number when the retry wave ends.
- A seed-43 replicate of all three arms launched 2026-10-20 21:29 UTC as the openathena.ai login, A on cw-us-east-02a, B and C on cw-rno2a: [A](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/5thdcjv5), [B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/v8o72kqn), [C](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/2rjy7l3n). C has been preempted three times by production-band jobs on rno2a and restarts from scratch each time.
- The recipe needs a drift fix before running past 8 steps: a stronger KL coefficient, a lower learning rate, dropping the entropy bonus, or a length penalty. The optional p arms (B-10, B-30) remain open; the second seed was prioritized.

spillover_issues.title: [post-training] Mix PivotRL pivots into broad RLVR for SWE and terminal gains

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
🤖  Snowball v0.1 (`open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14`, revision 6783e974, the base selected in #10283) takes about twice as many steps per task as Snowball v0 on agentic coding evals. Under the time and context limits of the eval policy (#10197) that turns into a large number of timed-out trials. Per trial that finishes, v0.1 is the stronger model.

cc @penfever

## What was measured and how

Both models were run on the same two agentic evals, with the same harness, task sets and limits:

- **SWE-bench Verified, random-100**: 100 fixed tasks, run with mini-swe-agent 2.1.0 through Harbor at commit 38742b0f. The agent must run the harness's submit command to hand in its patch. Context limit 32,768 tokens.
- **Terminal-Bench Lite, 100 tasks**: 100 fixed tasks, run with the Terminus-2 agent. Each task has an 1,800 second wall-clock limit. Context limit 32,768 tokens.
- Both models served with vLLM on H100s (non-preemptible serve, fixed eval-policy runner at commit 4d45932e39). Snowball v0 is `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign3-DARE-Linear-02-2026.10.12`. The two models share the tokenizer and chat template byte for byte.
- Step counts, submit commands and context-limit endings were counted from the saved trajectories of every trial. A "step" is one model turn (one tool call or one final message).

Results (one trial per task; a few tasks ran twice after infrastructure retries, hence 99 or 110 trials):

| | v0 | v0.1 |
|---|---|---|
| Terminal-Bench Lite: tasks solved | 20 of 99 | 23 of 99 |
| Terminal-Bench Lite: trials that hit the 1,800 s limit | 8 | 49 |
| Terminal-Bench Lite: solve rate on trials that finished in time | 22% | 40% |
| Terminal-Bench Lite: steps per trial, median | 14 | 26 |
| SWE-bench random-100: tasks solved | 33 of 100 | 26 of 100 |
| SWE-bench: trials in which the agent ran the submit command | 70 of 110 | 37 of 100 |
| SWE-bench: trials that ended at the 32,768-token context limit | not counted in that run | 59 of 100 |

A second measurement comes from a data-generation run in which each model writes the opening turns of a task before a larger teacher model continues it, on 2,100 SWE-bench-style tasks and 2,015 terminal tasks, eight samples per task, with a 30,000-token budget per episode:

- The median length of one model turn is the same for both (v0.1 872 tokens, v0 879 tokens, measured over several thousand terminal-task turns).
- The tail differs: v0.1's 99th-percentile turn sits at the 16,384-token per-turn cap, v0's at about 13,000.
- Episodes started by v0.1 run out of the 30,000-token budget before the teacher reaches the submit step more often (72% of the passing SWE episodes, against 64% for v0).

So the extra length is more steps per task and a longer tail per turn, not a longer typical turn.

## Why it matters

- The policy-level selection of v0.1 (#10283, mean paired win rate 0.684) and these agentic evals disagree on which base is better, and the disagreement is explained by the time and context limits rather than by capability.
- Any training that starts from v0.1 inherits the long episodes unless the training data pulls them back. Any v0-vs-v0.1 comparison on agentic evals should report the timeout count next to the score.

## Open questions

1. Is the extra length something the RL run rewarded (v0.1 is 14 updates of RLOO-N RL on the Campaign2 DARE-TIES-02 merge, #10305), or was it already present in that merge before RL? Running the pre-RL merge on the same two evals would separate the two.
2. Does fine-tuning v0.1 on data with short reasoning per turn reduce its step count? A fine-tune of v0.1 on such data is being trained under #10213 and will be measured on the same two evals; the result will be posted here.
3. Should the eval policy report timed-out trials separately from failed ones, so that this kind of base-level difference is visible at selection time?

Run the pre-RL Campaign2 DARE-TIES-02 merge at revision `153f5369` on the *same fixed* SWE-bench random-100 and TBLite-100 tasks, Harbor `38742b0f`, runner `4d45932e39`, 32,768-token context, and 1,800-second TBLite limit. comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Mechanism per harness, from the same reference runs:

- **Terminal-Bench Lite (Terminus-2)** never ends a trial at the context limit: when the transcript fills, the agent summarizes and continues. The limiter is the 1,800 s wall clock. v0.1: 49 of 99 trials timed out (v0: 8); among trials that finished in time it solved 20 of 50 (v0: 20 of 91). The typical step is barely longer (median completion 1,076 vs 952 tokens); the difference is the tail (66 steps of 16k+ completion tokens vs 6, at about 9 s per 1k tokens on the same server) and twice the steps per task (median 26 vs 14). Context pressure appears as 2.3x the summarization output (1.88M vs 0.83M tokens over the run).
- **SWE-bench (mini-swe-agent 2.1.0)** stops a trial at the 32,768-token context limit. v0.1: 59 of 100 trials ended there, 37 issued the submit command (v0: 70 of 110); median 42 steps per trial.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Frequent timeouts make the agentic scores hard to read. A Terminal-Bench Lite score mixes what the model can solve with how fast it is served: a trial that runs out of wall-clock time counts as a failure even if the model was on track.

| Terminal-Bench Lite, 100 tasks | v0 | v0.1 |
|---|---|---|
| Solved / scored | 20 / 99 | 23 / 99 |
| Trials stopped by the 1,800 s limit | 8 | 49 |
| Solved among trials that finished in time | 20 / 91 (22%) | 20 / 50 (40%) |

v0.1 solves almost twice as many of the trials it finishes, but its headline score is only 3 points higher. Proposals for the eval policy (#10197):
1. Report timed-out trials separately from failures (solved / failed / timed out), so a score drop from time can be told apart from a drop in capability.
2. Add a model-side token budget per trial (total generated tokens) next to the wall-clock limit. Wall-clock time depends on the serving stack and hardware, so the same model can score differently on different setups. A token budget gives the same limit everywhere; the wall-clock limit stays as a safety cap.

Per task, 1,800 s vs 5,400 s:

| | Tasks |
|---|---|
| Solved in both | 14 |
| Solved only at 5,400 s | 10 |
| Solved only at 1,800 s | 9 |
| Solved in neither | 66 |
| Unscored in one run | 1 |

- The one-point gain is smaller than the run-to-run churn (10 tasks gained, 9 lost).
- Only 3 of the 10 new solves used more than 1,800 s: server-log-analysis (3,897 s), raft-log-repair-concurrent-access (5,225 s) and rsa-jwt-token-api-redis-blacklist (5,410 s). The other 7 finished in 69–1,211 s, inside the old limit. They did not require the extra wall-time allowance; independent reruns cannot isolate its causal effect.
- Of the 49 trials that timed out at 1,800 s: 7 were solved at 5,400 s, 19 finished but failed, and 23 timed out again.
- Caveat: each 5,400 s trial is a fresh, independent sample, not a continuation of the 1,800 s trial. So this compares two runs, not one run given more time.

Per task, 1,800 s at 32k vs 1,800 s at 64k context: 11 solved in both, 15 only at 64k, 12 only at 32k, 58 in neither, 4 unscored in one run.

- Doubling the input context gives +3 solves, again inside the run-to-run churn (15 gained, 12 lost).
- Of the 49 reference timeouts: 7 solved at 64k, 18 finished but failed, 22 timed out again, 2 unscored.
- Caveat: the 64k trials also ran about 20% faster per completion token (median 11.3 vs 14.3 s of agent wall time per 1k tokens, which includes tool time). Some of the drop in timeouts may come from speed, not context.

Bottom line: neither a 3x timeout nor a 2x context window gives a gain larger than the run-to-run churn. With one run per setting, this does not establish that the settings are equivalent either.
